combined_text: enh ridge: support solver="cholesky" for array api inputs > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines. the svd is much more expensive than the cholesky path used for numpy inputs, so ridge on gpu is often slower than ridge on cpu with numpy, and sometimes much slower. i'd like solver="cholesky" (and so solver="auto") to work with array api inputs, and be fast on gpu. describe your proposed solution split the cholesky solver in two: compute the gram matrix on the device (x.t @ x, or x @ x.t in the dual case when n features > n samples), move it to the host, and solve it with the existing numpy/scipy code. then move the coefficients back to the device: python def solve cholesky array api(x, y, alpha, xp): n samples, n features = x.shape dual = n features > n samples g = x @ x.t if dual else x.t @ x the expensive part, on the device rhs = y if dual else x.t @ y g, rhs = convert to numpy(g, xp), convert to numpy(rhs, xp) same solve as for numpy inputs: scipy.linalg.solve(..., assume a="pos") if dual: coef = solve cholesky kernel(g, rhs, alpha) else: coef = solve cholesky gram(g, rhs, alpha) solve cholesky, minus the gram matrix coef = xp.asarray(coef, device=device(x)) if dual: coef = x.t @ coef return coef let's call this policy a. the system to solve is only (n features, n features) (or (n samples, n samples)), so the host solve and the transfers are cheap compared to the gram matrix. and the solve behaves exactly like for numpy inputs, whatever the namespace: same spd solver, same linalgerror handling for singular systems. solver="auto" could then resolve to "cholesky" for array api inputs, like for numpy inputs, and the warning would go away. i prototyped it by swapping solve svd during ridge.fit (fit intercept=true, alpha=1.0, one target, standard normal data, best of 3 after a warmup, torch 2.13). coefficients match the numpy cholesky solver to 1e-6 in float32 and 1e-14 in float64. fit times in seconds, policy b is the fully on-device alternative described below: nvidia l4, numpy on 8 vcpus (amd epyc 7r13): | shape | 0.66 | 0.27 | intel arc b390 igpu (panther lake), numpy on the 16 cores of the core ultra x7 358h: | shape | dtype | numpy cholesky | torch svd (current) | policy a | policy b | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 500,000 x 100 | float32 | 0.12 | 0.49 | 0.021 | 0.021 | | 50,000 x 1000 | float32 | 0.14 | 1.1 | 0.037 | 0.036 | | 50,000 x 1000 | float64 | 0.35 | 2.0 | 0.27 | 0.27 | | 463,810 x 990 | float32 | 1.1 | not run | 0.30 | 0.30 | | 2,500 x 20,000 | float32 | 0.27 | 10 | 0.11 | 0.075 | | 2,500 x 20,000 | float64 | 0.66 | 17 | 0.79 | 0.71 | | 5,000 x 40,000 | float32 | 2.5 | not run | 0.85 | 0.74 | policy a is 7x to 90x faster than the current svd, and in float32 2.5x to 13x faster than numpy on cpu. in float64, with 1000 features or more, it is only 0.8x to 1.5x the speed of numpy: both gpus have a low float64 throughput ( 450 gflop/s measured on the arc b390), and the gram matrix is a float64 matmul. describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant policy b: solve on the device with xp.linalg.solve, which is in the array api linalg extension. it is faster than policy a only when the system to solve is large, in practice in the dual case: up to 2.7x in float32 on the l4. elsewhere both are within noise, because the gram matrix dominates. but each namespace handles the solve its own way, and checking them all is hard. for instance, on a singular system torch.linalg.solve raises a linalgerror, while cupy.linalg.solve returns nans by default. some namespaces may also not implement the linalg extension. policy a avoids all of this by reusing the code path we already test with numpy. additional context 34793 (centering trick for the cholesky solver) would help here too: it avoids the centered copy of x, which halves the device memory needed by fit. i'd go with policy a. we could switch the solve to the device later for large systems if it turns out to matter.

featureagglomeration.inverse transform fails on list/dataframe input, including its own set output result > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines. describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact featureagglomeration.inverse transform indexes its input directly (x[..., inverse]) without validating it, so anything that isn't a numpy array fails, including the pandas/polars output that set output makes the estimator itself return. steps/code to reproduce python import numpy as np from sklearn.cluster import featureagglomeration x = np.random.randomstate(0).rand(10, 4) fa = featureagglomeration(n clusters=2).fit(x) fa.inverse transform([[1.0, 2.0]]) typeerror: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple fa.set output(transform="pandas") fa.inverse transform(fa.transform(x)) pandas invalidindexerror expected results same result as passing the equivalent ndarray (the docstring says x is array-like of shape (n samples, n clusters) or (n clusters,)). actual results - list: typeerror: list indices must be integers or slices, not tuple - pandas (including the estimator's own set output(transform="pandas") output): invalidindexerror / keyerror - polars: duplicateerror a plain ndarray works. versions shell scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6, polars 1.44.2, numpy 2.5.3 (main has the same code). interest in fixing the bug yes. i have a fix (validate with check array(x, ensure 2d=false) in inverse transform, plus tests for list/pandas/polars/1-d input) and would like to open the pr once this is triaged. found with ai assistance (claude); i verified the repro.

bug: trees fit(..., check input=false) silently ignores missing values > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines silently ignores missing values: with check input=false, fit skips compute missing values in feature mask, so missing values in feature mask stays none and the splitter treats nans as regular values. no error, no warning, just a wrong tree (nan thresholds, spurious depth). and there's no way around it from the public api: the mask can only be passed to the private fit. that's what forests do (they compute the mask once and pass it to each tree via tree. fit(..., check input=false, missing values in feature mask=...)). within scikit-learn, the only caller of the public fit(..., check input=false) is basegradientboosting ( gb.py), which is safe only because it rejects nans upfront. so this mostly affects third-party code using check input=false (which the docstring discourages: "don't use this parameter unless you know what you're doing"). more broadly, a single boolean isn't enough to express "this input was already validated" for trees anymore: callers also need to provide the missing-values mask (and, with categorical support, the encoding info). possible ways forward: 1. compute the mask even when check input=false on the public fit (when none is provided). it's one pass over x, cheap compared to building a tree, and makes the result correct. 2. document that missing values aren't supported with check input=false. cheap, but leaves a silent trap. 3. deprecate check input in the public fit of trees, and switch gradient boosting to fit (like forests). with 1. applied during the deprecation cycle. i'd go with 3. steps/code to reproduce python import numpy as np from sklearn.tree import decisiontreeclassifier x = np.array([[0.0], [1.0], [np.nan], [np.nan], [2.0], [3.0]], dtype=np.float32) y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0]) for check input in (true, false): tree = decisiontreeclassifier(random state=0).fit(x, y, check input=check input) print(f"{check input=}: depth={tree.get depth()}, thresholds={tree.tree .threshold}") doc: rfecv per-split ranking and support shapes omit the feature axis > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines ranking"] and cv results ["split(k) support"] as arrays with shape (n subsets of features,). both arrays actually have shape (n subsets of features, n features), where n features is the number of original input features, x.shape[1]. each row contains a rank or a selection indicator for every original feature. in contrast, split(k) test score has one scalar per evaluated subset and correctly has shape (n subsets of features,). user-facing impact the documented shape can mislead users interpreting per-fold rankings or selection masks, for example when examining feature-selection stability. indexing a ranking/support result by subset returns a vector over original features, not a scalar. code written around the documented one-dimensional structure could therefore use the wrong indexing or aggregation. this is a documentation mismatch. the reproducer does not show incorrect feature selection, scores, or predictions, and no change to the returned arrays is requested. minimal reproducer python import numpy as np from sklearn.feature selection import rfecv from sklearn.linear model import ridge x = np.column stack( (np.arange(10.), np.tile([0., 1.], 5), np.ones(10)) ) selector = rfecv( ridge(), cv=2, scoring="neg mean squared error" ).fit(x, np.arange(10.)) for key in ("split0 ranking", "split0 support", "split0 test score"): print(key, selector.cv results [key].shape) assert selector.cv results ["split0 ranking"].shape == (3, 3) assert selector.cv results ["split0 support"].shape == (3, 3) assert selector.cv results ["split0 test score"].shape == (3,) observed shapes text split0 ranking (3, 3) split0 support (3, 3) split0 test score (3,) the assertions pass. there are three evaluated subset sizes and three original features. verification scope runtime observation: scikit-learn 1.9.0, numpy 2.5.2, and python 3.14.7. the affected /1.9/ documentation page was inspected on september 11, 2026 and was labelled 1.9.1. the documentation version and tested runtime version are distinct: the 1.9.1 runtime was not tested for this report. the 1.9.0 implementation ranking : ndarray of shape (n subsets of features,) + split(k) ranking : ndarray of shape (n subsets of features, n features) - split(k) support : ndarray of shape (n subsets of features,) + split(k) support : ndarray of shape (n subsets of features, n features) please also clarify the axis meanings in the descriptions: - rows correspond to the evaluated subset sizes, ordered consistently with cv results ["n features"]. - columns correspond to the original input features, in their original order. this axis does not shrink as features are eliminated and is not the final selected-feature count, n features . for example, cv results ["split0 support"][i, j] indicates whether original feature j was selected for the subset represented by row i in split 0. the notes paragraph also describes the "size" of every cv results array using the subset-count formula. consider calling this the length of the first axis instead, since the ranking and support arrays are two-dimensional. this request concerns the docstring and generated api reference only; the existing two-dimensional outputs should remain unchanged.

bug: logisticregression (and other glms) can silently return badly wrong coefficients on off-centered data > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines before solving, then reconstructs the intercept afterward. centering is a pure reparametrization here: for any fixed coef, shifting x by a constant only shifts the intercept, and the l1/l2 penalty doesn't touch the intercept, so the optimal coef is mathematically invariant to any additive shift of the features. ridge/lasso exploit this to shield users from poor numerical stability on high mean to variance ratio features. - logisticregression, poissonregressor, gammaregressor, tweedieregressor (the linearmodelloss + newtonsolver/lbfgs/newton-cg/newton-cholesky family) do not do this. the intercept is just another free parameter solved jointly with the coefficients directly on the raw x. there is no preprocess data-equivalent step. the same invariance holds mathematically for this second family too (same argument: additive shift + unpenalized intercept), but because nothing centers the data first, the solvers can lose that invariance numerically. concretely: - newton-cholesky builds its hessian from the raw [x, 1] design. eliminating the intercept column during cholesky factorization implicitly computes x.t @ x - n mean(x) mean(x).t which can yield catastrophic-cancellation-prone quantity. the scipy solver normally fires a warning or an error in this case, so at least, it's visible for users something is wrong. - lbfgs doesn't have a cancellation problem in this sense, but its gradient-norm convergence check can be satisfied prematurely on badly-offset data, silently stopping far from the true optimum, with no warning at all . user-facing impact: any real dataset with a feature that's far from zero-mean relative to its variance (a year, a timestamp, an age, a physical measurement with an offset unit) can silently produce badly wrong coef /intercept for these estimators, without any indication something went wrong. i stumbled on this while investigating numerical-stability discussions in 34793 (ridge's cholesky centering trick). steps/code to reproduce sweep used to generate the plot below: python import warnings import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear model import ( linearregression, logisticregression, ridge, tweedieregressor, poissonregressor, elasticnet, ) def relative error vs mean variance ratio( linear estimator, dtype="float32", random seed=0, max ratio=1e5 ): rng = np.random.randomstate(random seed) n samples, n features = 5000, 5 x = rng.normal(size=(n samples, n features)) true coef = rng.normal(size=n features) proba = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(x @ true coef))) y = (rng.uniform(size=n samples) 0.1 we want coefs that aren't too small ratios = np.logspace(0, np.log10(max ratio), num=30) errors, has warnings = [], [] for offset in ratios: with warnings.catch warnings(record=true) as caught: linear estimator.fit((x + offset).astype(dtype), y) shifted = linear estimator.coef .copy() errors.append(np.linalg.norm(shifted - the shuffled score is computed on the subsampled rows only, and the two are subtracted. the difference therefore mixes in the gap between the full-data score and the subsample score, which has nothing doc/enh: standardscaler silently sets scale to 1.0 for zero-variance features with no warning > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines. while setting up a local editable build to start learning the codebase and look for ways to contribute, i was testing edge cases with standardscaler and noticed it silently returns a scale of 1.0 for zero-variance features (e.g. a single-sample fit) without any warning or documentation of this behavior. i dug into the source ( handle zeros in scale) to confirm it was intentional rather than a bug, and found the public docstring doesn't mention it. i'd like to help fix this if it's something the maintainers agree is worth addressing — happy to work on either a documentation update or a warning, whichever direction you'd prefer. describe the issue linked to the documentation standardscaler.fit() silently returns a scale of 1.0 (instead of erroring or warning) when a feature has zero or near-zero variance — e.g. a single-sample fit, or a constant column. this is implemented via the internal handle zeros in scale helper, but the behavior is not mentioned in the public standardscaler docstring or the user guide. minimal reproduction: ​python from sklearn.preprocessing import standardscaler import numpy as np x = np.array([[1, 2, 3]]) single sample — zero variance scaler = standardscaler() print(scaler.fit transform(x)) output: [[0., 0., 0.]] — no warning, no error raised ​ this could silently mask real data problems — e.g. an accidental single-row fit, or a constant column slipping through a preprocessing pipeline — producing all-zero output with no signal to the user that something unusual happened. suggest a potential alternative/fix adding a note to the standardscaler docstring (and the corresponding section of the user guide at doc/modules/preprocessing.rst) explaining that when a feature has zero or near-zero variance, its scale is set to 1.0 rather than raising an error or leaving a zero — so the transformed output for that feature will be 0. rather than nan or inf. this would at least make the existing behavior discoverable without changing any code.

rfc cpu oversaturation/oversubscription due to third-party libraries when running containers on linux > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, you can set a cpu quota, something like "this process gets 2 cores worth of compute." unfortunately, not all third-party c libraries know this. at minimum openblas does not seem to know about this limit (). so if you have 64 core machine, and run a kubernetes pod with 8 cores, and openblas will think it has 64 cores, and it will be much much slower. similarly libgomp and libomp. mkl builds on openmp so maybe no point in filing there until libgomp/libomp are fixed. this is a performance problem for scikit-lean users. demonstration my cpu has 12 cores. i set up a cgroup with equivalent of 2 cores, but openblas still reports 12 cores: $ systemd-run --user --scope --property cpuquota="200%" -- python -c "import threadpoolctl; import numpy; print(threadpoolctl.threadpoolcontroller().lib controllers[0].get num threads())" 12 potential fixes i am going to be fixing one case as a side-effect of when using joblib.parallel, the number of cores will be constrained using threadpoolctl, including in sequential cases. however, this is a strange fix where if you don't use joblib, you still have the same performance problem. so what else can be done until openblas any other relevant libraries fix this issue? option 1: joblib or scikit-learn set the limit correctly, on import instead of doing this in parallel in the sequential case, do it on import of joblib or maybe sklearn: threadpoolctl.threadpool limits(limits=joblib.effective cpu count(-1)). (technically this won't fix the above example because of but it will work in docker or kubernetes, and everywhere once that issue is fixed). pros: fixes the limit for all use cases. cons: importing a library changing global configuration. this is not very nice. option 2: sklearn sets the limit whenever calling into openmp or openblas pros: if you do with threadpoolctl.threadpool limits(limits=joblib.effective cpu count(-1)) it undoes the limits when done, so it's not a permanent global config change, it's just dtrt. cons: this adds performance overhead of all these calls. lots of code changes. option 3: documentation of the problem and how to solve it pros: no impacts on global behavior. cons: most people won't notice the documentation. if the situation improves or changes, most people won't re-read the updated docs. option 4: warn on import if os.process cpu count() > joblib.effective cpu count(-1) then that means cgroups is restricting cpu count further, so warn the user and tell them what to do. in practice should probably also docs to explain in more detail. pros: more likely to be noticed than docs. cons: users will still have to do work. my suggestion after further thought, i think setting the limit on import (option 1) is actually reasonable. the hope is that this is a stop-gap and can eventually be removed once the relevant libraries dtrt, and in practice for the vast majority of people this is the right thing to do. if that's not acceptable, docs + warning is what i would suggest doing. i can proceed with either, once there is some consensus.

caller's y score array is float32. model scores/predictions are very commonly stored as float32 (e.g. to save memory), so this is not an exotic input. this looks like a regression introduced this week by 34817 (merged 2026-08-31), which switched the unweighted cumulative-sum path to compute exact int64 counts and then cast them to output dtype: python y true int = xp.astype(y true, xp.int64) tps support infinite values in decisiontree/randomforest/extratrees (now that nan is supported) > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, i was wondering to what extent it would be possible to handle those. currently: import numpy as np from sklearn.tree import decisiontreeclassifier x = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [np.inf], [10.0]]) y = [0, 0, 1, 1] decisiontreeclassifier().fit(x, y) valueerror: input x contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float32'). this is because infinite value is explicitly rejected regardless, in basedecisiontree. compute missing values in feature mask (sklearn/tree/ classes.py): a second guard in validate x predict (same file) does the same at predict time. if not np.isfinite(overall sum): raise a valueerror in case of the presence of an infinite element. assert all finite element wise(x, xp=np, allow nan=true, common kwargs) both guards live on basedecisiontree, shared by all four tree classes; randomforest /extratrees call the same method rather than duplicating it. gradientboostingclassifier/regressor don't set allow nan and aren't affected either way. small number of call sites. describe your proposed solution the splitter already tolerates infinite values without modification. unlike nan, +inf/-inf are ordinary totally-ordered floats (-inf < finite < +inf), so <= comparisons already place them correctly, with no new split-evaluation logic needed like nan required. verified by monkeypatching out just the two guards: decisiontreeclassifier fits and predicts correctly on +inf/-inf data, including placing a real split threshold at -inf. checked sklearn/tree/ splitter.pyx too: thresholds are computed as feature values[p prev]/2.0 + feature values[p]/2.0 (sum-of-halves, to avoid overflow on large finite values), with a fallback to feature values[p prev] if the result lands exactly on +infinity/-infinity. with real -inf in the data this fallback is a no-op (-inf sorts first, so the fallback value is -inf too). check estimators nan inf (the common test for this) is already skipped entirely for these estimators (gated by one allow nan tag covering both nan and inf), so relaxing the guard doesn't remove existing coverage, though new tests would need to be added for inf specifically. proposal: relax the two guards (behind allow nan or a new dedicated tag), and add that dedicated inf/nan test coverage.

add population stability index (psi) as a model/data drift metric > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines. using population stability index - sum((new pct - base pct) log(new pct / base pct)) over aligned bins/categories is a standard for doing so. this is one of the most common "has my model gone stale" checks in production ml monitoring, sitting next to sklearn.metrics conceptually (it's a distance/divergence metric between two empirical distributions, similar in spirit to things like scipy.stats.entropy/kl divergence that sklearn already depends on via scipy). describe your proposed solution sklearn.metrics.population stability index(base, new, bins=10) for continuous input (auto-binning via quantiles of base) and direct category alignment for categorical/discrete input, returning the scalar psi (and optionally a per-bin breakdown table). possibly also some rolling psi method for evaluating the psi over different time periods. describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant checked scikit-learn's and statsmodels' issue trackers directly for prior discussion of psi - found none in either (no open request, nothing closed as wontfix). purpose-built alternatives exist as separate packages, but nothing really maintained, while psi is old and widely used operationally. additional context population stability index has been standard practice in credit scoring model monitoring since well before modern ml tooling (commonly attributed to the sas/banking scorecard literature from the 1990s-2000s); today it's also used more broadly for feature/data drift detection outside credit scoring specifically.

add information value (iv) / weight-of-evidence binning as metric and feature-selection > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines and computing information value: sum((pct event - pct nonevent) log(pct event / pct nonevent)) over bins. this is a standard univariate feature-screening step in binary classification, conceptually adjacent to things sklearn already ships in sklearn.feature selection (mutual info classif, f classif, chi2) as a way to rank/filter features before modeling. notably this metric does not depends on imbalance. describe your proposed solution 'sklearn.metric.iv(x,y, bins=10) would be useful for establishing information value. then 'sklearn.feature selection.information value(x, y, bins=10)' returning per-feature iv, using equal-frequency quantile binning by default (fast, matches the common textbook definition). describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant checked scikit-learn's issue tracker for "information value" and "weight of evidence" - found nothing (no open request, no closed-as-declined). the realistic existing option is optbinning, a purpose-built, actively maintained package that solves actual bin optimization (via a cp/mip solver) rather than plain quantile cuts. iv/woe binning is old and widely used, but specifically within credit-scoring-style binary classification rather than general ml - similar concern to the adjacent psi request i'm also filing. raising it mainly to get a maintainer judgment on record, since i couldn't find this discussed anywhere in scikit-learn's history. additional context mutual info classif already covers "how predictive is this feature" in a distribution-agnostic way; iv specifically gives interpretable, additive-across-bins output that credit-risk practitioners rely on for regulatory model documentation, which is the main reason it persists as a distinct metric rather than being subsumed by mutual information in that field.

documentation: incorrect description of statistic computed by maxabsscaler.partial fit > [!warning] > this issue is not yet ready for a pr. if you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines docstring. i’m opening this issue to clarify the documentation and make it consistent with the actual implementation. describe the issue linked to the documentation the x parameter description in maxabsscaler.partial fit() currently states that the data is used to compute the "per-feature minimum and maximum" . however, maxabsscaler computes the maximum absolute value for each feature and stores it in max abs . for example: python x = [[-2, 5], [-3, 1]] for the first feature: text minimum = -3 maximum = -2 maximum absolute value = 3 maxabsscaler uses 3 as the scaling value. it does not use the minimum and maximum as separate statistics. the implementation reflects this: python max abs = xpx.nanmax(xp.abs(x), axis=0, xp=xp) therefore, the current wording may confuse users into thinking that maxabsscaler computes and uses both the minimum and maximum values independently. this also appears inconsistent with the class-level documentation, which describes the scaler in terms of the maximum absolute value . i believe this is a documentation-only issue and does not require any change to the underlying algorithm. suggest a potential alternative/fix i suggest updating the x parameter description in maxabsscaler.partial fit() from: text the data used to compute the per-feature minimum and maximum used for later scaling along the features axis. to: text the data used to compute the per-feature maximum absolute value used for later scaling along the features axis. this would make the partial fit() documentation accurately reflect the statistic computed by the implementation and remain consistent with the class-level documentation.

[bug] compute class weight coerces class labels to int in 1.9, breaking dict lookup for string labels introduce yourself hi, i am a core developer for the aeon toolkit and an academic at the university of southampton. i found this bug when trying to raise our upper bound for scikit for context, we have a range of algorithms that use scikit components, in this case the extratreeclassifier and randomforestclassifier. we also maintain a range of data archives including the ucr archive, hosted here our classification data always loads class values as strings, so for example, "1"/"2" or "run"/"jump". the basic problem is that relevant parts of scikit 1.9 now always parse class value strings to integers, leading to dictionary errors. i had a good look and couldnt see this issue, sorry if its been fixed already. describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact in 1.9, fitting a forest ensemble with class weight="balanced" raises valueerror when the class labels are strings that happen to parse as integers ("1", "2", ...). the same code works in 1.8 and earlier. labels that are genuine integers, or strings that do not parse as integers ("a", "b"), are unaffected. the problem comes from a coercion added to the user-defined-dictionary branch of compute class weight in 32644 (commit 9ca766b, "fea add array api support for logisticregression with lbfgs"): python for i, c in enumerate(classes): try: c = int(c) except valueerror: classes contains strings c = str(c) if c in class weight: the intent looks like normalising array scalars to python scalars so that dict lookup by key works under a non-numpy namespace. but int("1") succeeds, so it never reaches the except clause that would have preserved the string. that branch is reached even though the user asked for "balanced", because baseforest. validate y class weight does not pass "balanced" straight through. it round-trips (sklearn/ensemble/ forest.py:861): python computing class weight (dict or list) for the "balanced" option. class weight k vect = compute class weight("balanced", classes=self.classes [k], ...) class weight k = {key: val for (key, val) in zip(self.classes [k], class weight k vect)} ... expanded class weight = compute sample weight(class weight, y original) it first expands "balanced" into an explicit dict keyed by the original labels — {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, string keys — investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than pypi (extratrees case) while looking at builds comparison results: -o3 in meson doesn't survive an environment cflags that also sets -o2 (which conda-forge's compiler activation does). 2. version of glibc (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a sysroot linux-64=2.17 (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). that old glibc's defines the isnan() macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal isnanf/ isnan functions instead of builtin isnan . gcc can't recognize or inline those, so sklearn/tree/ partitioner.pyx's isnan(value) calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (find min max, partition samples) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. this is fit-specific (confirmed: predict, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned. this is very likely not scikit-learn-specific : any conda-forge package with a hot-loop isnan()/isinf() call is plausibly exposed the same way. => todo: open an issue in conda-forge done: i posted a comment here: proposed fix replace from libc.math cimport isnan / isnan(value) in sklearn/tree/ partitioner.pyx and sklearn/tree/ utils.pxd (and any other tree/hgb hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality nan test value != value. pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever. root cause, in detail (pure llm write-up) sklearn/tree/ partitioner.pyx (densepartitioner.find min max, .partition samples) and sklearn/tree/ utils.pxd call isnan(value) on float32 t data, via from libc.math cimport isnan. this runs once per sample per feature scan during fit; never during predict. the feedstock's ci pin file (.ci support/linux 64 python3.12. cpython.yaml at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets c stdlib: sysroot, c stdlib version: '2.17'. that sysroot's math.h has: c define isnan(x) \ (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? isnanf (x) \ : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? isnan (x) : isnanl (x)) once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier isnan is gone from the translation unit — gcc has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so isnanf (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic) gets a real out-of-line call. modern glibc instead defines isnan(x) as builtin isnan(x) directly, which gcc folds to 2 instructions (ucomiss/setp). pypi/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler and modern headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc symbol versioning at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers. confirmed end to end: - perf-profiled real installed pypi vs conda-forge packages (extratreesregressor.fit, n features=30): conda-forge spends 12.6% of samples in isnanf alone; pypi doesn't show it in the top 15 at all. - disassembled both real .so files directly: conda-forge's find min max has call 0x1791f(%rip) ; pypi's has no call at all. - reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact matching gcc (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own .comment section) reproduced nothing until sysroot linux-64=2.17 was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte. - same isnan() call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on current main (the categorical-feature/breiman-shortcut work added since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — find min max compiles to the identical byte size on both). everything else that was tried and ruled out before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and did not reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge gcc linux-64/gxx linux-64 toolchain: - -o2 vs -o3 in isolation ( 1.7% effect — this is the meson bug above) - -march=nocona -mtune=haswell vs no override - gcc version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact 14.3.0-19 patch build (pinning gcc impl linux-64/gxx impl linux-64/binutils impl linux-64 precisely, since gcc impl linux-64 has its own build-number sequence independent of the gcc linux-64 wrapper) - cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up 3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect) - exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current main - editable install vs literal python -m build -w wheel build (matching build.sh exactly) - -fno-merge-constants (the extra flag conda-forge adds under conda build=1) - joblib version, core-count detection, blas threading config — all identical between real pypi and conda-forge installs interest in fixing the bug yes, i'll open the pr very soon.

add url rule leaves a route registered even after an endpoint conflict description ‘add url rule’ correctly raises an error when an endpoint already exists and you try to register a different view function with the same endpoint. however, after you catch the error and continue running the code, the url you tried to add (/b, for example) still exists. when a user requests /b, it is routed to the view function that was already registered for that endpoint, rather than the new view function whose registration failed. example python from flask import flask app = flask( name ) def first(): return "first" def second(): return "second" app.add url rule("/a", endpoint="same", view func=first) try: app.add url rule("/b", endpoint="same", view func=second) except assertionerror as e: print(e) client = app.test client() print(client.get("/a").status code, client.get("/a").data) print(client.get("/b").status code, client.get("/b").data) expected result text view function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same 200 b'first' 404 ... actual result text view function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same 200 b'first' 200 b'first' i think flask correctly rejects the view-function overwrite, but the failed registration has already added the url rule. environment: - python version: 3.11.2 - flask version: 3.1.3

stream with context: abandoned generator leaves the app context current on the worker thread; later requests skip teardown appcontext stream with context pushes the request's contexts onto whichever thread iterates the response body, and pops them only if the generator completes or is closed on that same thread. when a client disconnects mid-stream, the server abandons the body iterator and gc finalizes it later — often on a different thread. that cross-context pop fails (lookuperror/valueerror from contextvar.reset, swallowed as "exception ignored in ..."), and the app context stays current on the worker thread. because requestcontext.push reuses an ambient app context of the same app, every later request on that pooled thread runs under the stuck context and teardown appcontext never fires for it. anything keyed to the app context then leaks once per thread for the life of the process — with flask-sqlalchemy that is one connection held idle-in-transaction per poisoned thread, with nothing in the logs. related: 5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views; 5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite. neither covers the abandonment case. the docs mention that headers/session need care with stream with context, but not that a disconnect can leave the context stuck on the thread — a warning there would be helpful even if the behavior itself is hard to change. reproduction one long-lived "worker" thread serves two requests; the abandoned body iterator is gc-finalized on the main thread in between (in real deployments the reference is dropped by server machinery outside the worker — servers may never call close() on the iterator after a disconnect): python import gc import queue import threading from flask import flask, response, stream with context from flask.globals import cv app app = flask( name ) teardowns = [] @app.teardown appcontext def note teardown(exc): teardowns.append(threading.current thread().name) @app.route("/stream") def stream(): def gen(): for i in range(100): yield f"chunk{i}\n" return response(stream with context(gen())) @app.route("/plain") def plain(): return "ok" abandoned = queue.queue() holds the dropped iterator, like server machinery step2 = threading.event() def worker(): --- request a: streaming response, client disconnects after one chunk --- with app.test request context("/stream"): rv = app.full dispatch request() body = iter(rv.response) next(body) first chunk: stream with context pushes app+request ctx here abandoned.put((body, rv)) server-side reference outlives the request del body, rv print("a: ambient ctx after abandonment:", cv app.get(none)) step2.wait() main thread gc-finalizes the generator meanwhile --- request b: any later request on this pooled worker thread --- print("b: ambient ctx at request start:", cv app.get(none)) teardowns.clear() with app.test request context("/plain"): reuses the ambient ctx of the app.full dispatch request() same app -> no fresh app ctx print("b: teardown appcontext ran for b:", bool(teardowns)) print("b: ambient ctx after b finished:", cv app.get(none)) t = threading.thread(target=worker, name="wsgi-worker-0") t.start() abandoned.get() take the reference, then drop it on the main thread gc.collect() generator finalized here -> cross-context pop fails step2.set() t.join() output (flask 3.1.3, python 3.13): exception ignored in: .generator at 0x...> traceback (most recent call last): file ".../flask/helpers.py", line 130, in generator with app ctx, req ctx: file ".../flask/ctx.py", line 284, in exit self.pop(exc value) file ".../flask/ctx.py", line 264, in pop ctx = cv app.get() lookuperror: a: ambient ctx after abandonment: b: ambient ctx at request start: b: teardown appcontext ran for b: false b: ambient ctx after b finished: expected behavior request b runs under its own app context and teardown appcontext fires when it finishes. instead it silently runs under request a's leaked context, teardown never runs, and the thread stays poisoned indefinitely. environment: - python version: 3.13 (also reproduced on 3.11) - flask version: 3.1.3. the main branch (3.2-dev, post- 5639 merged context) looks affected as well: stream with context there enters the single context via with ctx: around the priming yield none, so the context is pushed at creation and only exited when the generator completes or is closed.

jsonify emits nan and infinity, which are not valid json jsonify serialises float("nan") and float("inf") as the bare literals nan and infinity. those are not valid json (rfc 8259 allows only decimal numbers), so the response is served as application/json but cannot be parsed by a strict parser, including the browser's json.parse. this inherits from json.dumps, whose allow nan defaults to true. defaultjsonprovider sets default, ensure ascii and sort keys, but never touches allow nan, so the permissive default applies. the path to it is ordinary: any average, ratio or division that can meet an empty input produces nan without anything looking wrong on the server. replication: python from flask import flask, jsonify app = flask( name ) @app.route("/stats") def stats(): values = [] mean = sum(values) / len(values) if values else float("nan") return jsonify({"count": len(values), "mean": mean}) with app.test client() as c: r = c.get("/stats") print(r.headers["content-type"]) application/json print(r.get data(as text=true)) {"count":0,"mean":nan} the response advertises application/json with a 200, but the body is not json: python import json json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":nan}') accepted, python is permissive by default json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":nan}', parse constant=lambda x: ( for in ()).throw(valueerror(x))) valueerror: nan <- what a strict parser, and json.parse in a browser, does so the failure surfaces in the client rather than the server, which makes it awkward to trace back. expected: either the same behaviour with it documented, or serialisation raises so the problem shows up server-side, where valueerror: out of range float values are not json compliant: nan names the cause immediately. there is currently no class attribute for this, although the plumbing already works, since dumps forwards kwargs to json.dumps: python app.json.dumps({"a": float("nan")}, allow nan=false) valueerror: out of range float values are not json compliant: nan defaultjsonprovider exposes sort keys, ensure ascii and compact as class attributes, so an allow nan attribute alongside them would fit the existing pattern and let applications choose, without changing the default for anyone. i could not find nan mentioned in the defaultjsonprovider or flask.json.dumps docstrings, so at minimum a documentation note seems worthwhile. happy to send a pr for whichever you prefer, an allow nan provider attribute or just the docs. environment: - python 3.14 - flask 3.1.3 - werkzeug 3.1.8

register blueprint name override bypasses dot validation the blueprint constructor explicitly prevents dots in names (if "." in name: raise valueerror) because dots denote nested blueprints. however, app.register blueprint(..., name="...") doesn't enforce this check on the overridden name. if a blueprint is registered with a dot via the name kwarg, it bypasses the restriction. this tricks the framework into treating it as a nested blueprint, causing the parent's callbacks (like before request) to unexpectedly execute for the unrelated child blueprint. how to replicate the bug `python import flask app = flask.flask( name ) parent = flask.blueprint("parent", name ) child = flask.blueprint("child", name ) parent.before request(lambda: setattr(flask.g, "hit", true)) child.add url rule("/", "index", lambda: str(hasattr(flask.g, "hit"))) app.register blueprint(parent) app.register blueprint(child, name="parent.fake") bypasses dot validation print(app.test client().get("/").get data(as text=true))

config.from file() silently ignores fewer oserror codes than from pyfile() summary config.from file() and config.from pyfile() behave inconsistently when silent=true and an oserror is raised. from pyfile() silences errors for these errno codes: python if silent and e.errno in (errno.enoent, errno.eisdir, errno.enotdir): return false but from file() only silences: python if silent and e.errno in (errno.enoent, errno.eisdir): return false it is missing errno.enotdir. reproduction enotdir is raised when a path component is a regular file, not a directory. for example, if /tmp/myconfig is a regular file and you try to open /tmp/myconfig/settings.json, the os raises enotdir (not a directory). python import os, tempfile from flask import flask app = flask( name ) create a file where we expect a directory with tempfile.namedtemporaryfile(delete=false, suffix="cfg") as f: f.write(b"") tmp = f.name from pyfile with silent=true returns false (correct) result = app.config.from pyfile(tmp + "/nested.cfg", silent=true) from file with silent=true raises oserror instead of returning false (bug) result = app.config.from file(tmp + "/nested.json", load=json.load, silent=true) expected behavior both methods should return false when silent=true and the path is not reachable due to enotdir, just like they both return false for enoent and eisdir. fix add errno.enotdir to the tuple in from file(): python if silent and e.errno in (errno.enoent, errno.eisdir, errno.enotdir): return false

add a built-in is safe redirect() helper to handle browser url normalization (backslash → forward slash) modern browsers normalize backslashes in navigation urls (e.g., \\evil.com) into forward slashes (//evil.com). this creates a discrepancy between how flask/werkzeug evaluates redirect targets and how user agents ultimately interpret them. a common pattern used by flask developers to prevent protocol-relative redirects is: python if not url.startswith("//"): return redirect(url) however, the following payload bypasses this logic: \\evil.com flask/werkzeug evaluates this as a safe relative path (startswith("//") == false), while browsers normalize it to: and perform an external redirect. this normalization behavior is consistent across chrome, firefox, and safari. as flask does not provide a built-in redirect validation helper, developers routinely implement ad-hoc string checks that do not account for browser normalization rules, resulting in an ecosystem-wide class of open-redirect flaws. feature request introduce an official, browser-aware redirect safety utility in flask or werkzeug, similar to django’s is safe url, to standardize redirect validation across the framework. the helper should: 1. normalize backslashes to forward slashes before validation. 2. reject protocol-relative urls (//example.com). 3. optionally enforce allowed host checks. 4. provide a documented, recommended pattern for safe redirects. rationale - this issue is not a flaw in flask’s redirect implementation but a recurring security footgun for developers due to inconsistent handling between application logic and browser url normalization. - providing an official helper reduces the likelihood of open-redirect vulnerabilities in applications built on flask. - this is framework hardening rather than a security bug report, and it aligns with the expectations set by other frameworks that offer standardized redirect-safety utilities. this feature would give developers a reliable and recommended approach to validating redirect targets securely, reducing reliance on fragile custom logic.

endpoint context cache keyed by id(func) can return stale context after gc bug extract endpoint context() in fastapi/routing.py caches per-endpoint context in endpoint context cache: dict[int, endpointcontext] keyed by id(func), holding only the ctx dict with no reference to func. after the endpoint function is garbage-collected, cpython reuses the address for a new function object, and the cache returns the old endpoint's file/line/function. the cache is also never cleared, so it grows unbounded. repro (fastapi 0.141.1, python 3.14.4, linux) python import gc from fastapi.routing import extract endpoint context def endpoint alpha(): pass ctx a = extract endpoint context(endpoint alpha) id a = id(endpoint alpha) del endpoint alpha gc.collect() for i in range(50000): g = {} exec(f'def endpoint beta {i}():\n pass\n', g) fn = g[f'endpoint beta {i}'] if id(fn) == id a: break del fn, g stale = extract endpoint context(fn) print(stale.get('function'), '| actual:', fn. name ) assert stale.get('function') == fn. name , f"stale: {stale} vs {fn. name }" output on my machine: endpoint alpha | actual: endpoint beta 0 assertionerror: stale: {...'function': 'endpoint alpha'...} vs endpoint beta 0 (the exact endpoint beta n index varies per run; id reuse triggered on the first try here.) expected / actual - expected: context always describes the function passed in. - actual: a recycled id() returns another endpoint's file/line/function, so validation-error messages and logs can point at the wrong endpoint. environment - fastapi 0.141.1 (also present on current master, fastapi/routing.py:275-297) - python 3.14.4, linux possible fix direction validate the hit against func identity instead of trusting the bare id() — e.g. store (func, ctx) and compare with is, key the cache by the function object itself (or a weak reference), or drop the hand-rolled dict for a bounded cache. related pr 16387 fixes the shared-mutation half with .copy() but leaves this key-recycling half in place.

fastapi silently ignores starlette's new max body size option summary starlette 1.6.0 adds a functional max body size option to starlette. init , but fastapi's subclass silently ignores the same keyword. fastapi reimplements both init and build middleware stack. the current code stores unknown constructor keywords in self.extra and does not consume max body size or install starlette's requestbodylimitmiddleware. this became observable after dependency commit fcf472e (starlette 1.3.1 -> 1.6.0). reproduction using the current checkout (50113da) with starlette 1.6.0: python from fastapi import fastapi from starlette.applications import starlette import inspect print('starlette option:', 'max body size' in inspect.signature(starlette).parameters) print('fastapi option:', 'max body size' in inspect.signature(fastapi).parameters) app = fastapi(max body size=1) print(app.extra['max body size']) 1 stack = app.build middleware stack() print(any(type(m). name == 'requestbodylimitmiddleware' for m in [ stack, getattr(stack, 'app', none), getattr(getattr(stack, 'app', none), 'app', none), getattr(getattr(getattr(stack, 'app', none), 'app', none), 'app', none), ])) false observed output: text starlette option: true fastapi option: false 1 false expected behavior either expose and enforce max body size in fastapi. init , or reject/document it as unsupported. it should not be accepted as an unused extra when the parent starlette class provides a feature with the same name. impact applications that pass this option expecting starlette's request-body limit receive no limit and no warning. this is a silent configuration failure; it does not change behavior for applications that never pass the option. suggested fix add a typed max body size: int | none = none parameter and include requestbodylimitmiddleware in fastapi's middleware stack, or explicitly document the supported integration path and add a regression test ensuring the option cannot silently no-op. relevant locations: fastapi/applications.py around the extra constructor argument and build middleware stack.

annotated[asynciterator[t], ...] return annotations fail route registration annotated[asynciterator[t], ...] return annotations fail route registration summary on fastapi revision 50113da16fec53b66b80d75e80a89296de4fa5a5, wrapping an async-stream return annotation in typing.annotated causes route registration to raise fastapierror, while the equivalent unwrapped annotation registers successfully. this is distinct from the apirouter.include router propagation issue in 15401: the failure happens while the route is first constructed, even when it is declared directly on fastapi. reproduction python from collections.abc import asynciterator from typing import annotated from fastapi import fastapi def plain app() -> fastapi: app = fastapi() @app.get("/plain") async def plain() -> asynciterator[int]: yield 1 return app def annotated app() -> fastapi: app = fastapi() @app.get("/annotated") async def annotated() -> annotated[asynciterator[int], "stream-item"]: yield 1 return app plain app() succeeds annotated app() raises fastapierror: invalid args for response field the reproduction was run against the current checkout with the same result for typing.asynciterator and collections.abc.asynciterator. actual behavior get stream item type() checks only whether the outer get origin(annotation) is one of the supported stream origins. for an annotated return annotation, the outer origin is annotated, so the helper returns none. the complete annotated[asynciterator[int], ...] object is then treated as a response model and route construction fails before the application can start. relevant code: - fastapi/dependencies/utils.py:261-268, get stream item type() - fastapi/routing.py:1086-1087, where the helper is called expected behavior annotated[asynciterator[int], metadata] should be accepted wherever the equivalent asynciterator[int] annotation is accepted. the metadata should be preserved or ignored according to fastapi's existing annotated conventions, and the stream item type should resolve to int. impact applications using metadata-bearing return annotations cannot start. this is a compatibility failure for valid pep 593 typing syntax and affects deployment before the first request. it also prevents the framework from generating the intended stream item schema. suggested fix unwrap annotated before stream-origin detection (or recurse through it inside get stream item type()), matching the existing annotation-unwrapping logic used for parameters. add regression coverage for annotated[asynciterator[t], ...] and annotated[asyncgenerator[t, none], ...] return annotations. environment - direct mutation of apirouter.routes bypasses the routes-version cache, causing stale/ghost routes found via a property-based audit (copy/clone independence, cache-invalidation consistency) run across several widely-used python libraries; repro was written and independently re-run twice (identical output both times) before filing. description since the lazy/cached router-inclusion rewrite ( 15745), includedrouter.effective candidates() (fastapi/routing.py) rebuilds and caches a resolved route list, gated by a version counter (apirouter. routes version, bumped by mark routes changed()). every tracked mutator (add route, add api route, add websocket route, add api websocket route, include router) correctly bumps the counter, including recursively through nested includes. however, apirouter.routes is still a plain public list (inherited from starlette.routing.router), and direct mutation of it is a documented pattern elsewhere (e.g. app.router.routes = [...] to remove routes). directly mutating that list -- router.routes.append(...), .remove(...), .clear() -- does not call mark routes changed(), so a parent router that already dispatched at least one request against an included child keeps serving from the stale cached candidate list, silently diverging from the router's actual current .routes contents. this is a different root cause from 15974 (a concurrent-rebuild race, already fixed with effective routes lock) -- that lock does nothing here, since the problem isn't concurrent rebuilding, it's that the version counter is never incremented at all for direct list mutation. minimal repro python from fastapi import apirouter, fastapi from fastapi.routing import apiroute from starlette.testclient import testclient app = fastapi() child = apirouter() @child.get("/child") def read child(): return {"msg": "v1-original"} app.include router(child, prefix="/api") client = testclient(app) trigger dispatch once so the parent's includedrouter builds and caches effective candidates() at the current routes version. client.get("/api/child") direction a: add a route directly to child.routes (bypass add api route). def read child2(): return {"msg": "v2-added-directly"} new route = apiroute("/child2", read child2, methods=["get"]) child.routes.append(new route) no mark routes changed() call happens here r1 = client.get("/api/child2") print(r1.status code) actual: 404 -- expected: 200, it's literally in child.routes direction b: remove the original route directly from child.routes. original = [rt for rt in child.routes if getattr(rt, "path", none) == "/child"][0] child.routes.remove(original) r2 = client.get("/api/child") print(r2.status code) actual: 200 (ghost route) -- expected: 404, it was just removed output (run twice, identical both times): after direct-append get /api/child2 -> 404 after direct-remove get /api/child -> 200 expected behavior the parent router's effective route resolution should reflect the current contents of child.routes at request time. actual behavior direct mutation of .routes after a router has been included and has served at least one request is silently ignored by the lazy cache -- an added route is invisible (404), and a removed route keeps being served as a "ghost" route (200). versions fastapi 0.140.0 (also confirmed present in fastapi/routing.py on master as of 2026-09-04), python 3.12.10, windows 11.

title, asset urls) into swagger ui / redoc html enables xss severity : high (cvss 8.8) cwe : cwe-79 repository : fastapi/fastapi description fastapi builds the /docs (swagger ui) and /redoc html pages by directly interpolating several values — the asgi root path, the application title, and the static asset urls — into html and javascript without any escaping. because these values can originate from the request url or from external configuration, an attacker or an untrusted config source can inject markup that executes as script in the browser of anyone viewing the documentation pages. the most severe path requires no developer misconfiguration. when a sub-application is mounted under a dynamic path segment (e.g. main app.mount('/{tenant}', sub app)), starlette sets scope["root path"] from the matched url segment, and fastapi leaves that attacker-controlled value in place. setup() in applications.py:1124-1125 reads it into openapi url and passes it straight into the docs generators, where docs.py:168 writes it inside a single-quoted javascript string and docs.py:293 writes it inside an html attribute. a crafted request path therefore breaks out of those contexts and runs arbitrary javascript. the same class of defect appears where the title is interpolated into {title} (docs.py:159 and docs.py:268) and where asset urls (swagger js url, swagger css url, swagger favicon url, redoc js url, redoc favicon url) are placed into href/src attributes (docs.py:157-158,164,278,294). any of these carrying html markup or a double quote — from an environment variable, config file, or per-tenant database — injects into the rendered page. impact arbitrary javascript execution in the browser of any user visiting /docs or /redoc, allowing the attacker to steal session cookies, make authenticated api requests as the victim, exfiltrate api responses, and inject content into the documentation ui. in multi-tenant deployments the exposure is broad: the dynamic-mount path needs only a crafted get request from an unauthenticated attacker, and a per-tenant title lets one tenant execute script against every other tenant's documentation page. remediation 1. escape openapi url for javascript string context before docs.py:168 using json.dumps(openapi url) to produce a properly escaped js string literal, and apply the same to oauth2 redirect url at docs.py:175. 2. html-attribute-escape openapi url before docs.py:293 using html.escape(openapi url, quote=true). 3. html-escape the title with html.escape(title) in both get swagger ui html() (docs.py:159) and get redoc html() (docs.py:268) before inserting it into the element. 4. html-attribute-escape each static asset url with html.escape(url, quote=true) — swagger css url, swagger favicon url, swagger js iter route contexts() yields an empty path for apiwebsocketroute, so prefixed websocket routes cannot be enumerated discussed in first check - [x] i added a very descriptive title here. - [x] i used the github search to find a similar issue and didn't find it. - [x] i already searched in google "how to x in fastapi" and didn't find any information. - [x] i already read and followed all the tutorial in the docs and didn't find an answer. - [x] i already checked if it is not related to fastapi but to pydantic — the helper added in 0.137.2 ( 15785) as the supported replacement for walking router.routes — yields path == "" for apiwebsocketroute, while http routes in the same router get their include prefix applied correctly. the mounted path is not recoverable from anything the returned bug: jsonable encoder does not propagate include/exclude to pydantic models nested in dict values description when using jsonable encoder with exclude (or include), the parameters are correctly propagated to pydantic models inside lists , but not to models inside dict values . this causes an inconsistency: filtering works for [usermodel(...)] but not for {"user": usermodel(...)}. reproduction python from pydantic import basemodel from fastapi.encoders import jsonable encoder class usermodel(basemodel): name: str password: str age: int user = usermodel(name="alice", password="secret123", age=30) list: exclude works correctly list result = jsonable encoder([user], exclude={"password"}) result: [{"name": "alice", "age": 30}] dict: exclude does not work on model fields dict result = jsonable encoder({"user": user}, exclude={"password"}) expected: {"user": {"name": "alice", "age": 30}} actual: {"user": {"name": "alice", "password": "secret123", "age": 30}} root cause in fastapi/encoders.py, the dict encoding path (lines 307-315) does not pass include/exclude to the recursive jsonable encoder call for dict values, while the list encoding path (lines 322-332) does. proposed fix add include=include and exclude=exclude to the recursive call for dict values. testing all existing tests continue to pass. i have verified the fix with additional tests.

"image/avif,image/webp,image/apng, / ;q=0.8" } print(client.get("/users/john", headers=browser nav).status code) 200, serves index.html print(client.get("/users/john.doe", headers=browser nav).status code) 404 print(client.get("/v/1.2.3", headers=browser nav).status code) 404 description hi 👋 i have been trying out the new app.frontend() helper to serve a single page app, using fallback="index.html" so that client side routes fall back to the shell and the frontend router can take over. this is the behavior described in the "client side routing" part of the docs, and it works fine for a path like /dashboard or /dashboard/settings. the problem shows up when a client side route has a dot in its last path segment. plenty of real apps have these, for example a profile at /users/john.doe, a version deep link at /v/1.2.3, or a slug like /files/report.2024. when i open one of those directly, or just hit refresh while i am already on that page, i get a 404 instead of the index.html shell, so the app never loads and the client router never gets a chance to handle the route. the part that surprised me is that setting fallback="index.html" explicitly does not change this. as far as i can tell there is currently no way to get these routes to fall back to the shell. i spent some time reading the code and i think it comes from is frontend navigation request() in fastapi/routing.py. it takes the last path segment and if os.path.splitext(...) finds an extension it returns early and treats the request as an asset request, before it ever looks at the accept header. because os.path.splitext("john.doe") returns .doe, any segment with a dot in it is treated as a file and never gets the index.html fallback, even when the browser clearly asked for text/html. what makes me think this is fixable without regressions is that the two situations are easy to tell apart. a real browser navigation sends accept: text/html, while a missing asset requested from a script tag, an image tag, or a fetch call sends / or a specific type like text/css. if i request a genuinely missing asset such as /assets/missing.js with accept: / it still returns 404 as expected, so checking the accept header first would fix the navigation case and keep the asset case working. i did notice there is already a test that pins the current behavior. test index fallback does not handle asset like or non html requests has a ("/users/jane.doe", "text/html") case that expects a 404, so before proposing a change i wanted to ask whether the current behavior is intentional. if the idea is that dotted client routes should be servable, would a change that treats an explicit accept: text/html request as navigation regardless of the path be acceptable? or would you rather keep the extension heuristic as the default for fallback="auto" and add an opt in for apps that use dotted client side routes? i am happy to open a pr with a failing test and the change for whichever direction you prefer. thanks a lot for the work on this feature. operating system windows operating system details also reproduced on current master. the logic involved is pure routing code, so it is not tied to any particular operating system. fastapi version 0.139.0 pydantic version 2.13.4 python version 3.11 additional context no response

race condition in includedrouter cache rebuild can 404 valid routes and permanently corrupt the candidate cache description since the router refactor in 0.137.0 ( 15745), includedrouter.effective candidates() and includedrouter.effective low priority routes() in fastapi/routing.py rebuild their cached lists lazily on first use, with no synchronization. the rebuild publishes an empty list on the shared attribute first, appends routes into it one by one, and only stamps the version at the end: python self. effective candidates = [] ... appends into self. effective candidates in a loop ... self. effective candidates version = routes version if several threads drive the app's first requests at the same time (for example per-thread testclients in a parallel test suite, or any embedding that serves one app object from multiple event loops), more than one thread can pass the version check and rebuild concurrently. every rebuilder appends into whichever list was assigned to the attribute last, so the cache ends up with duplicated candidates, and the corruption is permanent because the version gets stamped anyway. a request that runs while the list is still partially built can also get a 404 for a route that exists. the rebuild path additionally uses warnings.catch warnings() internally (via response field construction), so interleaved rebuilds can leak entries into the global warnings filters. reproduction python import sys import threading from fastapi import apirouter, fastapi from fastapi.routing import includedrouter from fastapi.testclient import testclient n routes = 120 n threads = 6 app = fastapi() router = apirouter() for i in range(n routes): def endpoint(i: int = i): return {"i": i} router.add api route(f"/r{i}", endpoint, methods=["get"]) app.include router(router) sys.setswitchinterval(1e-5) widen the rebuild window barrier = threading.barrier(n threads) def worker(): client = testclient(app) barrier.wait() client.get(f"/r{n routes - 1}") threads = [threading.thread(target=worker) for in range(n threads)] for t in threads: t.start() for t in threads: t.join() included = next(r for r in app.router.routes if isinstance(r, includedrouter)) print(len(included. effective candidates), "cached candidates, expected", n routes) on my machine this reliably prints around 600 cached candidates for the 120 route app. expected behavior the cache rebuild should be thread safe. building the list into a local variable and publishing it atomically (list first, version second) keeps readers from ever seeing a partial list, and serializing the rebuild avoids the duplicated appends and the warnings filter leak. environment - fastapi version: 0.139.0 - python version: 3.14.5 - os: windows 11 related report: discussion 15914 describes the same symptoms.

named type alias body loses openapi ref description fastapi generates different openapi schemas for a bare named pydantic type alias and the same alias wrapped in annotated[..., body()]. this came up while discussing the pydantic side in example: py from typing import annotated, literal from fastapi import body, fastapi from pydantic import basemodel, field app = fastapi() class cat(basemodel): pet type: literal["cat"] meows: int class dog(basemodel): pet type: literal["dog"] barks: float class lizard(basemodel): pet type: literal["reptile", "lizard"] scales: bool type pet = annotated[ cat | dog | lizard, field(discriminator="pet type"), ] @app.post("/bare") def bare(pet: pet): return pet @app.post("/body") def body(pet: annotated[pet, body()]): return pet expected: both routes should generate the same request-body schema shape, with a named pet component: json { "$ref": " /components/schemas/pet" } actual: /body references /components/schemas/pet, but /bare emits the discriminated union schema inline in the request body. why this matters for normal basemodel request bodies, fastapi supports the ergonomic form: py def create item(item: item): ... a named discriminated union is also a valid pydantic body type, but today it needs the more verbose form to get the same named openapi component behavior: py def create pet(pet: annotated[pet, body()]): ... rootmodel is not a good workaround because it adds a .root wrapper, while the desired request body is the flat union object itself. suggested fix fastapi should preserve the named alias when it auto-infers a body parameter. it looks like fastapi currently unwraps typealiastype / pep 695 aliases during parameter analysis. that may be useful for deciding whether the parameter is a body/query parameter, but the original alias should still be used when creating the inferred body field. so this: py def create pet(pet: pet): ... should produce the same openapi request-body schema as: py def create pet(pet: annotated[pet, body()]): ...

[compiler bug]: literal destructuring defaults (= [] / = {}) silently disable memoization when a hook call follows what kind of issue is this? - [x] react compiler core (the js output is incorrect, or your app works incorrectly after optimization) link to repro repro steps a destructuring default with a literal ({items = []} in props, or const {data: {user} = {}} = usequery()) silently stops memoization of downstream computations when both of these are true: 1. a hook call (any hook, usestate is enough) comes after the default. 2. the defaulted value is later used in a way the compiler treats as possibly mutating it, e.g. passed to a function created during render (createformatter(locale)(items)) or wrapped in an object literal passed to a function (format({items, count})). the fresh [] / {} gets a mutable range that extends past the hook call, so the scope is pruned and formatter(items) runs on every render. there's no diagnostic: the function compiles successfully, so nothing reports it and the eslint compiler rules stay silent. jsx // ❌ formatter(items) is not memoized export function defaultliteral({items = [], locale}) { const [count] = usestate(0); const formatter = createformatter(locale); return {formatter(items)}{count} ; } // ✅ memoized: same code, default hoisted to module scope (const empty = []) export function defaulthoisted({items = empty, locale}) { / same body / } // ✅ memoized: same code, no default export function nodefault({items, locale}) { / same body / } compiled output for defaultliteral, where only the jsx gets a cache slot, keyed on a value that changes every render: js const items = t1 === undefined ? [] : t1; const [count] = usestate(0); const formatter = createformatter(locale); const t2 = formatter(items); let t3; if ($[0] !== count || $[1] !== t2) { ... } the playground link has all five variants, including the hook-result case (const {data: {user} = {}} = usequery()). expected: defaultliteral memoizes like defaulthoisted / nodefault. suggestion: props and hook return values are already treated as frozen. a destructuring default of a frozen value (props.items ?? []) could be treated as frozen too, since mutating the fallback but never the real value would violate the same rules. alternatively, the compiler could emit a diagnostic or a logger event when a scope is pruned because it spans a hook call, so this is at least discoverable. this looks like the same underlying mechanism as 35237, but the destructuring-default form is very common in real code and easy to miss. removing a manual usememo in code like this leaves it with no memoization at all. some lint docs, e.g. eslint-react's no-unstable-default-props, also say literal defaults are safe under the compiler. how often does this bug happen? every time what version of react are you using? 19.2.4 what version of react compiler are you using? 1.0.0 (babel-plugin-react-compiler)

import { createroot } from "react-dom/client"; // log the types react passes to each view transition. const start = document.startviewtransition.bind(document); document.startviewtransition = (options) => { console.log("startviewtransition types:", json.stringify(options.types ?? null)); return start(options); }; const later = (ms, value) => new promise((resolve) => settimeout(resolve, ms, value)); const ready = (value) => object.assign(promise.resolve(value), { status: "fulfilled", value }); function text({ data }) { return {use(data)} ; } function app() { const [page, setpage] = usestate({ n: 1, data: ready("page 1") }); const [widget, setwidget] = usestate({ n: 0, data: ready("widget") }); function next() { // something unrelated starts loading behind a suspense boundary; it's ready after 200 ms. setwidget({ n: widget.n + 1, data: later(200, "widget") }); // a typed transition whose data takes 400 ms. starttransition(() => { addtransitiontype("forward"); setpage({ n: page.n + 1, data: later(400, page ${page.n + 1}) }); }); } return ( <> next loading widget }> page {page.n} ); } createroot(document.getelementbyid("root")).render( ); the current behavior on every click (10 of 10 on each version, production builds, chrome): startviewtransition types: ["forward"] . in a production build about 1 navigation in 20 lost its slide, and nearly all did when the response body was handed to the router one flight row per task. there is no unrelated update there. the commit that takes the types is an empty one, for a usedeferredvalue lane spawned during the navigation's own render: 1. next's innerlayoutrouter calls usedeferredvalue(cachenode.rsc, resolvedprefetchrsc). when it mounts, mountdeferredvalueimpl spawns a deferred lane d, even though the initial value equals the value. 2. the navigation lane l was suspended in an earlier attempt. a later render of l is pinged partway through (workinprogressrootpingedlanes) and then suspends again on a flight row that hasn't arrived. 3. markrootsuspended removes the pinged l before calling markspawneddeferredlane(root, d, suspendedlanes). so d is tied to nothing and isn't suspended. 4. getnextlanes prefers d, which isn't suspended, over the pinged but still-suspended l. d renders with no work, commits, and claims the types. l commits about 2 ms later and calls startviewtransition({ types: null }). lane trace from one navigation (ms after the click; lanes as bit strings; recorded through a stub devtools hook) 1.4 pendinglanes += 1000000000 (l) queue ["nav-forward"] 4.5 suspendedlanes += l; 4.8 pendinglanes += bit 19 (d1, tied to l) 318.0 ping l (headers); 318.7 pendinglanes += bit 20 (d2, tied to l) 1249.4 ping l, d2, d1 (body) 1251.9 pendinglanes += bit 21 (d3) from markrootsuspended, with no change to suspendedlanes (l was pinged mid-render) 1252.2 commit lanes {19, 20, 21}; l still pending -> claims ["nav-forward"]; the old page is still on screen 1254.3 commit l -> claims null -> startviewtransition({ types: null }) tracking types per lane, or claiming them only in a commit that includes the lanes they were queued with, would fix both cases.
