errors thrown in async setup are caught silently during ssr vue version 3.5.43 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce open the reproduction link, which performs the following steps: 1. throws an error from a component's async setup. 2. renders the component using rendertostring. what is expected? the error should propagate up to the rendertostring call, causing it to return a rejected promise. in the minimal reproduction, that rejection would be uncaught, so the error would appear in the node.js console. what is actually happening? there's no uncaught error or unhandled promise rejection. the console displays the following warnings: [vue warn]: unhandled error during execution of setup function at [vue warn]: component app is missing template or render function. at also, if there is a render function in the component throwing the error, it renders successfully as if no error occurred. any additional comments? this bug is caused by where onserverprefetch was added. originally, the bug only occurred when the setup synchronously calls onserverprefetch. that line intended to catch errors thrown from onserverprefetch callbacks, but the .catch was mistakenly applied to the entire setup promise. the bug was expanded to occur in all async setups in by no longer gating the .catch behind if (prefetches).

keepalive with max deactivates instead of unmounting the pruned current component when the render returned an already-mounted vnode (instance leaks) vue version 3.5.43 (the same code is on minor / 3.6) link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce 1. click "run". - the parent first re-renders and returns the vnode it rendered last time (already mounted), the way nuxt's does while a parent route is kept alive. - it then switches the child from a to b (a new cache key), so max: 1 prunes a. 2. look at the log. what is expected? a is unmounted: the log shows a unmounted. what is actually happening? the log only shows a deactivated. a is never unmounted: - isunmounted stays false, and its effect scope stays active. - it is moved into keepalive's storage container, but it is no longer in the cache, so nothing will ever unmount or reactivate it. - its watchers, router.aftereach registrations, and query observers keep running. onbeforeunmount / onunmounted / onscopedispose never run. in our nuxt app, every time the user leaves a kept-alive route and comes back to a different child, one more such instance piles up. their watchers then misbehave, e.g. a leaked page's watcher calls router.replace and hijacks later navigations. system info shell any browser / happy-dom. reproduced with vue 3.5.43 (nuxt 4.5.2 in the original app). any additional comments? cause. 1. the render returns an already-mounted vnode (vnode.el is set). keepalive clones it and stores the clone as current. 2. keepalive then returns that clone, which still has el. normalizevnode (cloneifmounted) in rendercomponentroot clones it once more, and it is this second clone that gets mounted (and cached by cachesubtree). 3. when prunecacheentry later prunes the entry of the currently displayed component, issamevnodetype(cached, current) is true. so it only calls resetshapeflag(current), which clears the keep-alive flag on a vnode that is not in the tree. 4. the mounted vnode keeps component should keep alive, so the following patch deactivates it instead of unmounting it. the same happens when the child is wrapped in (which is how renders it). there, clonevnode of the suspense vnode also clones sscontent. possible fix. in the else branch of prunecacheentry, also reset the flag on the cached vnode, which is the one actually mounted: js } else if (current) { resetshapeflag(current) if (cached) resetshapeflag(cached) } we are applying this as a pnpm patch to @vue/runtime-core@3.5.43. the minimal reproduction above, and the same reproduction with around the child, then unmount a as expected. it also fixed the leak in the real app. setting current from the mounted subtree in cachesubtree (onmounted / onupdated) would probably also work. i'm happy to open a pr with a test for either approach.

'undefined' : 'set' }} other is {{ other }} what is expected? after step 2 the page says "x is undefined", as it does on 3.5.43: the error in one subscriber is reported, and the other subscribers of x, here the component's render, still hear the change. what is actually happening? after step 2 the page keeps saying "x is set". it changes to "x is undefined" only at step 3, when other is written, which has nothing to do with x. flush() in packages/reactivity/src/system.ts has no try/finally. when effect.notify() throws, the loop stops with notifyindex and notifybufferlength left as they were, so the rest of notifybuffer is neither notified nor cleared, and the next endbatch() that finds notifybufferlength non-zero delivers it: ts export function flush(): void { while (notifyindex < notifybufferlength) { const effect = notifybuffer[notifyindex]! notifybuffer[notifyindex++] = undefined effect.notify() } notifyindex = 0 notifybufferlength = 0 } system info shell system: os: macos 27.0 cpu: (12) arm64 apple m2 pro shell: 5.9 - /bin/zsh binaries: node: 24.21.0 npm: 11.19.0 pnpm: 12.6.0 browsers: chrome: 154.0.8037.57 safari: 27.0 npmpackages: vue: 3.6.0-rc.9 any additional comments? - the same happens with plain reactivity and no component, whatever throws first: a computed read by a sync watch or by effect(), an effect() whose function throws, or a sync watch whose getter or callback throws (outside an app, where those rethrow). every subscriber of the same ref that sits after it in the batch, such as a later sync watch or a later effect(), runs only at the next unrelated write on 3.6.0-rc.9 and minor. on 3.5.43 they all run at once, and the first error is rethrown afterwards. - inside an app, an error from a watcher's getter or callback goes to app.config.errorhandler and stalls nothing. a computed that throws while a sync watcher checks whether it is dirty does not go there: that check runs in notify(), outside the watcher's call(...), so the error leaves flush() and comes out of the assignment. the escape itself also happens on 3.5.43; the stall does not. - alien-signals had the same bug and fixed it in stackblitz/alien-signals 97 (bfd4be520, "ensure effect queue is properly cleaned up after flush error") by putting its flush() in a try/finally that re-arms the effects it did not reach and resets the counters. 14813 synced system.ts to alien-signals v3.2.0, which includes that fix, but vue's own flush() was left as it was. porting that fix would stop the late delivery at an unrelated write; notifying the rest of the batch and then rethrowing, as 3.5 does, is what would also keep the page above correct. - found through 15673, where a vapor prop getter throws in that dirty check.

iterating a reactive array makes spread, array.from(array) and new float32array(array) 10–80× slower for the whole page vue version 3.5.43 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce open the playground link (or run the snippet) and compare the two columns. the arrays being spread and converted are plain, non-reactive arrays. what is expected? operations on plain arrays run at the same speed after a reactive array has been iterated. what is actually happening? from the playground, vue 3.5.43, chrome 153, macos, tab visible (median of 21 timings, ms): | operation | before | after one for…of over reactive([{}]) | |---|---|---| | [...arr] × 450 (1000 items) | 0.10 | 8.00 | | f(...arr) × 450 | 0.90 | 8.40 | | array.from(arr) × 450 | 0.10 | 6.20 | | new float32array(arr) (450k items, incl. building the array) | 1.50 | 15.40 | not affected in our measurements: for…of, f.apply(null, arr), array.from({ length }, fn), push, map/filter/slice/concat. importing vue alone changes nothing; the first iteration of a deep-reactive array does, and it lasts for the life of the v8 isolate (in chrome, the renderer process, so same-site pages sharing that process are affected too). in a nuxt 4 app it's triggered during startup (by the @nuxt/icon and @nuxtjs/supabase plugins iterating reactive arrays), so every page is affected, in dev and production. for us it makes a three.js layout step about 20% slower than the same code where the fast path is intact. system info shell chrome 153.0 (macos), vue 3.5.43, nuxt 4.5, macos version 26.6.2 (25g83) any additional comments? cause iterator() in packages/reactivity/src/arrayinstrumentations.ts (used by [symbol.iterator], values and entries on reactive arrays) adds an own next property to the native array iterator: js iter. next = iter.next iter.next = () => { … } v8 treats an own next on an array iterator as a change to array iteration and permanently invalidates its "array iterator" protector. after that, spread, array.from of iterables and typed-array construction from arrays take the generic, much slower path. possible fix return a wrapper iterator instead of mutating the native one. inheriting from %iteratorprototype% keeps [symbol.iterator] and the iterator helpers: js function iterator(self, method, wrapvalue) { const arr = shallowreadarray(self) const iter = arr[method]() if (arr !== self && !isshallow(self)) { const wrapped = object.create(object.getprototypeof(object.getprototypeof(iter))) wrapped.next = () => { const result = iter.next() if (!result.done) { result.value = wrapvalue(result.value) } return result } return wrapped } return iter } served in place of the original in our app, this kept spread at 0.2 ms and typed-array construction at its normal speed, and the app behaved the same (its computed readouts were identical). we haven't run vue's own test suite against it.

component update is skipped when object v-bind changes keys and the new prop value is undefined vue version 3.5.38 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce 1. open the reproduction. 2. notice that both child components initially display "add at least one item". 3. click "add item". 4. the click handler adds an item and schedules the counter update using nexttick(). 5. wait for the updates to complete. 6. observe that items contains one item, haserrors is false, and counter is 1. 7. compare the results of the "dynamic object shape" and "stable object shape" components. what is expected? both child components should clear the previous errormessage prop and display: text count: 1 when the object passed through v-bind changes from: js { errormessage: 'add at least one item', } to: js { counter: undefined, } the removal of errormessage should be detected even though the new prop value is undefined. the watcher for props.errormessage should be triggered with the previous error message and undefined as the new value. what is actually happening? the component using the stable-shaped binding works correctly: it clears errormessage and displays: text count: 1 the component using the dynamically shaped binding receives the updated counter but retains the stale errormessage. its effective props become: js { errormessage: 'add at least one item', counter: 1, } as a result, it continues to display: text add at least one item the computed binding in the parent is recalculated correctly, but the watcher for props.errormessage in the child is not triggered because the stale prop is never cleared. system info shell reproduces in the vue sfc playground using chrome. any additional comments? the reproduction uses nexttick() to intentionally split the state change into two render cycles: js const additem = () => { items.value.push('item'); nexttick(() => counter.value = items.value.length); }; this produces the following props transitions: js // initial render { errormessage: 'add at least one item', } // first render after adding an item { counter: undefined, } // second render after nexttick() { counter: 1, } during the first update, the previous and next props objects contain the same number of keys: js const prevprops = { errormessage: 'add at least one item', }; const nextprops = { counter: undefined, }; object.keys(prevprops).length === object.keys(nextprops).length; // true when vue checks the counter key from nextprops, the comparison is effectively: js nextprops.counter === prevprops.counter; // undefined === undefined // true counter is not present in prevprops, but reading a missing property also returns undefined. because the comparison checks the values without checking property presence, vue considers the props unchanged and skips the child component update. the child component therefore retains: js { errormessage: 'add at least one item', } however, after the skipped update, the component vnode has already advanced to: js { counter: undefined, } when counter is changed to 1 after nexttick(), vue detects that update and patches the child. at this point, the previous vnode no longer contains errormessage, so the stale errormessage stored in the component instance is not cleared. the child consequently ends up with both the stale error and the new counter: js { errormessage: 'add at least one item', counter: 1, } the stable-shaped version avoids the issue because vue can directly detect the errormessage value change: js const stablebind = computed(() => ({ errormessage: haserrors.value ? 'add at least one item' : undefined, counter: counter.value, })); a possible fix may be to account for property presence when comparing props, in addition to comparing their values: js !hasown(prevprops, key) || haspropvaluechanged(nextprops, prevprops, key) object-style v-bind is documented as equivalent to passing the object properties individually. the documentation does not state that the bound object must retain the same set of keys:

vapor: a branch with a key is never restored from the cache vue version 3.6.0-rc.9 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce 1. press +1 once, so the a branch shows count: 1. 2. press toggle branch to switch to b. 3. press toggle branch again to come back to a. what is expected? a comes back with count: 1, the way behaves outside vapor mode — the branch is restored from the cache and its setup runs only once. what is actually happening? a comes back with count: 0. it is a new instance, and the previous one is never unmounted: every round trip leaves another detached subtree behind in the keepalive storage container, with its effects still running, so the lost state comes with a leak. removing the key attributes from both branches makes it work correctly, so it only affects keyed branches. any additional comments? from a quick look, the entry seems to be written under the user key but looked up under the branch index — component.ts calls getcachedcomponent(component) without a key, and setblockkey only runs after the component has been created, so the lookup falls back to currentcachekey. the interop path passes vnode.key through, which may be why it doesn't show up there. happy to open a pr if that's useful, though i noticed the keepalive keys were reworked recently in 15516 — let me know if this overlaps with something already in flight.

[compiler-sfc] top-level await inside switch case generates invalid code (missing semicolon before rewrite) [compiler-sfc] top-level await inside switch case generates invalid code (missing semicolon before rewrite) vue version 3.5.42 — also reproduced on main (5409708) link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce 1. open the playground link above (or compile the sfc below with @vue/compiler-sfc). 2. the component setup() throws typeerror: object is not iterable (cannot read property symbol(symbol.iterator)). sfc: vue const a = true const b = 1 function qux() {} async function bar() { return 42 } if (a) { switch (b) { case 1: qux() await bar() } } what is expected? the compiled setup() should run fine: qux() and await bar() should be two independent statements. what is actually happening? the top-level await rewrite in compilescript emits the withasynccontext wrapper expression without a leading semicolon when the await is inside a switch case that is not the first statement: js async setup( props, { expose: expose }) { ... if (a) { switch (b) { case 1: qux() ( ([ temp, restore] = withasynccontext(() => bar())), await temp, restore() ) } } } because the next line starts with (, asi does not insert a semicolon, so the two lines are parsed as a single call expression qux()(...). bar() is never awaited in the intended way and the runtime throws typeerror: object is not iterable. the same code inside a plain block (not a switch) is compiled correctly with a leading ;: js if (a) { qux() ;( ([ temp, restore] = withasynccontext(() => bar())), await temp, restore() ) } additional comments root cause: in packages/compiler-sfc/src/compilescript.ts, the scope stack used to decide whether the rewrite needs a semicolon only pushes/pops on blockstatement. a switch statement's switchcase.consequent statement list is not tracked, so needssemi is misjudged as false for await expressions inside case branches (unless the await happens to be the very first statement of the case). related variants also affected: - two consecutive top-level awaits inside one case produce (...)(...) back-to-back (second one also parsed as a call of the first result). - any await that follows an expression statement inside a case branch. no prior issue found for this.

vapor: setdomprop skips the reflected attribute on a nullish→default transition version 3.6.0-rc.5 (minor branch, f11c8f2) reproduction link no playground link: the bug is in the vapor runtime internals. save this as packages/runtime-vapor/ tests /repro.spec.ts and run vp test --project unit-jsdom: ts import { nexttick, ref } from '@vue/runtime-dom' import { setprop } from '../src/dom/prop' import { rendereffect } from '../src/rendereffect' import { makerender } from './ utils' const define = makerender() test('nullish -> default', async () => { const t = ref (null) const { host } = define({ setup() { const el = document.createelement('input') rendereffect(() => setprop(el, 'type', t.value)) return el }, }).render() const input = host.queryselector('input')! t.value = 'text' await nexttick() expect(input.getattribute('type')).tobe('text') // received: null }) steps to reproduce 1. bind a reflected property that has a default value, for example . 2. set t to null. setdomprop coerces the value to '', writes it, then removes the type attribute. 3. set t back to 'text'. what is expected? the element carries type="text". vdom does write the attribute in that same sequence (patchprop(input, 'type', null, 'text')). what is actually happening? the attribute stays absent. el.type still reads 'text', because that is the element default, so nothing reaches the markup. --- cause setdomprop in packages/runtime-vapor/src/dom/prop.ts skips the write when the incoming value equals the current dom property and the $p$ cache flag exists: ts const prev = el[key] if (value === prev && cachekey in el) { return } the nullish call removes the attribute but leaves the flag set, and the property keeps reporting the default. the next call sees both conditions and returns, so the removal is never undone. method on behaves the same way. width and height are affected through the setprop api directly, but not from a template, since :width compiles to setattr. this is not a regression from 15341. the same spec fails on clean minor at f11c8f2, before that fix. 15341 closed the initial-set half of 15339, and this is the half that is left. (found in review on 15341.) open question the direct fix is to compare the last bound value instead of only checking that the flag exists: ts if (value === prev && cachekey in el && el[cachekey] === value) { return } that closes both cases. it also breaks one existing assertion in prop.spec.ts > "should remove attribute when value is falsy": after a nullish removal, setprop(el, 'id', '') then writes id="" instead of leaving the attribute off. vdom writes id="" in that same sequence, which i verified with patchprop, so the current vapor assertion already differs from vdom. which behaviour should vapor keep? 1. match vdom: apply the fix above and update that assertion. vapor and vdom then agree on all of these sequences. 2. keep the assertion: force the write only when the new value is not '' and not nullish, so the falsy case stays as it is today. i can send a pr for either one. please tell me which you prefer.

[vapor] a bound prop whose value equals the element's default property value writes no attribute (e.g. :type="text" on ) vue version 3.6.0-rc.5 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce inspect the rendered vapor and vdom subtrees. what is expected? both runtimes write the type attribute in all four cases, as vdom does. what is actually happening? vapor omits the attribute in exactly the two cases where the bound value equals the element's default property value: | bound value | equals el.type default? | vapor | vdom | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | yes | absent | text | | | no | checkbox | checkbox | | | yes | absent | submit | | | no | button | button | system info shell any additional comments? the same template is compiled twice in one app — once with vapor, once without — so the two runtimes can be compared side by side: vue x y with a = "text", b = "checkbox", c = "submit", d = "button". setprop sends type to setdomprop because 'type' in el, and setdomprop returns early on ts const prev = el[key] if (value === prev) { return } a fresh already reports el.type === "text" and a fresh reports "submit", so the assignment is skipped. type is a reflected idl attribute — the content attribute only comes into existence via that assignment — so nothing is written. the checkbox / button rows confirm this: as soon as the bound value differs from the default, the attribute appears. the property reads back correctly either way, so this stays invisible until something depends on the attribute: an input[type="text"] selector in css or queryselector does not match, and serialized markup differs between the runtimes. same file and same class of divergence as 15186.

[vapor] a bound :value writes no value content attribute, so form.reset() restores the wrong value vue version 3.6.0-rc.5 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce in each of the two forms: move the slider away from its initial position, then press its reset button. what is expected? reset returns the slider to 30, as it does in the vdom form. what is actually happening? the vapor slider lands on 50 — the midpoint of min/max, which is what a browser falls back to when a range input has no value content attribute to restore from. | | value attribute | .value property | after form.reset() | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | vdom | 30 | 30 | 30 | | vapor | absent | 30 | 50 | system info shell any additional comments? the same template compiled twice in one app — once with vapor, once without: vue reset with const rangevalue = 30. setvalue writes the property only: ts el. value = value // ... if (oldvalue !== newvalue) { el.value = newvalue } if (value == null) { el.removeattribute('value') } unlike type, value on an is not a reflected attribute — the content attribute is the element's default value — so a property write never produces one, and form reset restores from exactly that missing attribute. the initial render therefore looks correct and only reset misbehaves, which makes it easy to miss. any form containing a vapor-rendered control with a bound :value loses its initial value on reset instead of returning to it. related to 15186 (same file), and shares the "bound prop produces no attribute" shape with the :type issue i am filing alongside this one — though the mechanism differs, so they may need separate fixes.

suspense timeout + transition out-in: parent update during the fallback swap permanently drops the resolved branch version 3.5.41 reproduction link play.vuejs.org/. the repro is fully event-ordered (js transition hooks hold the leave open), so it fails on the first run, every run: 1. a keyed component inside inside navigates to a cold async component (defineasynccomponent, chunk not loaded yet). 2. timeout elapses → suspense starts the fallback swap; the old content's leave transition begins. 3. while the leave is in progress, the parent re-renders (in a real app: a resizeobserver callback, a store update — anything). 4. the async component resolves; the leave finishes. what is expected? the resolved page is mounted (with the fallback shown in between). what is actually happening? @resolve fires and the module is loaded, but the page is never inserted — the fallback stays on screen forever. no error, no warning. a later unrelated parent re-render "un-sticks" it, which is why this is so hard to catch in the wild. removing any one of the three ingredients — the timeout, mode="out-in", or the mid-swap parent re-render — makes it pass (all three controls verified). the bug is deterministic: 3.5.30 passes, 3.5.31+ fails (bisected). --- root cause (bisected + traced) regression introduced by 908c6ad05 ( 9392, first released in 3.5.31), which added isfallbackmountpending: - fallback() sets isfallbackmountpending = true and defers mountfallback to the leaving branch's afterleave. - a parent re-render hits patchsuspense's isinfallback path, which patches activebranch → newfallback and calls setactivebranch(suspense, newfallback) — mounting the fallback early without clearing isfallbackmountpending. - resolve() then skips unmount(activebranch) because the flag is still true, yet hooks the content move onto activebranch.transition.afterleave — where activebranch is now the fallback, which is never unmounted. the afterleave never fires; the resolved branch is lost. before 9392, resolve() unconditionally unmounted the active branch, so the fallback left and its afterleave inserted the content. a guard in patchsuspense fixes it — while isfallbackmountpending is true, activebranch is still the leaving content, so the patch(activebranch, newfallback) + setactivebranch(suspense, newfallback) calls in the isinfallback paths must be skipped. happy to submit a pr with the fix and an e2e regression test (prepared and passing locally, including the 9392 test for 7966). real-world impact: in our production spa (layout = routerview → transition out-in → suspense timeout, per the documented pattern) roughly 1 in 10 cold first navigations ended on an infinite spinner — console clean, all network requests succeed.

map/set values with different contents compare as not equal, so v-model selects the option that actually matches. what is actually happening? map and set fall through to the generic object branch. object.keys() on either is always [], so the key-count check passes and the for...in loop body never executes — entries are never compared. execution then reaches the final line: ts return string(a) === string(b) every map stringifies to '[object map]' and every set to '[object set]', so any two of the same type are reported equal. note this differs from date and symbol, which are given explicit branches above, and from arrays and plain objects, which compare correctly: ts looseequal([1], [2]) // false, correct looseequal({ a: 1 }, { a: 2 }) // false, correct packages/shared/ tests /looseequal.spec.ts has 13 cases but none for map/set, which is why this hasn't been caught. possible fix add explicit branches before the generic object check, mirroring the existing date/symbol pattern. ismap and isset already exist in packages/shared/src/general.ts. set needs content comparison rather than reference lookup to stay consistent with looseequal's semantics (e.g. new set([{ a: 1 }]) vs new set([{ a: 1 }])). worth confirming the intended semantics first: should map comparison be key-order-insensitive, and should set compare loosely (looseequal per element) or strictly? keepalive caches a never-mounted vnode when a switch lands while an ancestor suspense is pending vue version 3.5.41 (also reproduces on 3.5.40 and 3.6.0-rc.3) link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce the reproduction drives itself from onmounted — just open it and read the log. the tree is the one nuxt renders for a page with : 1. while rootdep is still pending (so parentsuspense.deps > 0), switch the inner page from pagea to pageb. 2. let the root boundary resolve. 3. switch back to pagea, then to pageb again. what is expected? the inner page follows the switches, and no errors are raised. what is actually happening? the rendered page is stuck on pagea forever — every later switch is a no-op — and the renderer throws: cannot read properties of null (reading 'suspenseid') // patchsuspense cannot read properties of null (reading 'm') // unmountcomponent in a production build the second one is the more familiar uncaught (in promise) typeerror: cannot destructure property 'bum' of 'instance' as it is null. removing the and changing nothing else makes both errors go away and navigation work. system info shell system: os: linux 7.0 ubuntu 26.04 lts cpu: (4) x64 intel(r) core(tm) i7-8700 cpu @ 3.20ghz memory: 5.86 gb / 11.67 gb binaries: node: 24.19.0 npm: 11.19.0 npmpackages: vue: 3.5.41 browsers: chromium (playwright 1.5x, headless) any additional comments? the chain , as far as i could trace it: 1. the route change re-renders keepalive, so the inner is patched with n1 != null. because an ancestor boundary is still pending, suspenseimpl.process takes its early return: js if (parentsuspense && parentsuspense.deps > 0 && !n1.suspense.isinfallback) { n2.suspense = n1.suspense n2.suspense.vnode = n2 n2.el = n1.el return } the incoming page vnode is therefore never patched: vnode.component === null, vnode.el === null. 2. keepalive's onupdated → cachesubtree still caches it, unconditionally: js if (issuspense(instance.subtree.type)) { queuepostrendereffect(() => { cache.set(pendingcachekey, getinnerchild(instance.subtree)) }, instance.subtree.suspense) } 3. the next render for that key hits the poisoned entry: keepalive copies cachedvnode.component (null) onto the new vnode and sets component kept alive, so patchsuspense reads newbranch.component.suspenseid on null, and the teardown that follows calls unmountcomponent(null). suggested fix — the same shape as the two guards already at that site, i.e. do not cache a vnode that never finished mounting: js const innerchild = getinnerchild(instance.subtree) if (innerchild.component) { cache.set(pendingcachekey, innerchild) } with that guard the page is simply not cached that one time, and the reproduction runs clean. this looks like a third path into the defect class fixed by 10912 (avoid caching vnode that not been mounted, for 10899) and 11479 (for 6028) — both guard keepalive's own subtree, while here it is an ancestor suspense that is pending. real-world context: this is how it surfaced for us — a nuxt 4 app rendering , where a link clicked before hydration finished intermittently left the user on a blank page with cannot destructure property 'bum' of 'e' as it is null in the console. the window widens with slower hydration, so it shows up under load / on slow clients. investigation and reproduction prepared with claude code, on behalf of drunomics.

vapor: components removed from v-for remain retained by the parent scope vue version 3.6.0-rc.3 link to minimal reproduction steps to reproduce 1. open the reproduction in chrome. 2. open devtools and select memory . 3. select heap snapshot and take a snapshot. 4. click run 100 x 1,000 mount/unmount cycles . 5. wait until completed cycles is 100 and attached children is 0. 6. click collect garbage three times. 7. take another heap snapshot. 8. select objects retained by detached dom nodes , or filter for detached. the second snapshot contains detached buttons from the removed child components. what is expected? 'dropped' }} middle does not declare class, so the class falls through onto its root - which is the child component. child declares class as a prop. what is expected child's classname prop receives "forwarded-marker". a declared prop is not an attr, so inheritattrs: false should have no say - which is exactly what the vdom renderer does with the identical files minus the vapor attributes: (renders class prop = forwarded-marker, and the div carries the class) what is actually happening under vapor the prop arrives undefined - the reproduction renders class prop = dropped and the div carries no class attribute. the fallthrough class is discarded by the receiver's inheritattrs: false before it is converted into the declared prop. two contrasts that isolate the mechanism, both measured on the same rc.3 playground: - passing the class directly ( , no middle component) works under vapor: the declared prop receives the value, inheritattrs: false does not interfere. - removing defineoptions({ inheritattrs: false }) from child (keeping the middle hop) also works under vapor. so it is specifically the fallthrough-then-inheritattrs:false combination: each half alone behaves. system info not relevant - reproduces in the sfc playground. any additional comments? found in an app where a modal hands its close button a positioning class (absolute end-3 top-1/2 ...), the close button's root is a tooltip component, and the tooltip declares class as a prop while setting inheritattrs: false (it teleports its floating panel, so attr inheritance is deliberately off). under vdom the x sits in the modal's corner; under vapor the class evaporates on the fallthrough hop and the x flows inline after the title. the userland workaround is to declare the class prop on the intermediate component and forward it explicitly - which restores identical behavior on both renderers, consistent with the mechanism above. related but distinct from 15227 (a class prop arriving unnormalized as an array - fixed by 15230) and 15274 (transition overwriting a wrapped root's own class - fixed by 15275): here the class never arrives at all, and only when it travels via fallthrough into a component whose inheritattrs is false.

vapor: dynamic slots from a v-for remount their content whenever the source array identity changes, losing all state vue version 3.6.0-rc.3 link to minimal reproduction all three sfcs carry and the playground is pinned to 3.6.0-rc.3. steps to reproduce 1. click one of the local state = 0 buttons twice, so a slotted component holds visible local state. 2. click recompute items once. the app is: a computed returns a new array of new objects on every recompute ([{ name: 'a' }, { name: 'b' }] - names, order and length never change), and that array feeds a dynamic-named-slot loop: html child renders two static outlets / ; content holds a local count ref and logs onmounted / onunmounted. what is expected the slotted components keep their state. nothing observable changed across the recompute: same slot names, same :keys, same component, same props. this is exactly what the vdom renderer does with the identical code minus the vapor attributes - same sequence there keeps local state = 2 and logs no unmounts: what is actually happening every dynamic slot is torn down and remounted, and all slot-content state is lost. console after one recompute click on rc.3: unmounted a mounted a total mounts: 3 unmounted b mounted b total mounts: 4 and both buttons reset to local state = 0. the mechanism, from reading the rc.3 runtime (vue.runtime-with-vapor.esm-browser.js): - the compiler emits the loop through createforslots, whose dynamicslot entries are { name, fn } - the template's :key is dropped, and each re-evaluation of the source expression mints fresh fn closures; - createslot's getboundslot caches by slot-fn identity, and the outlet's dynamicfragment.update(render, key = render) keys the mounted branch on function identity: if (key === this.current) return, otherwise it stops the branch scope, removes the branch and mounts a fresh one. so a recompute that yields a new source array identity - even when every item is observably identical - regenerates the slot closures and remounts every outlet. notably the props side already defends against exactly this kind of churn (stabilizedynamicsourcevalue in componentprops.ts keeps stable identities for plain objects), but dynamic slots have no equivalent: an array of slot entries plus fresh closures structurally bypasses it. system info not relevant - reproduces in the sfc playground. any additional comments? found in an app where the loop source is a computed reading store state: every store write recomputed the array, and every recompute silently remounted the mounted panel, resetting its selection state. the userland workaround is an identity-stable computed (return the previous array instance while the contents are shallow-equal), which fully restores the vdom-parity behavior - consistent with the mechanism above. if keying dynamic-slot branches on closure identity is an intended vapor trade-off rather than a defect, a statement of that contract would let userland stabilize loop sources deliberately - today nothing in the docs or the roadmap says dynamic slot content is remounted on source-identity change, and the template accepts (then drops) a :key that reads as if it controlled reuse.

facilitate external configuration wildcard composition in kubernetes (multiple application.yaml) problem i currently find it quite difficult to manage composable configuration when using kubernetes with spring boot. a single kubernetes configmap makes it easy to mount all contained configuration files (effectively behaving as a wildcard), but they can only be mounted into a single directory. spring boot, on the other hand, mainly supports importing a wildcard of directories, with each directory containing a single application.yaml. these two approaches are incompatible and you can't simply use wildcards end-to-end. there are several ways to workaround this (either mount the files in the "wildcard" format of kubernetes, but also pass the list of files to springboot; or mount the files in the "wildcard" format of springboot, but this requires explicitly listing all the file at the volumemount site) but in both cases you need to explicitely list all files. i find it rather cumbersome and error-prone. i'm not sure where the better fix would be. could spring boot make it easier to consume multiple configuration files from a single directory, in a way that matches how configmaps are naturally mounted? or do you think it should be kubernetes job to provide a more convenient way to mount a configmap in the layout expected by spring boot — one directory per file, with inside the right filename? exemple as a concrete example, imagine 3 spring boot deployments, a shared configmap, each one its specific configmap. you have multiple deployments variants, so you're configuration has to be composable. maybe in some cases you want to add a new timeout config file to all, and maybe a database connection credentials for 2 of the 3 microservices that use the database you have multiple possibilities: - change the volumemounts: - add the files to the corresponding existing configmap, and also at the volumemount level list all files to be mounted in subpaths (e.g. at /config/timeouts/application.yaml, /config/database/application.yaml) - or create new configmaps, modify the volumemounts of each microservice to mount to the correct folder /config/timeout and /config/database - put the files in the existing configmap and wildcard mount them, and get spring boot to read them by listing them explicitely (many ways to do this, using files or env vars or command line flags, activating profiles, setting confignames, or spring.config.additional-location pointing to the files or import: directives in an existing files; or even run init containers just to move things around) there are probably many more but arguably no simple solution ? what do you think ? ps: i'm working on this in the context of a kustomize deployments using components, but that's kind of at a higher level than the configuration problem ps2: as far as i understand, configtrees don't help with this, they only allow to work with configmaps that are "springkey": "value" instead of "filenamekey": "filenamecontent"

rainbow gum a logging framework supports loggingsystem (maybe a doc link?) rainbow gum is a logging framework similar to logback and log4j2 but newer and uses newer jdk features: best of all it integrates with spring boot. doc for spring boot is here: i have tried to make rainbow gum as much of a drop in replacement for the other two mainstream logging frameworks and as easy to use as possible. now here is a possible feature i was thinking of: i noticed is that while the loggingsystem (and the actuator loggersendpoint built on top of it) only exposes logger level state - getloggerconfigurations()/vgetloggerconfiguration()/setloglevel(). there's no way, at runtime or via actuator, to find out whether the logging system itself is healthy. for example did an appender fail to write, did a rolling policy break, did an async queue start dropping events. if you depend on log delivery for anything (audit logging, log shipping to a collector, compliance), that's currently a blind spot - the only signal is whatever got printed to stderr at the moment it happened, and only if someone happened to be watching. to get around that i added another actuator module and i think log4j2 has one as well: but i wonder if the loggingsystem could help guide that. the second feature and i know its very doubtful is a link to rainbow gum in the logging section. i get no money for rainbow gum and while i do think it is the best logging framework and could save a ton of money on general compute overhead (logging is actually a pretty significant cost at scale) it just does not have the decades network effect that the other two have.

tf.slice(v, v, v) on a length-1 tensor v = [19] is out of range. eager raises invalidargumenterror: expected begin[0] in [0, 1], but got 19. under jit compile=true, when begin/size come from a runtime computation, the process aborts with glibc heap corruption. the exact message varies: free(): corrupted unsorted chunks, malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted, free(): invalid next size (fast). it crashed in 6 of 6 runs across both versions. usually xla returns (0,) and the process then aborts; sometimes it aborts before printing. the uint8 cast matters. with w as int32 (or begin/size passed as constants), xla either raises the eager error or returns an empty tensor. with the cast, the inferred upper bound for the slice size is large enough for the out-of-range runtime size to write past the buffer. this is related to 110789 (heap corruption from tf.slice on a dynamically-shaped input), but it still happens in a nightly that includes the fix for 110789 (pr 126676). expected: xla should raise an error (or at least clamp safely). it should never corrupt memory. standalone code to reproduce the issue shell import tensorflow as tf def f(m, w): v = tf.linalg.matvec(m, tf.cast(w, tf.int32)) runtime value [19], shape [1] return tf.slice(v, v, v) begin=19, size=19 on a length-1 tensor m = tf.constant([[1, 5]]) w = tf.constant([4, 3], dtype=tf.uint8) try: print("eager", f(m, w).shape) except exception as e: print("eager", type(e). name , str(e).splitlines()[0][:100]) r = tf.function(f, jit compile=true)(m, w) print("xla", tuple(r.shape)) relevant log output shell eager invalidargumenterror {{function node wrapped slice device /job:localhost/replica:0/task:0/device:cpu:0}} expected begin[0] in [0, 1], but got 19 ... xla (0,) malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted aborted (core dumped)

tflite: interpreter(model path=) bypasses flatbuffer verification, causing sigsegv summary tf.lite.interpreter(model path=...) (the file-path variant of the official python api) loads .tflite models without invoking flatbuffer verification , causing a hard sigsegv on a maliciously crafted model. the same file loaded via model content= is correctly rejected by tflite::verify(). the two code paths of the same official api have inconsistent security behavior. this directly contradicts the security-boundary assumption stated in 122540 (comment by @dmiltr3, 2026-09-23): > interpreterbuilder is part of the core interpreter api, it operates under the assumption that the model has either been verified by tflite::verify() (which must catch this offset overflow safely) or is from a trusted source. the model path route of the official tf.lite.interpreter api is not a raw interpreterbuilder — it is the documented entry point used pervasively in google's own tutorials, the android/ios tflite sdk examples, and the model-serving samples. if verify() is a required precondition, the file-path variant must call it internally or the docs must warn loudly. currently neither is true. environment - tensorflow 2.19.0 (pip) - macos 14, arm64 (apple silicon) - python 3.9 - also reproduced on linux x86 64 + addresssanitizer (heap-buffer-overflow read, see poc repo) reproduction malicious model (gather overflow v2.tflite) contains a buffer whose offset triggers uint64 t overflow in the bounds check at interpreter builder.cc:671 (root cause originally reported in 122540). the same poc file is used for both tests below. test 1 — model content path (in-memory buffer, goes through buildfrombuffer → calls verify()) python import tensorflow as tf with open('gather overflow v2.tflite', 'rb') as f: data = f.read() interp = tf.lite.interpreter(model content=data) result: ✅ rejected cleanly. valueerror: the model is not a valid flatbuffer buffer test 2 — model path path (file path, goes through buildfromfile) python import tensorflow as tf interp = tf.lite.interpreter(model path='/tmp/gather overflow v2.tflite') interp.allocate tensors() result: ❌ sigsegv, exit code 139. no exception, no verify() rejection. process crashes. root cause the two interpreter entry points use different loading paths: - model content= → buildfrombuffer(...) in the python c++ shim → runs tflite::verify() on the input bytes before handing them to interpreterbuilder. - model path= → buildfromfile(...) → flatbuffermodel::verifyandbuildfromfile is not the default ; the standard path (buildfromfile) mmaps the file and constructs the model without running verify(). therefore, any user of the file-path api — which is the officially documented and most common way to load a .tflite model — is exposed to the entire class of flatbuffer parsing bugs (buffer-offset overflow, malformed subgraphs, etc.) that tf's security model explicitly delegates to verify(). why this matters (impact) 1. official google examples use model path. e.g. the tflite python quickstart, android/ios samples, and coral/edge tpu tutorials all use interpreter(model path=...) (or the equivalent newfromfile in the c++/java/swift api surface) with no explicit verify() call. 2. .tflite files are routinely loaded from untrusted sources — huggingface hub, community model zoos, on-device ml with ota model updates, federated learning aggregators, model-serving pipelines that accept user uploads. 3. the security boundary claimed in the previous issue does not hold in practice. applications following the official docs are, by definition, "violating the defined security boundary" — which means the boundary is documented in the wrong place. under any reasonable threat model where .tflite files can come from a non-trusted party (which google's own docs explicitly encourage: huggingface, mediapipe model zoo, litert community models), the file-path api is an unauthenticated remote crash primitive — and, given the earlier asan heap-buffer-overflow read result, potentially an information-disclosure primitive. requested fix any of the following would close the gap. in descending order of preference: 1. make buildfromfile call tflite::verify() by default , matching buildfrombuffer's behavior. provide an explicit unsafe=true / skip verification=true opt-out for trusted-source performance-critical paths. 2. fix the underlying integer overflow in the bounds check at interpreter builder.cc:671 (the fix originally proposed in 121262 / 122540) so verify() is not the last line of defense. 3. at minimum, prominently document in the tf.lite.interpreter docstring, tflite python guide, and android/ios sdk docs that model path= does not verify untrusted inputs and that callers must run tflite::verify() themselves before construction. proof of concept - poc dataset (malicious model + build script): - linux arm64 + addresssanitizer report showing heap-buffer-overflow read: reproduced in docker ubuntu 22.04 / clang-14, see previous issue 122540 for the asan trace. references - original overflow report: 121262 - fix pr discussion: 122540 - litert security policy referenced by the reviewer: --- filed as a follow-up to 122540. if the security boundary really is "callers must run verify() first", then the official model path api needs to enforce that itself, because right now it doesn't.

tf.linalg.svd under jit compile=true (xla) returns wrong singular values and a wrong reconstruction for a small-scale but well-conditioned float32 matrix; standard eager svd is correct issue type bug have you reproduced the bug with tensorflow nightly? yes source binary tensorflow version 2.22.0-dev20260921(git version v1.12.1-145339-g0181b74d80f) custom code yes os platform and distribution linux ubuntu 22.04(kernel 6.8, glibc 2.35) mobile device n/a python version 3.12.13 bazel version n/a(binary install) gcc/compiler version n/a(binary install) cuda/cudnn version cuda 12.9 / cudnn 9.26(pip nvidia- -cu12) gpu model and memory nvidia rtx a6000 (48 gb) current behavior? tf.linalg.svd under jit compile=true (xla) computes wrong singular values and a wrong reconstruction for a well-conditioned float32 matrix that has merely been scaled down. xla returns the diagonal entries as the "singular values" and reconstructs a diagonal matrix, dropping the off-diagonal entries; standard eager svd, and float64, are correct. although the individual u and v factors are not unique, the reconstructed product u·diag(s)·vᵀ must reproduce the input matrix; therefore factor sign/basis ambiguity cannot explain the observed reconstruction error — it is a genuine correctness error. root cause (hypothesis). a scale sweep with a fixed a0 (fixed condition number) shows the failure transition occurs between scales 1e-6 and 1e-7 , which is strongly consistent with the fixed absolute epsilon = 1e-6 used by the xla svd implementation. this strongly suggests that an absolute stopping/zeroing threshold is making the algorithm scale-sensitive : for this fixed matrix family, scaling the input below roughly this regime causes meaningful intermediate quantities to fall below the absolute threshold and be treated as negligible, breaking scale invariance. subnormal intermediates may further aggravate the problem, but they are not necessary to explain the failure: at scale 1e-7 the input quantities ( 1e-7) are already many orders of magnitude above the smallest normal float32 ( 1.17e-38), yet xla already fails. scale sweep (fixed a0 ⇒ fixed conditioning; residual computed in float64) a0 = [[1,2],[3,4]] fixed (cond ≈ 14.9 at every scale). relative reconstruction residual ‖u·diag(s)·vᵀ − a‖/‖a‖, computed after casting to float64 so the residual itself is scale-immune: | scale | eager resid | xla resid | |---|---|---| | 1 | 9.7e-8 | 9.7e-8 | | 1e-2 | 3.0e-7 | 1.7e-7 | | 1e-4 | 1.3e-7 | 2.4e-7 | | 1e-6 | 4.0e-7 | 2.0e-7 | | 1e-7 | 3.4e-7 | 0.658 ← xla breaks | | 1e-10 | 1.6e-7 | 0.658 | | 1e-15 | 1.3e-7 | 0.658 | | 1e-20 | 9.7e-8 | 0.658 | conclusion: the result depends on absolute scale, not on the matrix conditioning (cond is fixed throughout). the failure transition occurs between scales 1e-6 and 1e-7; conversion. for example, in aten/src/aten/native/kleidiai/kai pack.h, code such as: cpp bias.value().to(kfloat).data ptr () and: scales.to(kfloat).const data ptr () takes a pointer from the result of packing of the same inputs can produce different packed results, and the packed bias can be incorrect. reproducer: import hashlib import torch group size, k, n, repeats = 64, 768, 768, 20 def group size, k, n) def matmul(x, packed): return torch.ops.aten. dyn quant matmul 4bit(x, packed, group size, k, n) torch.manual seed(0) weight = torch.randint(0, 256, (n, k // 2), dtype=torch.uint8) describe the bug i compared a fp32 cpu training run against a fp32 cuda training run of the same resnet34 (torchvision, cifar stem: conv1 3x3 stride 1, maxpool replaced by identity) on identical combined_text: [rocm] sparse coo coalesce returns garbage values when the dense size exceeds one tile 🐛 describe the bug the issue was encountered during skipped fbgemm tbe tests re-enablement on rocm and became a reason of disabling the unit tests on rocm ci. sparse coo tensor output is used there and causes tests to compare against ill-formed reference. cuda pipeline on the other hand passes. on rocm, coalesce() of a sparse coo tensor on the gpu returns wrong values whenever the dense part of the values is wider than one kernel tile (warp size 4, so 256 on cdna) and nnz is at least 2. the affected columns are never written, so they contain whatever was in the memory returned by at::empty. there is no error. it reproduces for float32, float16, bfloat16 and bool. python import torch s = torch.sparse coo tensor(torch.tensor([[1, 5]]), torch.randn(2, 512), (10, 512)) print((s.cuda().coalesce().to dense().cpu() - s.coalesce().to dense()).abs().max()) expected: tensor(0.). observed on gfx950: a large value; columns 260 to 511 are wrong. > the following analysis was produced with claude code (ai assistant) and reviewed by me: > > 158281 moved the feature tile index of coalescevalueskernel from blockidx.y to blockidx.z on rocm, but the rocm branch computes the tile offset as blockidx.z nsegments sz instead of blockidx.z blockdim.x sz (aten/src/aten/native/sparse/cuda/sparsecudaapplyutils.cuh, both overloads). the host still sizes grid.z in tiles of warp size sz, so tiles overlap or leave gaps unless nsegments == warp size. the number of wrong columns measured on gfx950 for nnz in 2..128 and dense sizes 256..1024 matches this model exactly. the same root cause was reported for gfx1201 in a comment on 158281. using blockdim.x like the cuda branch fixes it: a 1794 case fuzz against cpu coalesce (11 dtypes, nnz up to 70000 including the batched grid path, several dense shapes) passes with that change. versions observed with the nightly torch==2.15.0.dev20260930+rocm10.0 (git 89ac0527b15d5d9e2d5389b4cc56c54ce5320ed0). code is unchanged on main as of d0b8bbb0151. rocm sdk used to build pytorch: 10.0.0 hip used to build pytorch: 7.15.26333 os: almalinux 8.10 (cerulean leopard) (x86 64) gcc version: (gcc) 13.3.1 20240611 (red hat 13.3.1-2) python version: 3.11.4 (64-bit runtime) python platform: linux-6.8.0-38-generic-x86 64-with-glibc2.28 gpu models and configuration: amd instinct mi350x (gfx950:sramecc+:xnack-) hip runtime version: 7.15.26333 miopen runtime version: 3.6.0 cpu: amd epyc 9575f 64-core processor [pip3] numpy==2.4.6 [pip3] triton-rocm==3.8.0+gitc01b6774 cc @nikitaved @pearu @cpuhrsch @amjames @bhosmer @jcaip @jeffdaily @sunway513 @jithunnair-amd @pruthvistony @rocmsupport @jataylo @hongxiayang @naromero77amd @pragupta @jerrymannil @xinyazhang

on intel xeon 6736p, with errors as large as the output values themselves. the issue appears to be in onednn's amx-fp16 convolution kernel and has been reported as uxlfoundation/onednn 6151. it affects both pytorch 2.14.1 and the 2.15 nightly build (both bundle onednn v3.12.0). i discovered the issue when a test comparing accelerator results against an fp16 cpu reference failed on this machine. as a workaround, i set onednn max cpu isa=avx512 core amx. the reproducer and analysis below were prepared with claude (ai-assisted); i ran and checked each result myself. > reproducer > > python > import torch > > torch.manual seed(0) > x = torch.randn(1, 6, 128, 128, dtype=torch.float16) > w = torch.randn(64, 6, 16, 16, dtype=torch.float16) > b = torch.randn(64, dtype=torch.float16) > > conv = lambda x, w, b: torch.conv2d(x, w, b, stride=(16, 16)) > ref32 = conv(x.float(), w.float(), b.float()) > print("max |fp32| =", ref32.abs().max().item()) > print("max |fp16 - fp32| =", (conv(x, w, b).float() - ref32).abs().max().item()) > > > observed: max |fp32| = 145.7, max |fp16 - fp32| = 159.3. the error is as large as the outputs, so this isn't fp16 rounding: the same fp16 inputs give 0.059 when onednn avoids the amx-fp16 kernel. > > | torch | bundled onednn | max \|fp16 − fp32\| | > |---|---|---| > | 2.14.1+cpu | v3.12.0 | 159.3 | > | 2.15.0.dev20261001+cpu | v3.12.0 | accuracy, as with the two settings above. > > onednn verbose=1 shows the kernel: > > > onednn verbose,v1,info,cpu,isa:intel avx10.1 and intel amx with bfloat16, float16 and 8-bit integer support > onednn verbose,v1,primitive,exec,cpu,convolution,brg conv fwd:avx10 1 512 amx fp16,forward training,src:f16:a:blocked:acdb::f0 wei:f16:ap:blocked:acdb16b32a2b::f0 bia:f16:a:blocked:a::f0 combined_text: cpu bf16/fp16 add(other, alpha=) rounds differently in the vectorized body and the scalar tail (and on x86 vs arm64); alpha is rounded to the tensor dtype 🐛 describe the bug on cpu, torch.add(self, other, alpha=a) for bfloat16 (and float16) gives different results for identical inputs depending on the tensor length and the element's index. neither result is the one-rounding value that mul/div give for reduced floats. python import torch g, p, a = 0.052978515625, -0.53125, 0.1 for n in (31, 32, 33): x = torch.full((n,), g, dtype=torch.bfloat16) y = torch.full((n,), p, dtype=torch.bfloat16) print(n, sorted(set(x.add(y, alpha=a).tolist())), x.add(y, alpha=a)[-1].item()) on x86 (avx512, torch.backends.cpu.get cpu capability() == 'avx512'): | n | elements 0..31 | trailing elements | |----|----------------|-------------------| | 31 | −0.000244140625 (all) | — | | 32 | −0.0001983642578125 (all) | — | | 33 | −0.0001983642578125 | −0.000244140625 | - exact g + a p = −0.0001464844; correctly rounded to bf16 = −0.0001468658447265625. - −0.0001983642578125 = fp32 fma with alpha rounded to bf16 (0.1 → 0.10009765625). - −0.000244140625 = bf16(g + bf16(a p)), two bf16 roundings. on apple m1 (arm64/neon) every element takes the two-rounding value, so the same op gives different results on x86 and arm64. torch. foreach add(..., alpha=) shows the same split. that is the path torch.optim.adam's l2 weight decay (grad.add(param, alpha=weight decay)) takes for bf16 parameters, and where we hit this. in our differential test, the same optimizer cell, seed and torch version produce different bf16 trajectories on x86 and arm64. cause (v2.14.1, unchanged on main) - aten/src/aten/native/native functions.yaml l564-569: add.out is a ufunc, generic: add (allandcomplex, bfloat16, half, complexhalf), so it is instantiated with t = bfloat16 and alpha is a bfloat16. - aten/src/aten/native/ufunc/add.h l15-17 (scalar): self + alpha other in bfloat16 arithmetic gives two roundings. - add.h l22-24 (vector): vec::fmadd(other, alpha, self). on x86 this widens to fp32 and rounds once. on neon, vec128 bfloat16 neon.h l647-663 implements bf16 fmadd as a b + c in bf16 (note [bf16 fma]), giving two roundings. - by contrast, cpu/binaryopskernel.cpp gives mul/div a reduced-float path that keeps the scalar as opmath t and computes in fp32 (l139-153, l171-185). expected the same result for every element regardless of position or isa. ideally that is bf16(float(self) + opmath(alpha) float(other)), as mul/div already do for reduced floats. this is a one-ulp-scale effect, but it is layout- and host-dependent, and it is largest under cancellation (self ≈ −alpha other). (not yet checked: cuda behaviour.) versions torch 2.14.1 (pypi wheel 2.14.1+cu130, run on cpu), python 3.13.14, linux x86 64, intel xeon @ 2.10ghz (avx512). also observed with torch 2.14.1 on macos arm64 (apple m1 pro), python 3.13.7. suggested labels: module: cpu, module: bfloat16 cc @jgong5 @mingfeima @xiaobingsuper @sanchitintel @ashokei @jingxu10 @aditew01 @snadampal @milpuz01 @nikhil-arm @fadara01 @robert-hardwick @nweidia

caching allocator: cross-stream memory when running two streams on green contexts previously, i opened 195378 related to sm green context memory mapping. this is another question related to memory in the same setup. currently, i'm working on llm prefill and decode running in parallel using green contexts. each of them runs in a separate stream. as you know, the caching allocator holds allocated memory only in the stream context in which the memory was allocated. it is intended by design (it is stated in the docs). i wanted to see how costly this can be in the above case and prepared a simple test. test 1: allocate 512 mib of memory on stream 1, free it and allocate 512 mib again. - same stream: reserved 512 mib - different streams: reserved 1024 mib test 2: allocate and free 8, 7, 8, 7, 8, 7 gib, alternating between two streams. 8 + 7 gib cannot be allocated simultaneously on the gpu, but each one separately. - same stream: 0 retries, less than 0.5 ms per allocation - different streams: a cache flush and retry on every allocation attempt; roughly 180 - 200 ms per allocation the setup: t4 (colab), pytorch [version]. sizes in test 2 are for a 15 gb gpu, so adjust accordingly. a=torch.empty(512 mb,dtype=torch.uint8,device="cuda") del a torch.cuda.synchronize() with torch.cuda.stream(s2): b=torch.empty(512 mb,dtype=torch.uint8,device="cuda") print("same" if same stream else in enumerate([8,7,8,7,8,7]): s=s1 if i % 2 == 0 else s2 t0=time.perf counter() with torch.cuda.stream(s): a=torch.empty(size gb,dtype=torch.uint8,device="cuda") del a torch.cuda.synchronize() print(i, revert broadcast array deprecation expirery (gh-26214 ) see discussion starting with: the original pr had some unintended changes on top of the expiration. but additionally, there is a change that buffer-protocol export cannot give a deprecationwarning so that some cython users who ingest such arrays have to use const. those users should prefer const and it is good that this get's fixed in scipy, but we should also revert it anyway at least for a while (maybe 3.0). one change that was not intended is that this changed arrays to read-only that didn't need broadcasting. i think when reverting we should add a test for this so that if we expire the deprecation in the future we don't accidentally change that part again.[^1] (there was an intermediate pr which added another new test to fix an initial issue. this test should be preserved as well.) [^1]: it might not be completely strange to do this, but it's really not necessary and probably wasn't deprecated. plus, i think if this was done then the code that relies on this would probably need a clearer api to achieve what it wants.

variant analysis: 1 unfixed sibling safety gap in numpy summary variant analysis of historical fixes in numpy identified 1 code site where an integer-overflow guard, bounds check, or safe-allocation wrapper exists at one location but is missing at a structurally identical sibling location (same file, same function, or same pattern family) elsewhere in the codebase. each finding below is code-confirmed against the current head (verified by cloning the repository fresh and checking the pattern is still present), with the exact file/line locations, the root cause, a description of the trigger path, and — where available — asan/execution verification output or a proof-of-concept. note on origin: these were surfaced by an automated variant-analysis pipeline that diffs historical fix commits against sibling code paths, then has each candidate manually reviewed. i'm posting them together per-project rather than as separate issues to respect maintainer time. happy to split, close, or reprioritize any of these as you see fit. --- finding 1: numpy — string add missing output buffer width check (sibling to fixed string multiply) verified against head: a98529df (2026-09-25) - project : numpy (numpy/numpy) - class : heap-buffer-overflow write (missing bounds check on fixed-width string output buffer) - status : code-confirmed, exec-blocked - sibling of : commit d0de6a1a9 — fixed heap overflow in string multiply by adding output width cap discovery method variant analysis. commit d0de6a1a9 fixed a heap overflow in string multiply where reps > width caused writes past the output buffer. the fix added min(reps , width) to cap characters written. string add in the same file combines two strings without checking whether len1 + len2 fits in the output buffer width. vulnerable code fixed — string multiply, after commit d0de6a1a9: cpp size t end index = reps > width ? width : reps ; // cap added buf1.buffer memcpy(out, end index); out.buffer fill with zeros after index(end index); unfixed — string add, lines 159-165: cpp static inline void string add(buffer buf1, buffer buf2, buffer out) { size t len1 = buf1.num codepoints(); size t len2 = buf2.num codepoints(); buf1.buffer memcpy(out, len1); // no width check buf2.buffer memcpy(out + len1, len2); // no width check out.buffer fill with zeros after index(len1 + len2); // no width check } no check that len1 + len2 descriptors[2]->elsize, normal ufunc dispatch correctly sizes the output via string addition resolve descriptors (line 735-776) which computes result itemsize = descr1->elsize + descr2->elsize. however , when using out= (in-place or pre-allocated output), the output descriptor retains its original size, creating a mismatch. root cause the string multiply fix added a cap (min(reps , width)) to prevent write past the output buffer. string add has the same vulnerability — len1 + len2 can exceed out.buffer width() — but was not fixed with the same pattern. the normal dispatch path computes correct output size, but the out= argument short-circuits this. concrete example python import numpy as np a = np.array(['hello'], dtype='s5') fixed-width 5-byte strings b = np.array(['world'], dtype='s5') 'hello' + 'world' = 10 bytes, but out=a is only 5 bytes wide np.add(a, b, out=a) writes 10 bytes into 5-byte buffer → heap overflow the buffer memcpy copies len1=5 bytes to out, then len2=5 bytes to out + 5. if out is only 5 bytes wide, the second memcpy writes 5 bytes past the allocation. trigger path 1. user (or fuzzer) creates fixed-width string arrays with narrow width 2. → calls np.add(a, b, out=a) where combined string length exceeds output width 3. → string add is called with output buffer width < len1 + len2 4. → buffer memcpy(out + len1, len2) writes past end of output allocation 5. → heap overflow, potentially corrupting adjacent numpy array data fuzz harness : standard numpy fuzzer or hypothesis-based property test with out= parameter on string operations. sibling-gap quality excellent. same file (string ufuncs.cpp), same class of bug, same mechanism (fixed-width string buffer width vs. operation result width mismatch), same mitigation pattern needed. the string multiply fix proves the developers recognized this class of bug; string add was simply missed. --- analysis date: 2026-09-22. code-confirmed, not execution-verified. --- methodology for each historical vulnerability fix in the codebase, we identified the safe pattern the fix introduced (an overflow guard, a safe allocator wrapper, a bounds check) and searched the rest of the codebase for structurally identical code that predates or postdates the fix but never received it. each candidate was then manually verified against the current head listed above. happy to provide anything else that would help triage — additional poc inputs, a minimal patch following the existing safe-sibling pattern, or a written reproduction script.

bug: set typedict() accepts non-dict objects and causes systemerror in later promote types() describe the issue: numpy. core. multiarray umath.set typedict() accepts arbitrary python objects and stores them as the internal typedict state without checking that the object is a dictionary. a later call to promote types() can then pass this invalid object to a cpython dictionary api, resulting in: text systemerror: objects/dictobject.c:1760: bad argument to internal function the relevant code in numpy/ core/src/multiarray/descriptor.c currently does: c if (!pyarg parsetuple(args, "o:set typedict", &dict)) { return null; } multiarray umath state state = get module state(module); py xsetref(state->typedict, py newref(dict)); there is no validation that dict is actually a dictionary before it is stored in state->typedict. the later dtype handling path uses this value as a dictionary, which is what leads to the internal systemerror. i believe the invalid value should be rejected by set typedict() before it replaces the existing internal dictionary. reproduce the code example: python import numpy as np m = np. core. multiarray umath install an invalid object into the internal development tree. python: text 3.12.14 compiler: text gcc 13.3.0 how does this issue affect you or how did you find it: i found this while running fusil against numpy's native multiarray umath module. the original fusil-generated testcase exercised a number of native functions. the failure was initially reported at promote types(). i then reduced the testcase and found that set typedict() was the important state-changing operation before the failure. the relevant sequence is: text set typedict(non-dict) | v invalid object stored in typedict | v promote types(...) | v cpython dictionary api | v enh: detect mixed bytes/text inputs during array conversion proposed new feature or change: follow-up to sebastian’s review comment on 32757 array(['a', 'b'], dtype=' >> np.concatenate(([b"a", "b"], ["c"])) array(['a', 'b', 'c'], dtype='<u1') we should add an opt-in mode (exposed to numpy python internals via array converter) that detects these mixtures during dtype discovery, before coercion happens and we lose track of the input dtypes. shared c conversion machinery would let concatenate detect mixtures within its inputs as well as between them. the same detection could support deprecating implicit unicode inference for mixed bytes/text inputs. these should eventually produce object arrays that preserve the original values. explicit conversions such as dtype="u" would remain supported. this has come up in the past, in particular: - [ 15327]( proposed deprecating implicit string/non-string promotion, including in concatenate. - [ 19078]( described downstream difficulties with promotion warnings: callers wanted numeric inference for numeric inputs and object arrays for mixed inputs. - [ 19101]( explored an opt-in object-fallback mode during dtype discovery; it was not merged.

bug: np.exp2 no longer raises underflow on windows 10.0.26100 and later (ucrt exp2 drops fe underflow) describe the issue: on windows builds 10.0.26100 and later (windows 11 24h2, windows server 2025), np.exp2 no longer raises on underflow, so np.errstate(under='raise') silently stops firing for it, and numpy. core.tests.test umath.testspecialfloats::test exp2 fails. the cause is outside numpy: the ucrt shipped with those builds returns 0.0 from exp2/exp2f on a total underflow without raising fe underflow (or even fe inexact). exp/expf on the very same runtime still raise correctly, and so does every other libm function i probed, so exp2 is the only one affected. numpy maps npy exp2 straight onto the platform exp2 (numpy/ core/include/numpy/npy math.h:196), so the missing flag is passed through to np.errstate. this is invisible to numpy's ci because every windows job in .github/workflows/windows.yml runs on the windows-2022 image, whose ucrt is 10.0.20348 and still behaves correctly. the windows-2025 image reproduces it. evidence i probed the ucrt directly through ctypes, so the measurement does not depend on numpy at all, and ran the same probe on both hosted runner images: | environment | ucrtbase.dll | exp2(-2000.0) flags | exp(-2000.0) flags | np.exp2(-2000.0) under errstate(under='raise') | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | my machine, windows 11 build 26200 | 10.0.26100.9444 | none | inexact,underflow | no raise | | github actions windows-2025 | 10.0.26100.33158 | none | inexact,underflow | no raise | | github actions windows-2022 | 10.0.20348.5622 | inexact,underflow | inexact,underflow | raises | exp2 returns the correct value in all three cases; only the exception flag is missing. it is specific to a total underflow: exp2(-1030.0), which lands in the subnormal range, still raises inexact,underflow,denormal on my machine, so the flag is being dropped only on the flush-to-zero path. i did not test the windows builds between 20348 and 26100 (23h2 and earlier windows 11), so i do not know where in that range the behaviour changed. reproduce the code example: python import numpy as np for dt in ('e', 'f', 'd'): try: with np.errstate(under='raise'): r = np.exp2(np.array(-2000.0, dtype=dt)) print('exp2 -2000', dt, '->', repr(r), 'no raise') except floatingpointerror as e: print('exp2 -2000', dt, '-> raised', e) and the numpy-independent probe of the c runtime: python import ctypes ucrt = ctypes.cdll("api-ms-win-crt-math-l1-1-0.dll") rt = ctypes.cdll("api-ms-win-crt-runtime-l1-1-0.dll") rt. clearfp.restype = rt. statusfp.restype = ctypes.c uint names = {0x1: "inexact", 0x2: "underflow", 0x4: "overflow", 0x8: "div0", 0x10: "invalid", 0x80000: "denormal"} for name in ("exp2", "exp"): fn = getattr(ucrt, name) fn.restype = ctypes.c double fn.argtypes = [ctypes.c double] rt. clearfp() value = fn(-2000.0) flags = rt. statusfp() print(name, "(-2000) =", value, "flags =", ",".join(n for b, n in names.items() if flags & b) or "none") error message: $ python -m pytest --pyargs numpy. core.tests.test umath -k test exp2 for value in [2000.0, -2000.0]: with np.errstate(over='raise', under='raise'): for dt in ['e', 'f', 'd']: > assert raises(floatingpointerror, np.exp2, np.array(value, dtype=dt)) e assertionerror: floatingpointerror not raised by exp2 numpy\ core\tests\test umath.py:1854: assertionerror the overflow half of the same test (+2000.0) still passes; only the underflow half fails. python and numpy versions: 2.5.3 3.12.10 (tags/v3.12.10:0cc8128, apr 8 2025, 12:21:36) [msc v.1943 64 bit (amd64)] also reproduced with 2.5.3 on the hosted windows-2025 image with python 3.12.10. runtime environment: windows 11 build 26200, amd64. numpy.show config() reports baseline x86 v2, found x86 v3. context for comment: two things numpy could do, and i am happy to send a pr for either: 1. make test exp2 tolerant of the platform defect. this is the same situation as the existing glibc older than("2.17") xfail directly above the test, and the smallest version keeps the overflow assertion and skips only the underflow one on affected builds, so no coverage is lost apart from the one thing the platform cannot do. 2. additionally consider whether numpy should compensate, since np.errstate(under='raise') quietly not firing is a behaviour change for user code on the most common desktop platform. that is a larger call and i would rather leave the design to you. worth flagging separately: because all windows ci runs on windows-2022, numpy's windows jobs currently do not exercise the c runtime that its users actually have.

bug: array converter.as arrays() can segfault when pyscalars is a self-referencing object array describe the issue: if a self-referencing object array is passed to the pyscalars argument of array converter.as arrays() then it may cause a native stack overflow and result in the python process being terminated by a segmentation fault. the crash seems to take place when the pyscalars argument is being validated. in the function pyscalar mode conv(), arbitrary python objects are compared with the allowed string values ("convert", "preserve", and "convert if no array") by means of pyobject richcomparebool(). for a self-referencing object array, this invokes ndarray/object-array equality recursively, eventually exhausting the c stack. the relevant path appears to be: text array converter.as arrays() -> pyscalar mode conv() -> pyobject richcomparebool() -> ndarray/object-array rich comparison -> recursive object comparison -> c stack overflow -> sigsegv i have reproduced the crash on both windows and linux/wsl2 using current numpy main. i am willing to investigate this issue and work on a fix/pr if the maintainers agree that this is an appropriate approach. reproduce the code example: python import numpy as np from numpy. core. multiarray umath import array converter obj = np.empty(2, dtype=object) obj[0] = obj obj[1] = [obj, obj] conv = array converter([1, 2, 3]) conv.as arrays(pyscalars=obj) error message: shell on linux/wsl2: segmentation fault (core dumped) on windows, the process terminates during the call without producing a python exception or traceback. python and numpy versions: 2.6.0.dev0+git20260919.9b2580b 3.12.3 (main, mar 23 2026, 19:04:32) [gcc 13.3.0] runtime environment: no response how does this issue affect you or how did you find it: no response
