baseexception as e: print(f"{type(e). name }: {e}") del p for in range(4): gc.collect() print("deleter calls:", deleter calls["n"]) error message: shell expected behavior buffererror: unsupported dtype in dltensor. deleter calls: 1 capsule released, producer free hook runs once (buffererror is the documented intent — see pr 31000 and dlpack dtype registry lookup() in numpy/ core/src/multiarray/dlpack.c.) actual behavior systemerror: returned null without setting an exception deleter calls: 0 deleter never invoked -> dlmanagedtensor + buffer leaked and the following is written to stderr (the smoking gun — the destructor runs with a pending exception): exception ignored on calling ctypes callback function: systemerror: returned a result with an exception set other unsupported dtype codes reproduce the same: code=4 (bfloat), 5, 7, 255, and a known code with unsupported bits (e.g. code=kdlint=0 with bits=24) all raise systemerror and skip the deleter. python and numpy versions: versions : numpy 2.5.2, python 3.12.14, linux x86 64 (cp312 wheel) runtime environment: versions : numpy 2.5.2, python 3.12.14, linux x86 64 (cp312 wheel) how does this issue affect you or how did you find it: why this happens in numpy/ core/src/multiarray/dlpack.c, from dlpack() falls through to the dtype registry on an unknown dtype code: c } else { descr = dlpack dtype registry lookup((uint8 t)dl tensor.dtype.code, bits); if (descr == null) { py decref(capsule); // <-- runs the producer destructor return null; // while the buffererror below is still set } } and the helper sets the exception first: c if (gres == 0) { pyerr setstring(pyexc buffererror, "unsupported dtype in dltensor."); return null; } so py decref(capsule) executes arbitrary producer code (the capsule destructor) while buffererror is pending. for a python-implemented destructor (ctypes, or any deleter that acquires the gil and touches python objects) the nested python call collides with the pending exception, raising systemerror inside the destructor. ctypes then clears the exception state ("exception ignored ..."), the destructor aborts before it can invoke the producer's deleter, and from dlpack returns null with no exception set — which cpython surfaces as the outer systemerror. this is the classic c-api rule "do not run arbitrary code (which py decref can trigger via destructors/finalizers) with a pending exception." note the same pyerr setstring(...); py decref(capsule); return null; pattern is used by the other error branches (device, lanes, maxdims) in this function, so they would be affected the same way. why the existing tests don't catch it test dlpack.py::testdlpack::test invalid dtype uses numpy itself as the producer (np.from dlpack(x) where x is an ndarray), so the capsule destructor is numpy's own c deleter (array dlpack deleter), which does not run python-level code — hence no systemerror and the test passes. a foreign, python-implemented producer (the standard way to build a dlpack capsule in tests, e.g. in iree/tensorflow) is what exercises this path. diagnostic registering the dtype makes the failure disappear, confirming the registry error path is the trigger: python np.dtypes.register dlpack dtype((3, 32), np.dtype("int32")) np.from dlpack(producer(3)) now succeeds and releases the capsule np.from dlpack(producer(3)) now succeeds and releases the capsule

bug: numpy.seterr() segfaults on a self-referencing object array describe the issue: if you pass a numpy object array that contains itself as the all argument to numpy.seterr(), it segfaults instead of raising an error. all is supposed to be one of 'ignore', 'warn', 'raise', 'call', 'print', 'log' (or none), so any other input should just raise typeerror/valueerror. tested this on numpy 2.5.3 from pip and also 2.6.0.dev0 built from git main, same result on both, so it's not something specific to a dev build. repro: python import numpy as np obj array = np.empty(2, dtype=object) obj array[0] = obj array obj array[1] = [obj array, obj array] np.seterr(obj array) crash: fatal python error: segmentation fault current thread 0x00007a5c6ba36740 (most recent call first): file "/home/bhuvansh/numpy/numpy/ core/ ufunc config.py", line 105 in seterr file "repro seterr segfault.py", line 13 in extension modules: numpy. core. multiarray umath, numpy.linalg. umath linalg segmentation fault (core dumped) i ran it under gdb to figure out what's actually happening: bash gdb -q -batch -ex "run" -ex "bt 30" --args python repro seterr segfault.py turns out it's a stack overflow, 19309 frames deep, stuck in this loop: array richcompare -> pyarray genericbinaryfunction -> pyobject vectorcall.warm -> ufunc generic fastcall -> call cached loop -> object equal -> pyobject richcompare -> back to array richcompare so seterr calls into make extobj (compiled, under numpy/ core/src/umath/) which checks all against the allowed strings using ==. for an object array enh: histogram bin edges: add an equal-frequency (quantile) binning strategy proposed new feature or change: np.histogram bin edges(x, bins=...) supports 'auto', 'fd', 'doane', 'scott', 'stone', 'rice', 'sturges', 'sqrt' - all equal-width strategies (they pick a bin width/count, then space edges evenly across the data's range). there's no built-in equal-frequency strategy (edges placed so each bin holds roughly the same number of observations), even though it's one of the two textbook-standard binning approaches and is what you reach for whenever the data is skewed and equal-width bins would leave most of the mass in one or two bins - a genuinely common histogram to want, not a niche one. today it has to be hand-rolled: np.unique(np.quantile(x, np.linspace(0, 1, n bins + 1))) describe the solution you'd like: np.histogram bin edges(x, bins='quantile') (naming open to bikeshedding - 'equal frequency' also reads clearly), using the number of bins from a paired range/bins=(strategy, n) argument or a sensible default, with np.unique applied to the resulting edges so duplicate quantiles collapse into fewer, wider bins rather than erroring or producing zero-width bins. describe alternatives you've considered: pandas.qcut does the equal-frequency binning itself, but returns pandas-specific categorical bin labels tied to a series, not raw histogram bin edges compatible with np.histogram/plt.hist - a different-shaped output for a different purpose (labeling data by bin vs. building a histogram). there's no numpy-native way to get equal-frequency edges as plain floats. additional context: happy to submit a pr - the core computation is a few lines (see the "solution" section above), the main design decision is naming and how to specify bin count for this strategy consistently with the existing string-strategy api.

(this is a tiny bug fix as well) if that fails, try current code with a warning. it would be nice to audit if there are remaining "i" uses that matters, because if there aren't we can be clearer about when the warning was introduced (i.e. we won't use it for more functions). additionally, it may be nice to do a check whether all integers are used in places where numpy may just want to directly transition to our integer conversion helpers. these differ in that numpy sometimes rejects booleans. bug: invalid quantile/percentile method error leaks a dict keys repr describe the issue: the error raised for an invalid method in np.quantile / np.percentile interpolates a dict keys object straight into the message, so the list of valid methods is wrapped in dict keys([...]): every other "invalid option" message in numpy formats the choices plainly, e.g. order must be one of 'c', 'f', 'a', or 'k' (got 'q') sort kind must be one of 'quick', 'heap', or 'stable' (got 'bogus') mode must be one of 'valid', 'same', or 'full' (got 'bogus') so this one is inconsistent with the surrounding convention, and the dict keys(...) wrapper is an implementation detail that means nothing to a caller. the source is numpy/lib/ function base impl.py:4791-4794: python except keyerror: raise valueerror( f"{method!r} is not a valid method. use one of: " f"{ quantilemethods.keys()}") from none reproduce the code example: python import numpy as np np.percentile(np.arange(4), 50, method="bogus") error message: valueerror: 'bogus' is not a valid method. use one of: dict keys(['inverted cdf', 'averaged inverted cdf', 'closest observation', 'interpolated inverted cdf', 'hazen', 'weibull', 'linear', 'median unbiased', 'normal unbiased', 'lower', 'higher', 'midpoint', 'nearest']) np.quantile gives the same message. expected behaviour: the valid methods listed without the dict keys(...) wrapper, so the names can be read and copied directly: valueerror: 'bogus' is not a valid method. use one of: 'inverted cdf', 'averaged inverted cdf', 'closest observation', 'interpolated inverted cdf', 'hazen', 'weibull', 'linear', 'median unbiased', 'normal unbiased', 'lower', 'higher', 'midpoint', 'nearest' additional context i checked whether this pattern appears elsewhere; searching numpy for a dict view interpolated into a message turns up only this one site, so it looks like an isolated slip rather than a general habit. the other matches are all inside vendored-meson. i have a one-line fix and a regression test ready and am happy to open a pr. runtime information: 2.6.0.dev0+git20260902.2f8bc80 on python 3.12.10, windows. also reproduces on the released 2.5.2.

enh: make "no" and "equiv" casting consistent for python scalars in ufuncs and copyto proposed new feature or change: for a python int or float operand, casting="no" is accepted where casting="equiv" is rejected, in ufuncs and in np.copyto: python >>> np.copyto(np.zeros(3, dtype="uint8"), 3, casting="no") >>> np.copyto(np.zeros(3, dtype="uint8"), 3, casting="equiv") typeerror: cannot cast python int to uint8 under the casting rule 'equiv' >>> np.add(np.zeros(3, dtype="float32"), 3.0, casting="no") array([3., 3., 3.], dtype=float32) >>> np.add(np.zeros(3, dtype="float32"), 3.0, casting="equiv") typeerror: cannot cast python float to float32 under the casting rule 'equiv' "no" is stricter than "equiv" for arrays, so the second call should not fail when the first succeeds. np.concatenate((np.zeros(1, dtype="uint8"), 3), axis=none, casting=...) accepts all five rules, so the functions also disagree with each other. the cause is npy update operand for scalar, added in 27091: when the target descriptor differs from the one discovered for the scalar, only npy equiv casting is rejected. npy no casting falls through, the operand is recreated with the target descriptor, and the later cast check compares identical dtypes. test copyto cast safety asserts the "equiv" error, and the comment in the code already questions the rule. this behavior was added in 27091 and no casting never came up in the review there. a python str converted to stringdtype or object ( 32040, 32356) goes through the same helper and has the same asymmetry. that behavior is new in the next release, so we're free to change it if we want, but i left things consistent with numeric types for now. possible fixes 1. reject "no" whenever "equiv" is rejected. consistent, but code passing casting="no" with a python scalar whose dtype changes starts raising. we may need a deprecation? 2. accept "equiv". under nep 50 the scalar takes the other operand's dtype, so there is no cast for either rule to reject. this is what concatenate already does. it changes behavior asserted in test copyto cast safety. @seberg i'd appreciate your opinion, especially if you can remember where you ultimately wanted to end up after 27091.

perf: avoid temporary boolean array in np.array equal for contiguous integer arrays proposed new feature or change np.array equal() currently implements its normal comparison path as: python builtins.bool((asanyarray(a1 == a2)).all()) this materializes an elementwise boolean array and then reduces it in a second pass. for same-shape, same-dtype, contiguous arrays of numpy's built-in signed/unsigned integer dtypes, equality can instead be fused, potentially with a bytewise comparison. this would avoid the temporary allocation and allow an early exit on mismatches. a conservative fast path would require both converted operands to be exact ndarrays, equal shapes and identical built-in signed/unsigned integer dtypes, and the same contiguous traversal order (both c-contiguous or both f-contiguous). unsupported cases would retain the current implementation. a raw-byte path should not initially include bool (distinct nonzero bytes can both mean true), floating-point (for example, 0.0 == -0.0), object, structured, flexible, or user-defined dtypes. for built-in integers, equal nan does not affect the result. conceptually: c if (same builtin integer dtype && same shape && compatible contiguous layout) { return memcmp(data1, data2, nbytes) == 0; } the implementation need not literally use memcmp; a numpy simd-aware fused compare/early-exit helper may be preferable. (2026-08-31). the helper uses memcmp only for identical built-in integer dtypes and compatible c/f-contiguous layouts, and otherwise returns notimplemented to the existing path. following the bug: matmul on apple silicon (accelerate) writes out of bounds — silent data corruption, not just spurious fpe warnings related to 28790 and 29820, which report spurious fpe warnings from matmul on apple silicon as "annoying but harmless". on our workload the same code path silently corrupts an unrelated live array . filing separately because the impact class is different. environment - macos 26.6.2 (build 25g83), apple m5 pro, arm64 - python 3.14.4 (homebrew), numpy 2.2.0, numpy.show config() → blas name: accelerate - scipy 1.17.1 (held constant throughout) 1. the known symptom reproduces in three lines python import numpy as np, warnings with warnings.catch warnings(record=true) as w: warnings.simplefilter("always") np.identity(15) @ np.identity(15) print([str(x.message) for x in w]) ['divide by zero encountered in matmul', 'overflow encountered in matmul', 'invalid value encountered in matmul'] — result is correct 2. the corruption in a scientific pipeline we have a float64 array of shape (255985,) — an owning copy, never assigned to anywhere in our source. across a loop that calls scipy.spatial.convexhull and then all pts @ hull eqs[:, :3].t + hull eqs[:, 3], that array's contents change between iterations . at the affected sites all inputs and outputs of the matmul are finite (|hull eqs| 42,130,944) with no error and no warning other than the fpe noise above. 3. it behaves as heap-layout dependence adding a statement that merely holds references to the arrays — keepalive = (a f, c f, d f, v f), computing nothing — makes the corruption vanish and restores the correct result. so does reversing an unrelated loop. any instrumentation that closes over the array suppresses it, which made it self-defeating to measure. 4. version isolation holding scipy at 1.17.1 and moving numpy alone: | numpy | identity-matmul warnings | our result | |---|---|---| | 2.2.0 | 3 warnings | corrupt | | 2.3.3 | none | correct | | 2.3.4 | none | correct | under 2.3.4 the result is byte-identical across clean / keepalive / reversed-loop builds. we have pinned numpy>=2.3.4. question: was the out-of-bounds write fixed deliberately between 2.2.0 and 2.3.3, or incidentally? if the underlying accelerate integration issue persists in any form, the harmless-warnings framing in 28790/ 29820 understates the risk — this silently changed a number that people make decisions on.

bug: series.str.pad/center/ljust/rjust with a negative width raises arrowinvalid on pyarrow-backed strings what happened : series.str.pad, series.str.center, series.str.ljust and series.str.rjust raise pyarrow.lib.arrowinvalid: negative buffer resize when width is negative and the dtype is a pyarrow-backed string dtype. reproduction (reproduced on 3.0.6 with pyarrow 25.0.1): python import pandas as pd s = pd.series([ab, +ab, , café], dtype=pd.stringdtype(pyarrow)) s.str.ljust(-5) pyarrow.lib.arrowinvalid: negative buffer resize: -70 center, rjust and pad raise the same error. the equivalent calls on object dtype, str dtype with python storage, and python's own str.ljust/str.center all return the strings unchanged, since a non-positive width is a no-op in python. expected behavior : negative (and zero) widths should return the values unchanged, matching object dtype and python string semantics. root cause (from reading the code): arrowstringarraymixin. str pad in pandas/core/arrays/ arrow string mixins.py passes width straight to pc.utf8 lpad/pc.utf8 rpad/pc.utf8 center for pyarrow >= 17/21. these kernels size their output buffer from width and raise arrowinvalid for negative values. unlike the elementwise fallback paths (which call the python str methods), the kernel path has no guard. notes : - this is pre-existing and present in released 3.0.x (unlike the str.zfill regression on main from 66339, tracked in 69486). - the same family of kernels is used for index.str as well. installed versions : pandas 3.0.6, pyarrow 25.0.1, python 3.13

bug: .str and .dt accessors raise on dictionary-encoded arrowdtype on current main, the .str and .dt accessors reject series backed by dictionary-encoded arrowdtype, even though the equivalent plain arrowdtype (and categorical, for .str) work fine. repro: python import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa import datetime .str on dictionary-encoded strings s = pd.series( pd.array(['a', 'b', 'a'], dtype=pd.arrowdtype(pa.dictionary(pa.int32(), pa.string()))) ) s.str.upper() attributeerror: can only use .str accessor with string values, not unknown-array .dt on dictionary-encoded timestamps arr = pa.dictionaryarray.from arrays( pa.array([0, 1, 0], type=pa.int32()), pa.array([datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1), datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2)], type=pa.timestamp('us')), ) s2 = pd.series(pd.arrays.arrowextensionarray(arr)) s2.dt.year attributeerror: can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values expected: both accessors work, decoding through the dictionary the way categorical does (pd.series(pd.categorical(['a', 'b', 'a'])).str.upper() works fine). what i found reading the code: - .str: stringmethods. validate does values = getattr(data, "categories", data) to blow up categoricals before inferring. arrowextensionarray has no .categories, so lib.infer dtype sees the raw arrow array and returns "unknown-array", which is not in the allowed list. - .dt: combineddatetimelikeproperties. init gates the arrow path on data.dtype.kind in "mm". arrowdtype.kind only returns "m" when pa.types.is timestamp(self.pyarrow dtype) is true, which is false for dictionary types, so it falls back to the numpy object kind "o". so both accessors need to look through dictionary encoding to the value type, similar to how categoricals are handled. environment: pandas main (3.2.0.dev1), pyarrow 25.0.1, python 3.12, linux.

if (armed && !fired && size == target size) { fired = 1; fprintf(stderr, "[failmalloc] returning null for size=%zu\n", size); return null; } return real(size); } python repro.py import ctypes, faulthandler import pandas as pd faulthandler.enable() frame = pd.dataframe({"t": pd.to datetime([1616409000123] 50, unit="ms").as unit("ms")}) ctypes.cdll("./failmalloc.so").failmalloc arm(ctypes.c size t(42)) print(frame.to json(orient="records", date format="iso")) $ pythonmalloc=malloc ld preload=./failmalloc.so python repro.py [failmalloc] returning null for size=42 fatal python error: segmentation fault current thread 0x0000004002102f00 [python] (most recent call first): file ".../pandas/io/json/ json.py", line 292 in write file ".../pandas/io/json/ json.py", line 241 in to json file ".../pandas/core/generic.py", line 2623 in to json file "repro.py", line 12 in current thread's c stack trace (most recent call first): ... binary file ".../pandas/ libs/json.cpython-314-x86 64-linux-gnu.so", at +0x8ae0 issue description a failed allocation inside the iso datetime conversion is dereferenced as a null string instead of raising, because the encoder's null signal is enc->errormsg and this path never sets it: 1. int64toiso (pandas/ libs/src/datetime/date conversions.c) allocates the output buffer and returns null after pyerr nomemory() if that fails. it also returns null when make iso 8601 datetime fails. 2. npydatetimetoisocallback (pandas/ libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objtojson.c) forwards that result unchanged, without setting ((jsonobjectencoder )tc->encoder)->errormsg. 3. ultrajsonenc.c, case jt utf8, tests only enc->errormsg before using the value: c value = enc->getstringvalue(obj, &tc, &szlen); if (enc->errormsg) { enc->endtypecontext(obj, &tc); return; } buffer reserve(enc, reserve string(szlen)); ... if (!buffer escapestringunvalidated(enc, value, value + szlen)) { so buffer escapestringunvalidated runs on value == null, which segfaults. sibling callbacks in the same file follow the opposite convention and do set errormsg before returning null — pytimetojson and the type-check branch of pydatetimetoisocallback both do ((jsonobjectencoder )tc->encoder)->errormsg = "";. two more callbacks look to have the same gap as the one above: - npytimedeltatoisocallback forwards int64toisoduration, which has the same two null returns. - pydatetimetoisocallback sets errormsg for the type check, but forwards the result of pydatetimetoiso (which has several null returns) unchecked. this looks like a remaining instance of the class of bug reported in 66356 and fixed by 66357 and 66797 — neither of those passes touched the iso datetime/timedelta callbacks. reproduced on 3.0.5 and on main at 3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e, both python 3.14 / linux-x86 64. 3.0.6 contains no changes to these files. for context on why this isn't only theoretical: we hit a sigsegv in pandas/ libs/json...so beneath dataframe.to json(orient="records", date format="iso") in ci, serialising a 45k-row frame with a tz-aware datetime64[ms, utc] column under memory pressure from several parallel test workers. i can't attribute that crash with certainty — the shipped extension module is stripped, so the c stack has no symbols — but this is the only unchecked-null path i could find on it, and the per-value allocation count makes a transient failure plausible. expected behavior memoryerror (or the relevant exception) propagates to the caller, consistent with how other allocation failures in the encoder are handled — e.g. buffer realloc calls seterror(null, enc, "could not reserve memory block"). setting errormsg in the three callbacks before returning null would be enough; enh: add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations feature type - [x] adding new functionality to pandas - [x] changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] removing existing functionality in pandas problem description long-running series.apply() and dataframe.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination. currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. if the python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed. it would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution. for example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. if execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows. this could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as api requests, machine learning inference, llm calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations. the goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards. feature description result = df[“column”].apply( expensive function, checkpoint=“apply checkpoint.pkl”, checkpoint every=10, ) alternative solutions for i, value in df["column"].items(): df.at[i, "result"] = expensive function(value) if i % 10 == 0: df.to pickle("checkpoint.pkl") additional context no response

api: should the supports 2d contract require repeat(axis=...)? extensiondtype. supports 2d documents what a third-party array must provide to declare itself 2-d capable (pandas/core/dtypes/base.py): > arrays that support 2d values should: > > - implement array.reshape > - subclass the dim2compattests in tests.extension.base > - concat same type should support axis keyword > - reduce and reductions should support axis keyword repeat is not on that list, and the base implementation actively rejects an axis: python pandas/core/arrays/base.py def repeat(self, repeats, axis: axisint | none = none) -> self: nv.validate repeat((), {"axis": axis}) while the backing-array implementation both defaults to and honours one: python pandas/ libs/arrays.pyx def repeat(self, repeats, axis: int | np.integer = 0): in-tree this never shows, because the only dtypes with supports 2d = true are datetimetzdtype and perioddtype, whose arrays are ndarraybacked. a third-party array that implements the four documented requirements and inherits extensionarray.repeat would raise valueerror: the 'axis' parameter is not supported in the pandas implementation of repeat(). this matters because the gate internals use to decide "may i treat this as 2-d" is python def is 1d only ea dtype(dtype) -> bool: return isinstance(dtype, extensiondtype) and not dtype. supports 2d so anything reaching a 2-d code path is exactly the supports 2d audience. broadcasting a 1-d value across several columns wants value.reshape(1, -1).repeat(ncols, axis=0), which works for both in-tree types and for any ndarraybacked array, but is not something the documented contract entitles pandas to call. two ways to resolve it: 1. add repeat with axis support to the supports 2d requirements, and relax the base signature/validation for 2-d-capable arrays. this documents what pandas already needs and costs existing third-party authors nothing until they opt into supports 2d. 2. treat repeat(axis=) as out of contract and require internals to spell 2-d broadcasting with only the four documented operations, e.g. value.repeat(ncols).reshape(-1, ncols). that is contract-clean but produces a c-contiguous result where the current spelling gives an f-contiguous one, which changes the stored block's layout on the numpy path. no in-tree caller passes axis= to an extensionarray's repeat today, so nothing is broken right now; this is about whether such a call is legitimate going forward.

bug/depr: low memory keyword in read csv low memory=true (the default) can give incorrect results in corner cases, which is the reason why the keyword exists. minimal example: n = 65536 rows in the first internal chunk of an 8-column table data = ( "a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h
" + "1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1
" n chunk 1 -> int64 + f"{2 64 - 1},1,1,1,1,1,1,1
" chunk 2 -> uint64 + f"{2 64 - 2},1,1,1,1,1,1,1
" ) res = pd.read csv(stringio(data))["a"] exp = pd.read csv(stringio(data), low memory=false)["a"] assert exp.iloc[-1] != exp.iloc[-2] assert res.iloc[-1] != res.iloc[-2] <- fails because of unwanted casting in the low memory=true case, we do dtype inference in chunks. in cases where different chunks get different dtypes, the concat does a cast which can be lossy. low memory=false avoids that by doing the dtype inference on the whole column instead of in chunks. the alternative i think we should consider is to detect when this casting occurs and then re-parse (with usecols restricted to the affected column) in the low memory=false mode. then we get the correct result and don't need the user-facing keyword. the downside is a perf penalty in these corner cases. passing low memory=false disables the parallel path, which is what brought this to my attention.

depr: cache dates in read csv a review of github code shows that cache dates is the least-used keyword, with 8.4k uses (compared to 1.01m of dtype). moreover, the cases where cache dates=false improves performance are fewer and fewer now that iso cases get excluded by default. i think we should deprecate the keyword and have a slightly simpler api. cc @mroeschke

api: select dtypes we made a bunch of changes to select dtypes in july. i advocate reverting the most niche use cases to simplify the code. summarizing the support that was added : 1) passing an extensiondtype class matches every instance of that dtype (instead of raising) 2) passing a partially-specified intervaldtype e.g. intervaldtype(np.int64) (without specifying "closed") matches all intervaldtypes that match that partial specification. 3) passing a partially-specified categoricaldtype e.g. categoricaldtype(my categories, ordered=none) matches all categoricaldtypes with those categories regardless of orderedness. summarizing the behavior that changed as bugfixes 4) passing a specific dtype e.g. np.dtype(np.int64) matches exactly that dtype, not every integer dtype. 5) passing a type (that isn't an extesnsiondtype subclass) raises instead of matching object dtype. 6) passing eadtypes like int64dtype() would match numpy integer dtypes. summarizing deprecations 7) deprecated accepting "datetimetz" and "datetime64tz" since item 1 now means you can pass pd.datetimetzdtype explicitly. i advocate reverting items 2 and 3 before 3.1 is released, as they contribute a lot of complexity for very niche use cases. also we don't have a mechanism to do similar partial-specification matching for datetimetzdtype or 3rd party eas.

unbind → setitem(undefined) fires editor events synchronously | | src/vs/editor/browser/widget/multidiffeditor/virtualizeditemmanager.ts | root cause (producer) | l228-l247: clearbinding() disposes the binding with no guard; the autorun at l149-l155 re-enters it during that synchronous dispose | repro steps this is a timing-dependent re-entrancy, reproduced by closing/hiding a multi-diff item whose diff editor fires a synchronous model-change event during disposal. 1. open a multi-diff editor (e.g. a source-control / agent sessions diff view) with at least one visible diff item that has loaded its diff model. 2. trigger disposal of a bound, visible item — close the editor, switch the active editor, or scroll the item out while it is being cleared. 3. during clearbinding(), binding.dispose() → unbind() → setitem(undefined) → editor.setdiffmodel(null) fires an editor event that re-enters the item's autorun, calling clearbinding() a second time on the same binding. 4. the nested unbind() sees viewmodel === undefined, undefined !== item, and throws bugindicatingerror. how the fix works chosen approach — src/vs/editor/browser/widget/multidiffeditor/virtualizeditemmanager.ts, managedvirtualizeditem. clearbinding(): add an isclearingbinding guard flag. on entry, if a clear is already in progress the method returns immediately; it is simply no longer reached on this re-entrant path because the duplicate dispose never starts. why this is correct : the guard makes the unsupported "dispose during dispose" ordering unrepresentable at the producer, which is the lifecycle-fix priority (reorder/serialize the producer's state mutations), instead of teaching the consumer unbind() to tolerate inconsistent state. no logservice.error or telemetry path is removed, and no try/catch swallows the error. alternatives considered : - guard inside unbind() / diffeditoritembinding.dispose() by comparing viewmodel and returning early — rejected: that is a crash-site guard that silently tolerates double-dispose and would mask the same re-entrancy for every other binding type, hiding the producer bug. - defer editor.setdiffmodel(null) to a microtask so events do not fire synchronously — rejected: broader behavioral change to editor teardown timing with higher regression risk than serializing the clear. recommended owner @hediet — author of the multi-diff virtualization refactor (10de1b93436) and the follow-up lifecycle fixes; fix: guard terminal scroll operations before renderer is attached (fixes 339313) summary terminalinstance.sendtext() (reached via runcommand) calls this.xterm?.scrolltobottom(), which forwards to xtermterminal.scrolltobottom() → bundled xterm.js scrolltobottom → scrolllines → get dimensions. when this runs against a terminal whose renderer has not been initialized yet (the xterm instance exists but attachtoelement/raw.open() has not run, so the render service and its dimensions object do not exist), xterm.js throws typeerror: cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'dimensions'). 389 users / 448 hits across windows, mac, and linux on 1.140.0. fixes microsoft/vscode\ 339313 recommended reviewer: @meganrogge culprit commit no single culprit commit — this is a pre-existing latent race that surfaced as a new stable bucket in 1.140.0. the entry path sendtext → scrolltobottom (terminalinstance.ts line, authored 2022) and the xtermterminal.scrolltobottom wrapper (authored 2021) both long predate the baseline, and git blame on the throwing call sites points to commits years older than the regression window. the anomaly is a timing/re-bucketing shift (bundled xterm.js scroll internals), not a logic change in a commit within the 1.139.1→1.140.0 range. | field | value | |-------|-------| | commit | not identified — pre-existing | | author | n/a | | pr | n/a | | message | trigger | l1422: this.xterm?.scrolltobottom(); inside sendtext, which can run before the instance is attached to the dom | repro steps this is a timing-dependent race, so it is non-deterministic: 1. trigger sendtext/runcommand on a terminalinstance whose xterm object has been created but not yet attached to the dom (attachtoelement / raw.open() not yet called) — e.g. programmatic command execution against a backgrounded or just-created terminal, or a restart that re-creates the xterm before re-attaching. 2. sendtext reaches this.xterm?.scrolltobottom(). 3. xterm.js walks scrolltobottom → scrolllines → get dimensions and dereferences the render service's dimensions, which is undefined because the renderer was never opened. 4. typeerror: cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'dimensions') is thrown. increase likelihood by executing commands against terminals immediately on creation or during a restart, before layout/attach completes. how the fix works chosen approach (src/vs/workbench/contrib/terminal/browser/xterm/xtermterminal.ts): add an early-return guard if (!this. attached) { return; } to the renderer-delegating scroll wrappers (scrolltobottom, scrollupline, scrolldownline, scrolluppage, scrolldownpage, scrolltotop). attached is set only after attachtoelement runs this.raw.open(container) — the exact point at which xterm.js constructs its render service and the dimensions object the throwing code reads. the producer of the violating value is bundled third-party xterm.js, which cannot be modified in this repo, so the fix is placed at vs code's own boundary wrapper and gated on the real lifecycle signal ( attached) rather than suppressing the symptom at the crash site. scrolling a terminal that has no renderer yet is a no-op anyway, so the guard changes no user-visible behavior. the guard is not a try/catch and does not touch any logservice.error path. alternatives considered : - wrapping the scrolltobottom call in terminalinstance.sendtext in try/catch — rejected because it hides the error from telemetry instead of preventing the invalid lifecycle call, and would mask other legitimate failures. - optional-chaining into xterm.js internals (this.raw.scrolltobottom?.()) — rejected because the method is always callable; the undefined value is deep inside xterm.js's render service, unreachable from the wrapper, so chaining would not prevent the throw. recommended owner @meganrogge — terminal area owner; authored the sendtext → scrolltobottom call path and is an active core maintainer with write claude agent host: between-turn 'resume rebuild' kills subagents and drops replies summary. the agent host sometimes discards a healthy, live claude sdk session between turns and rebuilds it from transcript on the next turn. any in-process background subagents (agent tool tasks) are killed mid-flight by the rebuild, and the assistant's reply is sent but not rendered to the agents window. mechanism (read from the minified out/vs/platform/agenthost/node/agenthostmain.js): claudesdkpipeline attaches a "rematerializer" which rebindquery(reason) invokes whenever desired state drifts from applied state — rebindforrestart(), rebindforclienttools() (client tool-set changes mark tooldiff.markdirty()), mcp launch-enablement revision changes, additional-directory changes, and transport switches. the rematerializer starts a fresh sdk session with isresume: true and the live one is discarded, logging [claude] session : resume rebuild agent=(none). consequences observed (agenthost.log, 2026-10-02, hostprocessagems continuous across the event — i.e. no host restart): 1. seven running background subagents died and reported on the next turn as "didn't finish before the previous session ended". 2. their stopped-notices ran as their own tiny turn (queue yielded → result 23 ms later), which closed the pending user turn; the assistant's actual reply then logged as result for sdkuuid=undefined and was never rendered to the user. 3. related variant: a user message sent mid-turn is folded in as steering (injectsteering: enqueued id=…, queue yielded … steeringpendingid=…); the turn again closes on the first result, dropping the reply to the second message. log signature sequence for one occurrence: 11:03:42 [claude: ] result for sdkuuid=request 49dfe40f-… ← turn ends normally, 7 subagents still running 11:06:01 [claude] session : resume rebuild agent=(none) ← between turns; kills the subagents 11:06:03 [claude: ] queue yielded sdkuuid=request 26892093-… 11:06:03 [claude: ] result for sdkuuid=request 26892093-… ← 23 ms stopped-notice turn 11:08:56 [claude: ] result for sdkuuid=undefined ← the real reply, never rendered expected behavior. a between-turn rebind should be deferred while background subagents are running (or hand them off to the new session), and an sdk-initiated notice turn must never consume the pending user turn's result slot. environment. vs code 1.139.1, linux; anthropic.claude-code 2.1.284. the 1.140 release notes mention no fix, and no chat.agenthost. setting governs rebind behavior. related, but distinct: 332073 (replies lost after background subagents complete — analyzed there as a turnid === undefined discard), 337904 (mid-turn steering messages never shown), pr 326270 (removes the rematerializer pattern; does not claim to preserve running subagents across a rebuild), pr 336753 (renders sdk-initiated turns when the prompt queue is empty).

copilot token refresh that finishes after an account switch is adopted for the new account found while fixing 339239. problem a copilot token fetch that started for one github account can finish after the user has switched accounts, and the result is then stored as the current token for the new account. the post-fetch guard in vscodecopilottokenmanager.getcopilottoken (extensions/copilot/src/platform/authentication/vscode-node/copilottokenmanager.ts) only checks that the auth provider and the github enterprise uri haven't changed. it doesn't check that the github account is still the same. baseauthenticationservice.getcopilottoken then stores the result and fires ondidcopilottokenchange. sequence 1. account a is signed in, and its copilot token refresh is in flight. 2. the user switches to account b. b's token mint fails (network error, enterprisemanagederror, ...), and ondidauthenticationchange fires with no token. 3. a's refresh finishes. its token is stored and ondidcopilottokenchange fires while the session is b. impact - requests made while signed in as b use a's copilot token until it expires or the identity changes again. - anything that evaluates policy from the current token reads a's entitlements for b. one example is byok provider registration (byokcontrib), which re-applies policy on ondidcopilottokenchange. suggested fix tie each token result to the account (or an identity generation) that started the fetch. discard stale results before they update the token store or fire token change events.

copilot agent host: every /.copilot/instructions file is in the system prompt twice - copilot chat extension version: built into vs code 1.140.0 (bundled @github/copilot 1.0.73, @github/copilot-sdk-win32-x64 1.0.15-preview.4) - vs code version: 1.140.0 (commit 07f806f999227108933c2e30515b26eecc1fda74, x64) - os version: windows 11 enterprise 26200 - feature (e.g. agent/edit/ask mode): agent mode, agent host session (copilot cli in vs code) - selected model (e.g. gpt 4.1, claude 3.7 sonnet): claude-sonnet-5 - logs: not attached; events.jsonl holds the full private instructions. the relevant system.message excerpt can be shared on request. steps to reproduce: 1. put user instruction files in /.copilot/instructions/, e.g. a.instructions.md: markdown --- name: 'rule a' description: 'test rule a' applyto: ' ' --- rule a always say marker-a when asked for the marker. 2. optionally add a project instruction in .github/instructions/p.instructions.md of the open folder, same format. 3. quit vs code completely, start it, open the folder, start a new copilot cli session and send any prompt. 4. open /.copilot/session-state/ /events.jsonl and look at the content of the system.message event. expected: each instruction file once. actual: every file from /.copilot/instructions appears twice , byte-identical including its frontmatter: first together with the project instruction files, then again on its own, directly after. /.copilot/copilot-instructions.md and the project's .github/instructions files appear once. the model notices it too ("some instructions appear twice in the prompt"). the local agent loads each file once. things that do not change it: - chat.instructionsfileslocations with " /.copilot/instructions": false (the local agent stops loading the files; the agent host session still has them twice) - /.copilot/instructions as a real folder instead of a symlink - a full restart of vs code (rules out the instruction cache) likely cause (from the bundled, minified code): 1. the runtime reads /instructions/ / .instructions.md itself and merges the files into one source: { id: "user-copilot-instructions", label: ".copilot/instructions", type: "vscode", location: "user" }. 2. the agent host (out/vs/platform/agenthost/node/agenthostmain.js) runs its own customization discovery: discoverrules calls rpc.instructions.discover, turns the sources into rule customizations, and lme turns those into a plugin. only rules that are alwaysapply and whose name ends in .md are skipped (which is why copilot-instructions.md appears once). buildsessionconfig then passes instructiondirectories: lz(snapshot.plugins.flatmap(p => p.instructions)), i.e. the folders of those rule files, which includes the user instructions folder. 3. the runtime loads each file of an instructiondirectories entry as a separate source: type: "vscode", id: "vscode-instructions/external/ " (outside cwd / git root), label: " [external]". 4. the final dedup hashes content only for type home, repo and model, and otherwise dedups by id. the merged user source and the per-file sources are both vscode and have different ids, so both are kept. project files get the same id vscode-instructions/ on both paths and are deduped. i could not confirm from the minified code which discovery source makes the agent host include the user folder in step 2; steps 1, 3 and 4 are in the @github/copilot js bundle, and the same ids (user-copilot-instructions, vscode-instructions/external) are in the sdk's runtime.node. impact: about 9 kb of duplicated context per request with 12 small instruction files; no functional error. possible fixes: - agent host: do not pass folders the runtime already discovers itself (user /instructions) as instructiondirectories. - runtime: dedup vscode sources by resolved file path or content as well, or skip files of an additional directory that are already part of user-copilot-instructions.

git.worktreesymlinkfolders: removing a worktree deletes symlink target does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: yes report issue' dialog can assist with this. --> - vs code version: 1.140.0 - os version: windows 10 steps to reproduce: 1. enable the git.worktreesymlinkfolders setting: 2. create a git worktree for a repository. 3. verify that the configured folder inside the worktree is a symbolic link pointing to the corresponding folder in the main worktree. 4. remove the worktree using vs code's git worktree ui/command. 5. observe that the target directory pointed to by the symbolic link is deleted instead of the symbolic link itself. expected behavior: when removing a worktree, vs code should remove the symbolic link created by git.worktreesymlinkfolders, leaving the target directory and its contents untouched. actual behavior: vs code follows the symbolic link during worktree removal and deletes the contents of the target directory instead of removing only the symbolic link. this can result in data outside of the worktree being unintentionally deleted. additional information: the issue appears to be specific to the handling of symbolic links created by git.worktreesymlinkfolders during worktree cleanup/removal. the symbolic link itself should be removed using an operation that does not follow the link.

git: stash messages appear garbled when i18n.logoutputencoding is set does this issue occur when all extensions are disabled?: yes - vs code version: 1.140.0 / main - os version: windows / macos / linux in extensions/git/src/git.ts, repository.getstashes() runs git stash list without forcing the output encoding to utf-8. if a repository or global gitconfig sets i18n.logoutputencoding (or i18n.commitencoding), non-ascii stash messages appear as corrupted characters (mojibake) in the source control stashes view and related quickpicks. this is a follow-up to 331086 / pr 331087, which added -c i18n.logoutputencoding=utf-8 to log, logfile, blame2, getcommit, and showchanges, but missed getstashes. steps to reproduce: 1. initialize a repository with non-utf-8 encoding configured: sh git init test-repo cd test-repo git commit --allow-empty -m "initial" echo "sample" > file.txt git add file.txt git config i18n.commitencoding euc-jp git config i18n.logoutputencoding euc-jp 2. create a stash with a non-ascii message (e.g., euc-jp text): sh git stash push -m "$(printf '\xa5\xc6\xa5\xb9\xa5\xc8 stash')" 3. open the folder in vs code with extensions disabled (code --disable-extensions .). 4. inspect the stash in the source control panel or via git: pop stash.... expected behavior: the stash message is decoded and displayed as on master: テスト stash. actual behavior: the stash message displays as on master: ƥ stash. direct cli comparison: sh current git.ts behavior (garbled output) $ git stash list stash@{0}: on master: ƥ stash expected git.ts behavior (with -c i18n.logoutputencoding=utf-8) $ git -c i18n.logoutputencoding=utf-8 stash list stash@{0}: on master: テスト stash cause: in extensions/git/src/git.ts:3022: typescript async getstashes(): promise { const result = await this.exec(['stash', 'list', --format=${stash format}, '-z']); return parsegitstashes(result.stdout.trim()); } because this.exec() decodes stdout using bufferresult.stdout.tostring('utf8') (line 657), git stash list needs -c i18n.logoutputencoding=utf-8 prepended to ensure git converts the commit message to utf-8 before writing to stdout: typescript const result = await this.exec(['-c', 'i18n.logoutputencoding=utf-8', 'stash', 'list', --format=${stash format}, '-z']);

reverse provider migration (provider back to regular service) is untested and converges only by accident "this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report." context 14264 fixed the forward migration: a deployed service switched to provider: now has its stale replicas condemned by the plan before the relay takes over the service's canonical container name. this issue tracks the mirror direction , which is currently untested: a provider-backed service (with a standing relay) switched back to a regular container service. what happens today (by accident, not by contract) after the reverse migration, the relay container is still there, holding the service's canonical name ( - -1), its network alias, and standard compose labels — including a confighashlabel whose value is the relay identity (image+routes hash), stamped so label-driven commands treat the relay as the service. on the next up, the reconciler — now on the regular-service path — observes the relay as replica 1 with a config hash that cannot match the service's expected hash, and recreates it like any diverged container. the outcome (relay replaced by a real service container) is plausibly correct, but it holds through a coincidence of label choices, not through any stated semantics: - nothing distinguishes "diverged replica" from "leftover relay" in the plan or its events (the user sees a recreate, not a migration); - the recreate path was never designed with a relay as input (e.g. inherit-volumes decisions, notrecreated-style expectations, the relay's own lifecycle normally belonging to ensureservicerelay); - no test locks any of this — a future change to relay labels (confighashlabel = identity) or to the recreate gate could silently break the reverse migration with the same symptom class as the forward one (name conflict on - -1). ask define the reverse-migration semantics explicitly (most likely: a relay observed for a non-provider service is condemned, mirroring 14264's forward rule) and lock it with an e2e scenario — the fromfile model switch introduced by 14264 makes the scenario symmetrical to testprovidermigration (deploy with provider:, switch back to a regular service, up, assert recreated and the service serving its own workload).

pre start hooks: per replica: true is accepted by the schema but always rejected at runtime what this issue is about pre start hooks support a per replica attribute in the compose-spec model (types.prestarthook.perreplica, compose-go's types/hooks.go): "runs the hook once per service replica instead of once per service." docker/compose's engine, however, does not implement it: runprestart (pkg/compose/pre start.go) validates every declared hook up front and rejects the whole service if any hook sets per replica: true: go for i, hook := range service.prestart { if hook.perreplica { return fmt.errorf("service %q pre start[%d]: per replica is not yet supported; remove per replica or set it to false", service.name, i) } } so today, per replica: true is accepted by the loader/schema but always a hard error at runtime — there is no path to actually use it. illustration yaml services: app: image: alpine command: sleep infinity deploy: replicas: 3 pre start: - image: alpine command: ["sh", "-c", "echo initializing replica"] per replica: true console $ docker compose up -d service "app" pre start[0]: per replica is not yet supported; remove per replica or set it to false the only way to get this compose file to run at all today is to drop per replica: true, at which point the hook runs once for the whole service (against the lowest-numbered replica only, per the current one-hook-one-runner model) instead of once per replica — a different, sometimes unacceptable behavior for hooks that need to prepare per-replica state (e.g. per-replica config files, per-replica volume initialization). suggested scope for an implementation the reconciliation-plan work in 14221 (pre start hook runners as first-class plan resources) planned one createhookcontainer operation per declared hook , targeted at a single resolved replica. supporting per replica: true would mean planning one runner per hook × per replica instead, with: - a deterministic name/label scheme distinguishing replicas (e.g. extending the existing com.docker.compose.hook-index label with a replica index, or a dedicated label), - volumesfrom resolved against that replica rather than the lowest-numbered one, - the corresponding execution-phase change in runprestart/execprestarthook to run and account for one runner per replica. this issue only tracks the feature gap; the reconciliation-plan groundwork from 14221 already discussed and worked around it (see its planprestarthookrunners, which explicitly skips planning entirely for a service with any per replica: true hook, to avoid orphaning runners that could never execute).

provider relay cannot reach loopback-bound published endpoints on a standalone linux engine description the provider extension lets a provider announce service endpoints with publish-endpoint messages; compose then deploys a relay container carrying the service's name on the project networks, so dependent services reach the provider's resource at the compose-native address ( the relay rewrites host-relative upstreams (localhost, loopback or unspecified addresses) to host.docker.internal (pkg/compose/relay.go, relayupstream), provisioned through extrahosts: host.docker.internal:host-gateway on engines that do not resolve it natively. this transport is not equivalent across platforms when the provider's endpoint is bound to the host's loopback interface: - on docker desktop (all oses), host.docker.internal traffic is proxied by the vm through the host's own loopback, so a 127.0.0.1-bound endpoint is reachable from the relay. - on a standalone linux engine , host-gateway resolves to the bridge gateway address. a connection from the relay container arrives on the bridge interface with that destination address, which a listener bound only to 127.0.0.1 (or ::1) cannot accept. the endpoint publishes successfully, the relay deploys, and dependent services then get connection failures at the compose-native address. the consequence for provider authors: a published endpoint must be bound to an address reachable from the bridge (in practice the wildcard) to work on standalone linux engines, which exposes the port on every host interface — or bound to loopback to stay off the lan, which limits the provider to docker desktop. the bundled example provider documents and works around this by binding 0.0.0.0 (docs/examples/provider.go): go // all interfaces, not loopback: on a plain linux engine host-gateway // is the bridge ip, which cannot reach a host loopback bind. server := exec.command(os.args[0], "serve-demo", "0.0.0.0:0") reproduction on a standalone linux engine (not docker desktop), run a provider that binds its endpoint to 127.0.0.1: and publishes it, with a dependent service consuming 1. docker compose up succeeds — the endpoint is published and the relay starts. 2. the dependent service's requests to the compose-native address fail to connect. the e2e suite does not cover this case: testproviderpublishendpoint (pkg/e2e/providers test.go) exercises the full relay path on linux ci, but with the example provider's wildcard bind. a variant with a loopback-bound endpoint fails on a standalone linux engine today.

stop/kill/pause/logs/rm/down/ps/events silently no-op or give a raw error when targeting a job name "this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report." what this issue is about pr 14093 fixed create and start so that targeting a declared jobs: entry (instead of a services: entry) gives a clear, actionable error instead of compose-go's raw no such service: — and, when compose project name is set, instead of silently doing nothing. that fix was scoped to create/start only. the same underlying helper, projectorname (cmd/compose/compose.go), also backs stop, kill, pause, unpause, logs, rm, down, ps and events — none of which got the fix, so they still show both problems: 1. confusing raw error — without compose project name, targeting a job by name surfaces compose-go's generic no such service: instead of a message pointing the user at docker compose run. 2. silent no-op — with compose project name set, projectorname falls back to a label-driven, file-less project on any project-load failure (including "no such service"), swallowing the error entirely. since a job that was never run left no container behind, the label-driven command finds nothing to act on and exits 0 as if it had succeeded. illustration given: yaml services: web: image: nginx jobs: migrate: image: alpine command: ["echo", "migrating"] triggers: manual: true without compose project name: console $ docker compose stop migrate no such service: migrate nothing here tells the user migrate is actually a valid job name and that docker compose run migrate is what they meant. compare with start, fixed in 14093: console $ docker compose start migrate job "migrate" can only be triggered with "docker compose run" with compose project name set — as ci pipelines and scripts commonly do: console $ export compose project name=myproj $ docker compose stop migrate; echo "exit=$?" exit=0 no error, no output: stop silently did nothing. suggested fix generalize the jobtargeterr/unselectedjobs helpers introduced in 14093 (cmd/compose/run.go) to the other projectorname callers — or fold the check directly into projectorname so every caller benefits at once, rather than repeating the wiring per command.

add opt-in ordered replica startup with health-based readiness description description docker compose supports ordering between different services using depends on and condition: service healthy. however, this ordering cannot be applied between replicas of the same service. for example: yaml services: app: image: example/app deploy: replicas: 3 healthcheck: test: ["cmd", "/app/healthcheck.sh"] interval: 5s timeout: 3s retries: 20 compose starts all three replicas without waiting for one replica to become healthy before starting the next. although container start api calls may be issued sequentially, application initialization occurs concurrently. desired behavior i would like an opt-in mode that starts replicas in sequence and waits for each replica to become ready: text app-1 starts ↓ app-1 post start hooks complete ↓ app-1 becomes healthy ↓ app-2 starts ↓ app-2 post start hooks complete ↓ app-2 becomes healthy ↓ app-3 starts this would provide behavior similar to chaining separately declared services: yaml services: app-0: image: example/app app-1: image: example/app depends on: app-0: condition: service healthy app-2: image: example/app depends on: app-1: condition: service healthy that workaround loses the benefits of compose replicas and requires manually duplicating each service. suggested configuration the exact syntax is open for discussion. one possible configuration is: yaml services: app: image: example/app deploy: replicas: 3 startup config: order: sequential condition: service healthy failure action: pause startup config should be optional. when it is not provided, docker compose should preserve its existing replica startup behavior without requiring an explicit order: parallel setting. this makes ordered, health-gated startup opt-in and maintains backward compatibility with existing compose files. expected semantics when ordered startup is enabled: 1. start the lowest-numbered missing replica. 2. run and complete its post start hooks. 3. wait until its healthcheck reports healthy. 4. start the next replica. 5. stop the sequence if a replica exits, becomes unhealthy, a hook fails, or the readiness timeout is exceeded. 6. apply the same behavior during initial up and later scale-up operations. 7. leave the current behavior unchanged when the option is omitted. a service using condition: service healthy should require a healthcheck. a separate condition could support applications that only need the previous replica to be running. use case this is useful for stateful or clustered applications where each member must register, join the cluster, initialize data, update shared configuration, or elect a leader before another member starts. in our case, multiple replicas start concurrently and attempt to update the cluster configuration at the same time. two clients can read the same available port before either client finishes writing its configuration. both clients are then assigned the same port, resulting in a configuration mismatch error and preventing the cluster from starting correctly. the expected sequence is: text app-1 starts ↓ app-1 updates the cluster configuration ↓ app-1 completes its post start work and becomes healthy ↓ app-2 starts and receives the next available port ↓ app-2 becomes healthy ↓ app-3 starts environment docker compose version text docker compose version v5.3.1 docker post start / pre stop hook stdout/stderr is discarded in up -d and up --wait — only attached mode shows it, and nothing persists it description service lifecycle hooks (post start, pre stop) run their command, but their stdout/stderr is only forwarded to the terminal when docker compose up runs attached (foreground). in every non-interactive form — up -d, up --wait — the hook output is dropped: - success: completely silent, no indication the hook ran. - failure: a single summary line on stderr ( hook exited with status ) plus a non-zero exit code, but the hook's own output (the actual error from the migration tool / script) is never shown. the output is also not recoverable after the fact from any other source: | source | has hook output? | |---------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------| | docker compose up (attached) | ✅ streamed, prefixed svc-1 -> \| | | docker compose up -d | ❌ (only hook exited with status n on failure) | | docker compose up --wait | ❌ same as -d | | docker compose logs / docker logs | ❌ | | docker inspect | ❌ | | docker events payload | ❌ | | dockerd logs (journalctl -u docker) | ❌ | this makes lifecycle hooks effectively undebuggable for any tool or ci pipeline that shells out docker compose up -d (the standard non-interactive invocation). when a post start migration/seed/warm-up step fails, the operator sees hook exited with status 1 and has no way to find out why. related but distinct issues (hooks not running in certain paths): 13593 (compose run), 13318 (compose restart), 12513 (service.up api). this report is about hooks that do run, but whose output goes nowhere. steps to reproduce compose.yaml: yml services: ok: image: alpine:3.20 command: sh -c "sleep 600" post start: - command: sh -c "echo hook stdout; echo hook stderr 1>&2; exit 0" bad: image: alpine:3.20 command: sh -c "sleep 600" post start: - command: sh -c "echo why it failed; exit 7" 1. attached — output is visible: $ docker compose up --no-color ... ok-1 -> | hook stdout ok-1 -> | hook stderr bad-1 -> | why it failed bad hook exited with status 7 2. detached — output is gone: $ docker compose up -d ; echo "exit=$?" ... container proj-ok-1 started bad hook exited with status 7 exit=1 hook stdout, hook stderr, and why it failed are nowhere. same with --wait. 3. nothing recovers it afterwards: $ docker compose logs main container output only $ docker logs proj-bad-1 main container output only $ docker inspect proj-bad-1 no hook output / exit code field also observed: a failing post start hook does not mark the container unhealthy (health check keeps passing, failingstreak=0), so --wait cannot surface the failure via health state either — the only signal is the exit code of up itself. expected behavior a hook that runs and fails should leave its output somewhere retrievable. at minimum one of: 1. when a hook exits non-zero, its stdout/stderr is included in the cli output alongside the existing hook exited with status line (this is the actual bug — the failure is reported without the reason). 2. hook output is written to a retrievable location — e.g. surfaced through docker compose logs for the owning service, or an ephemeral hook container whose logs survive like a failed pre start hook's do. 3. up -d / up --wait forward post start / pre stop hook stdout/stderr to the cli (prefixed like attached mode), so a wrapping process can capture it. compose version text docker compose version v5.1.2 docker environment text docker engine 29.4.0 os: macos (darwin 25.6.0) anything else? no response

support mounts and secrets in compose provider extensions compose provider extensions are useful for provisioning or configuring resources that are not managed directly by compose. they can also inject information about those resources into the application, commonly through environment variables—for example, providing managed database credentials. however, credentials and other sensitive values are often better distributed as mounted files rather than environment variables. environment variables can unintentionally leak through process inspection, debugging output, logs, crash reports, or other tooling. at present, compose providers appear to only have the ability to add or override environment variables. there does not seem to be a way for a provider to inject a mount, secret, or other file-based credential into the resulting compose service. proposed feature allow compose provider extensions to contribute file-based (secrets) resources such as, and overall align them better with existing capabilities like cdi extensions which in principle can mutate containers at runtime with additional volume and/or bind mounts. for example, a database provider could expose credentials through a secret: services: app: providers: database: type: managed-db secrets: - db password secrets: db password: provided by the provider the application could then consume the credential from the mounted secret file rather than receiving it through an environment variable. motivation this would allow providers to follow more secure secret-distribution practices while retaining the convenience of provider extensions. in particular, it would: better align the feature with security recommendations/best practices, and align the feature for images that exclusively be used with such password files.

allow overriding entrypoint for pre start init containers description pre start init containers are useful for preparing files or other resources before a service starts, but currently there is no way to override the image's entrypoint for an individual init container. this becomes problematic when using purpose-built utility images whose functionality is exposed through their default entrypoint. for example, i have some services that require tls and does not support a non-tls bootstrap mode. an init container could generate a self-signed certificate before the service starts. a natural choice would be to use an openssl image. however, if alpine/openssl has an entrypoint that is not appropriate for the desired initialization command, there is no way to replace it. the workaround is to use a generic alpine image and install openssl at runtime, but when using services that require self signed certificates multiple "apk add --no-cache openssl" compounds and slow down initialization. services: app: image: example/app pre start: - command: - sh - -c - | apk add --no-cache openssl openssl req -x509 ... please consider to allow entrypoint to be specified for pre start init containers, overriding the image's default entrypoint in the same way that entrypoint can be overridden for regular compose services. this would allow init containers to use existing utility images without having to create wrapper images or install their tooling at runtime.

compose provider extensions/plugins can only execute ".exe" on windows the windows plugin discovery currently appears to restrict plugins to .exe files. i'm not sure this is desirable behavior. on windows, executable command resolution normally respects pathext, which allows extensions such as .cmd, .bat, and potentially .py (depending on the environment) to be invoked without explicitly specifying the extension. restricting compose plugins to .exe therefore prevents lightweight script-based plugins. for example, a plugin could be implemented as a python, batch, or other script rather than requiring a compiled executable. i think plugin discovery should probably respect pathext (or otherwise use the same executable-resolution semantics as windows), rather than hard-coding .exe. this would also make compose plugin behavior more consistent with how commands are normally resolved on windows.

[bug] ttywriter.done still hangs forever when the context was canceled before done runs description the 13639 fix (25b29d77) makes ttywriter.done send on the unbuffered done channel before taking the render mutex, which fixes the completion-path deadlock. a second wedge path survives it. the render goroutine started by ttywriter.start has three exits: ctx.done(), receiving from w.done, and the 100ms tick. the done channel has exactly two users in the codebase: that receive, and the send in done. adaptcmd cancels the command context on the first sigterm/sigint. when that happens, the render goroutine exits through the ctx.done() branch and never receives. pkg/compose.run then calls bus.done unconditionally, and its send blocks forever: the only receiver is gone. there is also a narrower window when the cancel and the send race: the select can pick the ctx.done() branch while the sender is already blocked. interactive use masks this: the signal handler unregisters itself after the first signal, so a second ctrl-c kills the process by default disposition. an unattended caller that sends a single term to a tty-attached compose command gets a process that never exits. expected: done returns after a canceled operation and the process exits with status 130. steps to reproduce the mechanism reduces to a deterministic unit test. on current main (f729794), add this to cmd/display/tty cancel test.go: go // a single sigterm/sigint cancels the command context (adaptcmd). the render // goroutine started by start then exits through its ctx.done() branch and never // receives from the unbuffered done channel. pkg/compose.run still calls // bus.done unconditionally afterward, and its send blocks forever: the only // receiver is gone. func testdoneaftercontextcanceldoesnothang(t testing.t) { w, := newtestwriter() ctx, cancel := context.withcancel(context.background()) w.start(ctx, "down") cancel() // let the render goroutine observe the cancellation and exit. time.sleep(100 time.millisecond) finished := make(chan struct{}) go func() { w.done("down", false) close(finished) }() select { case <-finished: case <-time.after(2 time.second): t.fatal("ttywriter.done blocked forever after context cancellation") } } --- fail: testdoneaftercontextcanceldoesnothang (2.10s) tty cancel test.go:46: ttywriter.done blocked forever after context cancellation fail github.com/docker/compose/v5/cmd/display operationally this corresponds to: docker compose down on a tty with a slow-stopping service, one sigterm while the progress ui renders, and the process never exits. we found it while root-causing 13639 on an embedded device fleet, where we captured on-target goroutine dumps of that deadlock. compose version text built from main at e8c21434 plus a backport of 25b29d77; the involved code paths are unchanged at f729794. docker environment text embedded linux devices, docker 29.x; the analysis is environment-independent. anything else? replacing the send in done with close(w.done) fixes it: close never blocks, and the select exits on the closed channel. with that one-line change, the test above and the whole cmd/display suite pass, race detector included.

build.provenance: false is ignored with the containerd image store; up --build recreates unchanged containers description with the containerd image store enabled, build.provenance: false in the compose file does not stop the default provenance attestation from being attached. the attestation carries build timestamps and a unique invocation id, so every docker compose up --build produces a new manifest-list digest for an unchanged build, and compose recreates the container even though nothing changed. setting buildx no default attestations=1 in the environment suppresses the attestation and the container is left running, so the compose-file setting appears to not reach buildkit in this path. 13146 describes the same behavior and is closed as completed, but the issue is still reproducible on the versions below. steps to reproduce dockerfile: dockerfile from alpine:3.20 cmd ["sleep","infinity"] compose.yml: yaml services: app: build: context: . provenance: false init: true 1. docker compose up --build -d → container created, started. 2. docker compose up --build -d again, no file changed → container recreated (new container id). 3. buildx no default attestations=1 docker compose up --build -d twice → second run prints running and keeps the same container id. compose version text docker compose version v5.1.1 docker environment text docker engine 29.3.1 (docker desktop, macos) image store: containerd (io.containerd.snapshotter.v1, overlayfs) anything else? expected: with build.provenance: false, an unchanged up --build leaves the container running, the same as with buildx no default attestations=1.

hooks: missing defensive copy in outputtail.string() append this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report. in outputtail.string() (hook.go, pr 14091), the partial-line append uses the lines slice directly: go lines = append(lines, partial) without a defensive copy this can mutate the underlying array if the slice has spare capacity. the original code used append(append([]string{}, lines...), partial). low impact in practice (the function is called after the copy goroutine has exited), but fragile. mentioned in 14091 review by @ndeloof (hook.go:221).

hooks: retained pre start containers removed before service containers on compose down -v this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report. removeprestarthookcontainers is called before service containers are stopped in down() (pr 14091, down.go:110). hook containers share volumes with the service container via volumesfrom. removing them with -v before stopping the service container may cause volume leaks if the service container holds anonymous volume references. suggested fix: move the hook-container sweep to after service container removal, or at minimum verify the ordering is safe. mentioned in 14091 review by @ndeloof (down.go:110).

hooks: containerlist failure in removeprestarthookcontainers aborts compose down teardown this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report. in removeprestarthookcontainers (down.go, introduced in pr 14091), a containerlist error returns early and causes the whole down() to return an error, leaving networks and volumes unremoved. the call should warn-and-continue (matching the removal-failure behaviour below it) rather than aborting teardown. mentioned in 14091 review by @ndeloof (down.go:419).

hooks: compose down skips retained hook containers of dependent services this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report. pr 14091 added removeprestarthookcontainers to clean up retained pre start hook containers on compose down. when services are specified, the cleanup is scoped to those services. however, if a listed service has a dependency whose hook container was retained, that dependency's hook container is not cleaned. compose down web does not sweep hook containers of db (a dependency of web) mentioned in 14091 review by @ndeloof (down.go:406).

source build secrets from .env files description in docker-compose.yml, runtime environment variables may be defined in .env files. but at build time, secrets can't be sourced from an .env file. they must be defined in an environment variable or in a dedicated text file on the host. i'm using the following setup to try to mitigate the effect of any supply chain attacks on my development environment: - [1password's environments feature]( which locks access to an .env file behind an auth dialog. - visual studio code's [dev containers plugin]( which automatically runs docker compose build commands and doesn't allow passing alternate build arguments. my choices for build secrets are currently: - load them into my host's environment - place them in individual files both leave them open to a malicious process on the host, and neither works with 1password to give me an auth screen on access. it would be nice to be able to define a secret like this: yml secrets: github token: file: ./my secrets.env key: gh token then i would be prompted to grant access to the token automatically when vs code sends docker compose a build command.
