epic: converge the start phase into the plan engine "this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report." context two lifecycle engines coexist today ( 14074, section c). the plan-based reconciler (reconcile.go → executor.go, single entry point create.go) is pure, deterministic and golden-tested — but create-only : containers leave the plan in created state, and opstartcontainer is only ever emitted for exotic states (paused/dead). everything that makes an application actually start lives in the second, imperative engine (independencyorder): waitdependencies (health/completion polling), secret/config injection, pre start/post start hooks. up chains the two with two different daemon snapshots , no canonical project object across the phases, two event-emission systems, and latent bugs at the seam (startmx not held on the path actually exercised; the start-phase containerlist skips the config-hash filter; dependency-wait timeouts swallowed by ctx.done() → nil). this epic tracks converging the start phase into the plan engine, one reviewable pr at a time. target architecture guiding split: decision vs execution — not "plan vs imperative". the plan is the pivot execution format of compose; the reconciler is just one producer of plans. - one snapshot, one project, one plan with two phases. reconcileoptions gains a scope (create, start, or both); plannode gains a phase field. up -d builds a single create+start plan; start/scale/watch-rebuild use scope start (never recreating); compose create keeps scope create unchanged — the existing golden tests do not change . - new operations (explicit numbering, 40+): - opwaitcondition — one node per (awaited service, condition ∈ healthy / completed successfully / running or healthy), deduplicated across dependents (a waitnodes map, like networknodes). required: false is absorbed locally: skipped event, node succeeds — same pattern as the existing besteffort. condition: service started needs no node : a plain dag edge expresses it. health is re-observed at execution time (the node runs today's waitdependency polling); observedstate deliberately does not grow a health field — it would be stale by construction. - oprunprestart — per service. emitted at plan time only when no replica was running at observation (today's rule in startservice), targeting the lowest-numbered replica (lowestnumberedcontainer). - oprunpoststart — per container, after its start. - opstartcontainer enriched : secret/config injection folds into execstartcontainer (they always run as a pair right before start — a separate node would be noise), and the target resolves either from an observed container or from the createnodeid of a create in the same plan (the reconciliationcontext mechanism already used by oprenamecontainer). side effect by construction: every containerstart in the codebase now goes through the one call site that holds startmx. - replica chains : inject→start→post start of replica n+1 depends on the end of replica n's chain — today's sequential start order, preserved and now visible in golden plans. servicenodes[svc] points at the end of the chain, so a service started dependent waits for the whole service, matching independencyorder semantics. - events : on converged paths the executor is the only emitter. exact parity of observable sequences (waiting→healthy|exited|skipped, starting→started with started emitted after post start) via a start: : group on the existing grouptracker. - interactive up : prepare the plan once; execute the create phase; set up attach/printer/monitor (upsession unchanged); execute the start phase under context.withoutcancel with the printer as listener. the phase boundary replaces today's create/start seam without reintroducing a second snapshot. - --wait stays post-plan: it is a final verification with a global timeout and synthetic conditions (getdependencycondition), running on the shared waitdependency primitive. - shared primitives, no decisions inside : waitdependency, injectsecrets/injectconfigs, runhook, createmobycontainer — consumed by the executor and by what stays imperative (restart, run, --wait). startservice/startservicecontainer/waitdependencies are deleted at the end of the series. - executor constraint (to document in code): never add errgroup.setlimit to the plan executor while it schedules one blocking goroutine per node — instant deadlock. a concurrency cap requires moving to a ready-queue scheduler first. non-goals (explicit) - stop / down : reverse-order teardown converges later as a plan-builder producing a plan directly (no reconciler — down without a compose file has no desired state to diff; --rmi, anonymous volumes and duplicate-named networks don't fit a diff model). separate epic. - restart : containerrestart is atomic on the daemon side; decomposing it into stop+start changes semantics. stays imperative on the shared primitives. - kill / pause / unpause : unordered by design; a plan would introduce an ordering that doesn't exist. - run one-off container : by definition outside desired state (number=-1, autoremove, unique slug). its dependencies converge for free (they go through create/start); its own creation stays imperative on the shared primitives. - parallel replica starts (relaxing today's sequential order): becomes a trivial edge change after this series; not mixed into it. pr breakdown lot 0 — foundations (no behavior change except deliberate bug fixes; independent, can start immediately) - [x] test: unit-lock the imperative start path — characterization tests only (start idempotence, "no container to start", pre start gating ×3, inject→start→post start order, required:false skip, getdependencycondition, restart restart:true). the imperative engine is currently locked only by e2e. → 14104 (merged) - [x] fix: dependency wait timeout silently ignored ( 14074 c) — waitdependency returns the error on deadlineexceeded; user cancellation stays silent; audit of the 4 callers. → 14105 (merged) - [x] fix|chore: startmx on the real start path — maintainer decision requested below . → 14106 (merged) - [x] refactor: newgraph stops mutating the project — pruning of unresolvable optional deps becomes an explicit step; precondition for a canonical project object. → 14124 (+ compose-spec/compose-go 922 for the upstream project.withoutunresolvedoptionaldependencies) lot 1 — vocabulary (the plan learns to start; inert code, no consumer) - [x] feat: reconciler plans the start phase — new ops, phase field, planstartphase (deduplicated waits reproducing shouldwaitfordependency, started-edges, plan-time pre start gating, replica chains, exited/created → start chain under scope start). golden tests only; epic: make the codebase agent-legible — fix misleading self-description, ambiguous contracts, and legacy leftovers "this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report." goal coding agents (and new human contributors) navigate this codebase by reading it locally: file names, doc comments, option structs, docs, and error messages are their map. today several of those signposts are inaccurate, ambiguous, or point at code that no longer exists , so a reader who trusts them lands on wrong conclusions and produces plausible-looking regressions. this epic tracks making the codebase self-describing and truthful : fix documentation and comments that lie, make implicit invariants explicit, remove legacy leftovers, and add guardrails so the map stays accurate. the findings below come from a systematic legibility review (5 parallel deep dives: lifecycle backend, cli layer, pkg/api contract, build/watch, cross-cutting), with each claim spot-verified against the current code. every item lists file references. items marked 🐛 are arguably user-facing bugs discovered along the way and may deserve extraction into standalone issues. a. the code misdescribes its own structure — split into focused prs (supersede 14075) - use annotations instead of labels for compose-managed container runtime state context spun off from (@thajeztah): > compose is already heavily depending on labels to store state, but we should start looking if we could transition to using annotations, especially for state that shouldn't be persisted (doing a docker commit on a container, or running a container from an image that already has labels set could probably still provide "interesting" results) problem compose stores both identity and runtime state as container labels (com.docker.compose.project, service, container-number, oneoff, config-hash, image, depends on, replace, version, project.working dir, project.config files, environment file, …). labels have two persistence problems annotations don't have: - docker commit on a compose-managed container bakes all of this state into the resulting image; - containers inherit image labels, so running a container from such an image (or any image shipping com.docker.compose. labels) makes it look like compose-managed state: wrong config-hash comparisons, orphan detection, ps/down matching, etc. hostconfig.annotations is per-container, non-identifying runtime metadata — exactly the right home for state that must never leak into images. proposal split the current label set by role: - runtime state → annotations : config-hash, image, depends on, replace, container-number, oneoff, version, project.working dir, project.config files, environment file — none of these should survive a docker commit. - identity stays as labels (for now) : project and service are used in server-side filters (docker ps --filter label=…, events, networks/volumes listing); the engine api has no annotation-based filtering, and annotations don't exist on networks/volumes/images at all. per the original comment, containerd namespaces may eventually be the right primitive for project scoping — that's engine-side work to track separately. backward compatibility migration must be invisible to users with running stacks: 1. phase 1 (dual write, fallback read) : new containers get both labels and annotations; all readers prefer the annotation and fall back to the label. stacks created by older compose keep working (up recreates, down, ps). 2. phase 2 (annotation-first) : stop writing the state labels on new containers; keep the fallback read path for at least a major-version window. 3. filters keep using the identity labels throughout; nothing changes for docker ps --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=… consumers, and third-party tooling relying on identity labels is unaffected. a container recreated by a newer compose gets the new layout; mixed projects (old + new containers) must reconcile correctly during phase 1, which the fallback read gives us. open questions - exact split for container-number/oneoff: they are identity-adjacent but not used in server-side filters everywhere — audit each call site. - annotations are only available for containers: networks, volumes and images keep labels regardless (their divergence-detection labels like com.docker.compose.network/volume and config-hash stay as-is). - whether third-party ecosystems read the state labels (not just identity) — a deprecation note in release notes should cover phase 2. known direct label consumers compose labels were never a documented api, yet some external tools are known to read com.docker.compose. labels directly from docker ps output instead of using compose ps or another supported interface — docker desktop has been identified as one such consumer. these consumers will need to be updated; the phase 1 dual-write window is their migration period, and does not turn the state labels into a compatibility commitment. blocker: the engine api has no annotation filter containerlist returns annotations since engine v27.0.0 (moby/moby ca0529f984, hostconfig.annotations in each summary — verified empirically against v29.6.1 / api 1.55), so list-driven reads keep working once state moves to annotations. but server-side filtering by annotation does not exist (invalid filter 'annotation'; label only). this is a blocker for moving any filtered label, and compose filters on more than identity today: | label | filter kind | server-side usage | |---|---|---| | com.docker.compose.project | equality + presence | containerlist (all lookups, ls project discovery), networklist, volumelist, imagelist (pruner, watch), events (up monitor), stats | | com.docker.compose.service | equality | containerlist (getdefaultfilters), imagelist (watch), stats | | com.docker.compose.oneoff | equality | containerlist (getdefaultfilters, start, monitor initial state), events (up monitor) | | com.docker.compose.config-hash | presence ("compose-managed" marker) | containerlist: ls, getdefaultfilters (i.e. virtually every container lookup), monitor initial state | | com.docker.compose.container-number | equality (--index lookup) | containerlist (getspecifiedcontainer) | | com.docker.compose.network | equality | networklist (down) | consequence: two labels from the runtime state basket are filtered on today. migrating them requires either an annotation filter landing engine-side, or compose first rewriting those filter usages — the config-hash presence marker can be replaced by the project label presence, and the container-number equality by client-side selection over a service-scoped list. both rewrites are compose-local and should land as a phase 1 prerequisite; identity labels (project, service, oneoff, network) stay labels regardless until the engine offers annotation filtering.

[bug] second up recreates image pulled by first up with containerd store this issue was filed by an ai agent on a human's behalf. the human submitter may not have independently verified the report. description on an engine using the containerd image store, compose 5.4.0 can recreate a container on the second identical docker compose up when the first up had to pull a multi-manifest image. current behavior: - the first up pulls the missing image and creates the container. - the second identical up, without another pull or any configuration/image change, reports the service as recreate and replaces the container. expected behavior: - the second up recognizes that the image and configuration are unchanged and leaves the container running. this can destroy state held in the container writable layer. we encountered it with a stateful infrastructure container initialized between the two compose invocations. steps to reproduce use docker engine with the containerd image store and api >= 1.48. start with the selected multi-platform image absent locally. yaml services: app: image: alpine:3.22.2 command: ["sleep", "infinity"] console docker image rm alpine:3.22.2 only to make the first compose invocation pull docker compose up -d first id=$(docker compose ps -q app) docker inspect -f '{{index .config.labels "com.docker.compose.image"}}' "$first id" docker compose up -d second id=$(docker compose ps -q app) test "$first id" = "$second id" on the affected setup, the second up prints recreate and the final comparison fails. compose version text docker compose version v5.4.0 docker environment text docker engine 29.7.2 api version 1.55 storage driver: overlayfs driver-type: io.containerd.snapshotter.v1 containerd 2.3.3 linux/amd64 anything else? this appears to be a digest-type inconsistency introduced when getimagesummaries was changed by fd794ea8421812cd0604d5ebae632eb4a098513c to select the platform runnable-manifest digest: - during the initial pull, pullrequiredimages stores the value returned by pullserviceimage in the project image map. - pullserviceimage currently returns plain imageinspect.id. with the containerd image store, this can be the top-level image-index digest. that value becomes the new container's com.docker.compose.image label. - during the next up, the image is already local. getimagesummaries requests manifests and contentdigest returns the platform runnable-manifest digest. - reconciliation compares the runnable-manifest digest with the existing container's index-digest label and treats the unchanged image as stale. in the observed failure, the existing container label held sha256:46302bcb91a7e8008e6394be8afafdbfa40fb77a54d4046a38be35992042d5de, while the later local-image lookup selected a different platform manifest digest for the same unchanged tag. the compose configuration hash and mounts were identical, and no pull occurred during the second invocation. compose 5.1.4 does not reproduce this because both paths use plain inspect.id. a patch that resolves the post-pull image through the same getimagesummaries path fixes the mismatch. this is related to the containerd multi-manifest handling in 14007, but it is a different path and symptom: 14007 rejects a locally available non-native platform and attempts a pull; this issue successfully pulls a same-platform image and then unnecessarily recreates it on the following up.

[bug] "docker compose up -d --dry-run" performs a real container swap when recreate is needed description docker compose up -d --dry-run (with -d/--detach) does not stay dry when it decides a service needs to be recreated: it performs a real stop/remove of the old container, creates a new one, and renames it into place — exactly as a real up -d would — despite the --dry-run flag. no error, warning, or indication is given that a real change was applied. the output itself also looks like normal dry-run output (container recreate / recreated), but crucially is missing the dry-run mode - prefix that a correctly-dry run shows on every line (see the example output in 13040 / pr 13042, which fixed a related build-path issue). dropping -d (running in the foreground) correctly stays dry for the same scenario — the old container is left untouched. so the bug appears specific to the -d/detached code path for the up/recreate step, not dry-run handling in general. this is a real-world data-loss risk: any tooling that uses docker compose up -d --dry-run to check whether an update is available (a common pattern) will silently apply that update instead of just detecting it. steps to reproduce 1. create a minimal compose project and bring it up for real: yaml compose.yaml services: test: image: nginx:alpine container name: dryrun-test environment: - foo=bar docker compose up -d 2. change a value that forces a recreate (e.g. foo=bar -> foo=baz). 3. run: docker compose up -d --dry-run 4. check the container's actual state: docker compose ps -a expected behavior the original container (age/id) is unchanged — --dry-run should not apply anything, per its name and documented purpose. actual behavior container dryrun-test recreate container dryrun-test recreated container 015cbd0f386c dryrun-test starting container 015cbd0f386c dryrun-test started --- state immediately after dry-run --- name image command service created status ports dryrun-test nginx:alpine "/docker-entrypoint.…" test 23 seconds ago up 22 seconds 80/tcp the container was genuinely swapped for a new one (new image id, fresh created/uptime) — not left as-is. running the same reproduction without -d (docker compose up --dry-run, foreground) correctly leaves the original container untouched, confirming the -d combination specifically is what breaks dry-run's guarantee. compose version docker compose version v5.4.0 docker environment server: 29.7.2 debian gnu/linux 13 (trixie), kernel 6.12.96+deb13-amd64 docker-compose-plugin 5.4.0-1 debian.13 trixie (previously 5.3.1, upgraded via the standard docker apt repo) anything else? possibly related to 13040 ("build --dry-run actually builds the image", fixed by pr 13042) — but that fix was scoped to the build/bake path and its own example output correctly shows the dry-run mode - prefix on every line, which is absent entirely from the output above, suggesting the up -d/recreate path takes a different, still-broken code path.

[bug] up --abort-on-container-exit aborts on one-off compose run containers (regression in 2.39.0) description since 2.39.0, an attached docker compose up --abort-on-container-exit tears down the project when an unrelated one-off container created by docker compose run exits. those containers are labelled com.docker.compose.oneoff=true and were never part of the up set, so their exit shouldn't count as "a container exited". i ran into this through rubymine. its docker compose interpreter starts the app with up --exit-code-from --abort-on-container-exit , and separately shells out docker compose run --rm id -u to introspect the container (it runs rubocop the same way, on every edit). each of those probes now kills the debug session: manualprobe-idler-run-cb1884bd4e99 exited with code 0 compose stopping aborting on container exit... container manualprobe-idler-1 stopping error response from daemon: can not get logs from container which is dead or marked for removal i bisected it to 2.39.0 and then went looking in the source. i think it comes from pkg/compose/monitor.go, added in 485b6200ee00 ("(refactoring) introduce monitor to manage containers events and application termination") and first shipped in 2.39.0. the initial container list excludes one-offs, but the event subscription immediately below it doesn't: go initialstate, err := c.api.containerlist(ctx, container.listoptions{ all: true, filters: filters.newargs( projectfilter(c.project), oneofffilter(false), // excluded here hasconfighashlabel(), ), }) ... evtch, errch := c.api.events(context.background(), events.listoptions{ filters: filters.newargs( filters.arg("type", "container"), projectfilter(c.project)), // but not here }) the only thing between a one-off's die event and the listeners is the service guard a few lines further down: go if len(c.services) > 0 && !c.services[event.actor.attributes[api.servicelabel]] { continue } a one-off carries com.docker.compose.service for the service it was run from, so it passes. that also predicts the trigger matrix below, which is what i measured: | up target | run target | result | | --- | --- | --- | | up main | run main | aborts | | up main | run other | survives (service guard catches it) | | up (no services) | run other | aborts (len(c.services) == 0, nothing filters it) | in 2.38.2 this went through attach.go, which sourced containers via getcontainers(ctx, project.name, oneoffexclude, true, selectedservices...), so one-offs never entered the picture. adding oneofffilter(false) to the events filter args looks like the one-line fix; checking the oneoff label on event.actor.attributes inside the loop would also work. happy to open a pr. monitor test.go seems like the right home for a regression test, though 13990 is touching that file at the moment. this exact behaviour was reported and fixed once before, in docker/compose-cli 1955 (pr docker/compose-cli 1987, "ignore one-off container events"). on whether this is intended: the docs for --abort-on-container-exit say "stops all containers if any container was stopped", which doesn't address one-off containers either way. elsewhere they're consistently excluded from project-wide operations (ps, logs, kill all apply oneofffilter), and monitor.go itself excludes them when building its initial container set — only the event subscription doesn't. combined with docker/compose-cli 1987, which established this exclusion deliberately, i read the current behaviour as an oversight in the refactor rather than a decision. happy to be corrected if the intent changed. not the same as 13800, which is about declared services exiting during an up. i checked that case separately and it behaves identically on 2.38.2 and 5.1.2 (aborts on both), so it isn't a regression. the two do interact though: the workaround suggested in that thread, moving side jobs to docker compose run, is broken by this bug. steps to reproduce yaml compose.yml services: main: image: alpine command: ["sleep", "infinity"] bash shell 1 docker compose up --abort-on-container-exit main shell 2, once main is running docker compose run --rm main true shell 1 prints aborting on container exit... and stops main. expected: the one-off container's exit is ignored and main keeps running, as it does on 2.38.2 and earlier. compose version bisected on macos/arm64 using the official docker-compose-darwin-aarch64 release binaries, same host and daemon throughout: - not reproducible: 2.10.2, 2.20.3, 2.29.7, 2.34.0, 2.35.1, 2.36.2, 2.37.3, 2.38.2 - reproducible: 2.39.0 , 2.39.1, 2.39.2, 2.39.4, 2.40.3, 5.1.2, 5.4.0 docker environment docker engine 29.4.0, cli 29.4.0, macos (darwin 25.6.0) arm64, running under orbstack 2.2.3. orbstack bundles compose 5.1.2, which is how i hit it, but it reproduces with the upstream binaries too.

image store is enabled and a locally tagged multi-platform image contains both the host platform and a non-native platform, docker compose incorrectly treats the image as unavailable for the non-native platform and attempts to pull it from a registry. in this reproduction, the docker host is linux/arm64, while the compose service requests linux/amd64. the unpublished local image tag contains runnable variants for both platforms. current behavior: - docker image inspect --platform linux/amd64 finds the requested local variant. - docker run --platform linux/amd64 runs the local variant successfully. - docker compose up reports that the local image does not match linux/amd64, treats it as missing, and attempts to pull the unpublished tag (which fails). - docker compose up --pull never runs the same local linux/amd64 variant successfully. expected behavior: with the default missing pull policy, compose should recognize that the requested linux/amd64 variant is available [bug] config --hash does not match container config-hash for services using env file description description for a service using env file, the output of: console docker compose config --hash does not match the com.docker.compose.config-hash label written to a newly created container. this happens even immediately after docker compose up --force-recreate, so the difference is not caused by an outdated container. actual behavior the hashes differ, and the final test command returns non-zero. removing env file and declaring the same environment variable inline avoids the discrepancy. expected behavior immediately after forcing container recreation, docker compose config --hash app should match the container's com.docker.compose.config-hash label. this comparison previously worked and was reported in: suspected regression the following commit added cli.withoutenvironmentresolution to several config --... operations, including runhash: it was introduced in compose v2.22.0 through: as a result: - config --hash hashes the service without resolving its service-level env file. - container creation hashes the resolved service environment before writing com.docker.compose.config-hash. skipping env file resolution makes sense for commands such as config --services and config --volumes, but it prevents config --hash from representing the configuration used to create the container. version comparison - v2.21.0: last release where runhash still resolved env file. - v2.22.0: first release containing the suspected regression. - v5.2.0: still affected. steps to reproduce create compose.yaml: yaml services: app: image: alpine:latest command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do sleep 3600; done"] env file: - direct command to compose down services a specific profile without down default services problem description there’s no proper way to compose down only a profile’s services without specifying specific service names or getting default services down along as well. i understand the current ideology of having default(core) services getting up along with any profile(s). though now i want to keep my core services running but compose down my other profiles. the only way is to: bash docker compose down … as if you do bash docker compose --profile=xyz down removes the default services along, which is expected as per docs: however that’s inconvenient. we might nest command to get services names dynamically from config maybe. but hard to get around such complex command. is there some ideal way. or can we introduce something for this? proposed approaches & community discussion after discussing on community forum: metin y suggested an argument addition --profile-only in the compose down action. i comma separated profile: bash docker compose --profile="hi,bye" up then we can introduce something like a tilde at the beginning to indicate only this profile(s): bash docker compose --profile=" hi,bye" down this may seem to be a bit confusing as well, there's a requirement for a convenient way. additional proposal: container labels for profiles additionally there should be proper and easier files. docker inspect already contains com.docker.compose.project, com.docker.compose.project.config files, com.docker.compose.project.working dir in [0].config.labels which i'm assuming are there for [bug] attached up never exits after external stop+down when a container is in restart backoff (regression in v2.39.3) description since compose v2.39.3, an attached docker compose up never exits when the project is stopped externally (docker compose stop + docker compose down from another process) while one of the containers is in restart backoff (status=restarting with restart: unless-stopped). up to v2.39.2 the attached up exited a few seconds after down completed. from v2.39.3 on it hangs forever, even though all containers are stopped and removed. the behavior is still present in v5.3.1 (latest at the time of writing). the apparent mechanism, observed via docker events during the stop window: - a container that is stopped while it is in restart backoff emits only stop → destroy events — there is no die event, because no process is running at that moment; - containers that are running normally when stopped emit the full kill → stop → die → destroy sequence; - since v2.39.3 ( 13210), the attached up appears to wait for a die event per container to detect termination, so it waits forever for the container that never emits one. this matters for supervisors that spawn an attached up as a child process and stop the project externally: the leftover up process keeps holding resources it inherited (in our case, flock file locks on the compose files taken by a wrapper), long after the project is gone. steps to reproduce docker-compose.yml: yaml services: crasher: image: busybox:latest command: ["false"] restart: unless-stopped sleeper: image: busybox:latest command: ["sleep", "3600"] 1. docker compose -p repro up --remove-orphans --force-recreate & (attached, in background) 2. wait until the crasher is in restart backoff: docker inspect repro-crasher-1 --format '{{.state.status}} {{.restartcount}}' shows restarting with restartcount >= 5 3. from another shell: docker compose -p repro stop -t 5 && docker compose -p repro down -t 5 4. observe the backgrounded up process: - v2.39.2 and earlier: exits within a few seconds after down - v2.39.3 and later (incl. v5.0.2, v5.3.1): never exits (waited 120+ s) bisect over official release binaries (same engine, same procedure, pass = up exits / fail = up hangs): | version | result | |---|---| | v2.15.1 | pass | | v2.26.0 | pass | | v2.33.1 | pass | | v2.37.3 | pass | | v2.38.2 | pass | | v2.39.0 | pass | | v2.39.1 | pass | | v2.39.2 | pass | | v2.39.3 | fail (first bad release) | | v2.39.4 | fail | | v5.0.2 | fail | | v5.3.1 | fail | we also verified on a separate machine (same engine v29.3.0) that swapping only the compose cli plugin between v5.0.2 and v2.38.2 toggles the hang with an identical docker events sequence, so the regression is in compose, not in the engine. compose version text docker compose version v5.0.2 (also reproduced with v2.39.3, v2.39.4, v5.3.1; not reproducible with v2.39.2 and earlier) docker environment text reproduced on: - docker engine 29.6.2 (amd64, wsl2) — bisect environment - docker engine 29.3.0 (amd64, embedded linux device) — production environment client: docker compose cli plugin, official release binaries anything else? the first bad release v2.39.3 contains 13210 ("use events to detect container exit"), which matches the observed mechanism (no die event is emitted for a container stopped during restart backoff). possibly related: moby/moby 50908 (open) adds a restarting attribute to die events for 13210's event-based detection. however, in this scenario the container emits no die event at all (only stop → destroy), so the attribute alone would not cover this case.

taint eviction controller pod deletion duration seconds records nanoseconds scaled by 1e9, not seconds what happened? deletepodhandler in pkg/controller/tainteviction/taint eviction.go records the pod deletion latency as float64(time.since(fireat) time.second). time.since already returns nanoseconds, so the multiplication scales the value by another 1e9. taint eviction controller pod deletion duration seconds is documented as "latency, in seconds" with buckets from 0.005 to 240. any latency below about 9.2s is recorded as a huge positive number and lands in the +inf bucket. above about 9.2s the multiplication overflows int64 and wraps around, so the recorded value is arbitrary. for example 10s is recorded as -8446744073709551616 and counts in the lowest bucket, while 20s is recorded as 1553255926290448384. sum is meaningless in all cases. what did you expect to happen? the metric records the latency in seconds, the same way devicetaintevictioncontroller does in pkg/controller/devicetainteviction/device taint eviction.go with poddeletionlatency.seconds(). how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? call deletepodhandler with a fireat 10s in the past and read the histogram. the regression test in 141742 does this. before the fix it records -8.44e+18, after the fix about 10. anything else we need to know? introduced in ccda2d6fd413d02b9df2dd76ca643dfb42d62aaf (kep-3902, which split taintevictioncontroller out of nodelifecyclecontroller) and first released in v1.29.0. the metric is alpha. open prs with the fix: 141742, and 141311 which was opened earlier. 141568 also includes it as part of a larger change. /sig scheduling /kind bug kubernetes version v1.29.0 and later, including master. found by reading the code, not on a running cluster. cloud provider n/a, not provider specific. os version no response install tools no response container runtime (cri) and version (if applicable) no response related plugins (cni, csi, ...) and versions (if applicable) no response

kube-apiserver built with go 1.27 returns 431 for impersonated or front-proxy users with about 500 groups what happened? we're reporting this ahead of v1.38 because it only appears when several conditions combine, and it's easy to miss until someone with a large group membership hits it. go 1.27 added http.server.maxheadervaluecount with a default of 500 (golang/go 79936 - x-remote-group (request-header authentication, used by authenticating proxies) as a result, kube-apiserver v1.38.0-alpha.1 (go1.27.1) returns 431 request header fields too large for requests that impersonate, or are proxied on behalf of, a user with about 500 groups. for the curl request below, 495 groups produce 431 over http/2 but 200 over http/1.1, and 500 groups produce 431 over both; the exact threshold depends on the other request headers. v1.37.1 (go1.26.8) accepts the same requests, tested up to 1,000 groups. the rejection happens in net/http before kubernetes request handlers run. in our run with metadata-level auditing and default log verbosity, the rejected requests had no audit record and no related kube-apiserver log message. go 1.27 has no godebug override for this limit; one was proposed and declined (golang/go 80020, for users with roughly 500 or more groups, on servers built with go 1.27. users with fewer groups are unaffected. groups taken from client certificates, oidc or webhook token authentication are not sent to kube-apiserver as headers, although aggregated api servers still receive them that way. we hit this with an enterprise directory in which some users belong to more than 1,000 groups. what did you expect to happen? requests for users with several hundred to over a thousand groups keep working through impersonation and request-header authentication, as they do with go 1.26 builds, or the limit becomes explicit and documented rather than an implicit net/http default. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. start etcd (listening on 127.0.0.1:2379) and kube-apiserver v1.38.0-alpha.1 with a static token in system:masters, then wait until /readyz returns 200: sh openssl genrsa -out sa.key 2048 && openssl rsa -in sa.key -pubout -out sa.pub echo 'admintoken,admin,admin-uid,"system:masters"' > tokens.csv kube-apiserver --etcd-servers= --bind-address=127.0.0.1 --secure-port=6443 \ --cert-dir=./serving --token-auth-file=tokens.csv --authorization-mode=rbac \ --service-account-issuer= --service-account-key-file=sa.pub \ --service-account-signing-key-file=sa.key --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/16 2. impersonate a user with 495 groups: sh { echo 'header = "authorization: bearer admintoken"' echo 'header = "impersonate-user: alice"' echo 'header = "impersonate-group: system:masters"' for g in $(seq 2 495); do echo "header = \"impersonate-group: group-$g\""; done } > impersonate.cfg curl -sk --http2 -o /dev/null -w '%{http version} %{http code}\n' -k impersonate.cfg \ this prints 2 431 (curl must support http/2; check curl -v). with 490 groups, or with kube-apiserver v1.37.1, it prints 2 200. we also tested request-header authentication separately: --requestheader-client-ca-file, --requestheader-allowed-names, --requestheader-username-headers=x-remote-user and --requestheader-group-headers=x-remote-group, with x-remote-user and repeated x-remote-group headers sent using a client certificate signed by that ca. it gave the same results as impersonation. results (get /api/v1/namespaces/default, the group count includes system:masters): | groups | v1.37.1 (go1.26.8), http/2 and http/1.1 | v1.38.0-alpha.1 (go1.27.1), http/2 | v1.38.0-alpha.1 (go1.27.1), http/1.1 | |---|---|---|---| | 480 | 200 | 200 | 200 | | 490 | 200 | 200 | 200 | | 495 | 200 | 431 | 200 | | 500 | 200 | 431 | 431 | | 1000 | 200 | 431 | 431 | impersonation and request-header authentication gave identical results in every case. other request headers count toward the same limit, which is why the threshold is slightly below 500 groups. anything else we need to know? - staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/secure serving.go sets maxheaderbytes (1 mib) but not maxheadervaluecount. under go 1.27, golang.org/x/net/http2.configureserver (v0.59.0) hands http/2 to the net/http server, so the limit applies to both protocols. - kube-aggregator forwards the user's groups to aggregated api servers as separate x-remote-group headers (round trippers.go. 82468 also discusses a single structured user-info header, which would avoid the per-group header count entirely. - a possible direction: an explicit, bounded and, if appropriate, configurable maxheadervaluecount in k8s.io/apiserver secure serving that supports the intended group sizes while keeping protection against floods of small headers, tested over both http/1.1 and http/2. we're happy to help with a fix once there's agreement on the approach. /kind bug /sig api-machinery /sig auth kubernetes version console $ curl -sk kube-apiserver: /openapi/v3 is never gzip-compressed, unlike /openapi/v2 what happened? kube-apiserver serves /openapi/v3 and /openapi/v3/ uncompressed even when the client sends accept-encoding: gzip. /openapi/v2 on the same server is gzipped. same client and headers against a v1.34.11 kube-apiserver: | path | identity size | with accept-encoding: gzip | content-encoding | |---|--:|--:|---| | /openapi/v2 | 5,333,236 b | 484,949 b | gzip | | /openapi/v3 | 13,653 b | 13,653 b | none | | /openapi/v3/api/v1 | 1,452,085 b | 1,452,085 b | none | | /openapi/v3/apis/apps/v1 | 665,580 b | 665,580 b | none | what did you expect to happen? /openapi/v3 and /openapi/v3/ honour accept-encoding: gzip, as /openapi/v2 does. why the v2 endpoint is wrapped in a gzip handler in kube-openapi (pkg/handler/handler.go): go handler.handle(servepath, gziphandler.gziphandler(http.handlerfunc( the v3 handlers are registered without one, both in kube-openapi (pkg/handler3/handler.go, registeropenapiv3versionedservice) and in kube-aggregator, which serves these paths in kube-apiserver (pkg/controllers/openapiv3/aggregator/aggregator.go, register). the apiserver's own response compression does not apply either: kep-2338 scopes it to api object responses and lists "openapi endpoints which provide their own compression" as out of scope. that is true for v2 but not for v3. why it matters v3 is designed around client-side caching: the discovery document hands out ?hash= urls served with cache-control: public, immutable, and every response has an etag. a client that uses them downloads each document once. not every client does. a client that requests group-version documents without the hash and without if-none-match gets the full body each time. helm does this when rendering a chart, so a helm-based operator repeats it on every reconcile. at around 800 kb per response, one fetch every few seconds adds up to roughly 10 gb per day from a single controller, where gzip would make it about 1 gb. possible fix wrapping the two v3 handlers in kube-aggregator in the gzip handler v2 already uses is enough: | path | before | after | |---|--:|--:| | /openapi/v3 | 13,653 b | 5,295 b | | /openapi/v3/api/v1 | 1,452,085 b | 117,651 b | | /openapi/v3/apis/apps/v1 | 665,580 b | 77,036 b | that compresses on every request. kubernetes/kube-openapi 646 moves v2 to gzip once per cache rebuild; the same could be done for v3 in handler3, which already caches the json and protobuf serializations per group-version. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? bash for p in /openapi/v2 /openapi/v3 /openapi/v3/api/v1 /openapi/v3/apis/apps/v1; do curl -s --cacert ca.crt --cert client.crt --key client.key \ -h 'accept: application/json' -h 'accept-encoding: gzip' \ -o /dev/null -d - -w "$p wire=%{size download}\n" " \ | grep -i -e 'content-encoding|wire=' done kubernetes version v1.34.11. the handler registration is unchanged on master. /sig api-machinery

kube-proxy config validation reports internal field paths what happened? kube-proxy configuration validation reports error field paths using internal go type and field names instead of the public kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1 json/yaml field names. for example, a config with invalid values for: yaml apiversion: kubeproxy.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1 kind: kubeproxyconfiguration bindaddress: "10.10.12.11:2000" healthzbindaddress: "0.0.0.0" metricsbindaddress: "127.0.0.1" iptables: masqueradebit: 32 is reported by the validator as: text kubeproxyconfiguration.kubeproxyiptablesconfiguration.masqueradebit: invalid value: 32: must be within the range [0, 31] kubeproxyconfiguration.bindaddress: invalid value: "10.10.12.11:2000": not a valid textual representation of an ip address kubeproxyconfiguration.healthzbindaddress: invalid value: "0.0.0.0": must be ip:port kubeproxyconfiguration.metricsbindaddress: invalid value: "127.0.0.1": must be ip:port those paths do not match the fields users put in kube-proxy config files: text iptables.masqueradebit bindaddress healthzbindaddress metricsbindaddress the same pattern appears in other kube-proxy validation paths, for example: - kubeproxyconfiguration.kubeproxylinuxconfiguration.kubeproxyconntrackconfiguration.tcpestablishedtimeout instead of conntrack.tcpestablishedtimeout - kubeproxyconfiguration.kubeproxylinuxconfiguration.oomscoreadj instead of oomscoreadj - kubeproxyconfiguration.kubeproxyipvsconfiguration.excludecidrs instead of ipvs.excludecidrs the external field names are defined in staging/src/k8s.io/kube-proxy/config/v1alpha1/types.go, but pkg/proxy/apis/config/validation/validation.go constructs paths with internal pod-level memory.low should follow the pod's memory request after a request-only resize, as it does after a limit resize. kep-2570 says that after an in-place resize, memory.min/memory.low "are recalculated during the next cgroup reconciliation cycle" (kep? memoryqos: container memory.high is not reset when an in-place resize makes the memory request equal the limit what happened? with memoryqos on and a memorythrottlingfactor set, i resized a burstable container's memory request up to its limit in place. the container kept the memory.high computed for its previous request, so it stays throttled below its limit. it doesn't recover on later syncs. measured on v1.37.0 (kind, containerd, cgroup v2, memorythrottlingfactor: 0.9), container with limit 512mi: | memory request | container memory.high | |---|---| | 256mi (created) | 510025728 | | 400mi (resize) | 525123584 (recomputed, correct) | | 512mi = limit (resize) | 525123584 (stale, should be max) | | 90s later | 525123584 | i saw the same on v1.36.1. what did you expect to happen? when request equals limit the kubelet deliberately doesn't set memory.high, so after the resize the container should end up with memory.high=max, the same as a container created with request == limit. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? yaml kind node, kubeletconfiguration featuregates: {memoryqos: true} memorythrottlingfactor: 0.9 sh kubectl run a --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10 \ --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"a","image":"registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"256mi","cpu":"100m"},"limits":{"memory":"512mi"}}}]}}' kubectl patch pod a --subresource resize -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"a","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"512mi","cpu":"100m"},"limits":{"memory":"512mi"}}}]}}' then read memory.high in the container's cgroup on the node anything else we need to know? i think the cause is in generatelinuxcontainerresources. with memoryqos enforced, memory.high is added to unified only when memoryrequest != memorylimitspec (and memoryhigh > memoryrequest). otherwise the key is simply absent, and the runtime leaves an absent key untouched on updatecontainerresources; cri-o copies only the keys it's given. the memoryqos-off branch already writes memory.high=max for exactly this stale-after-resize reason, but the memoryqos-on branch has no equivalent. this matters for vpa-driven resizes: a vpa requestsonly policy produces request == limit whenever the target is above the limit (kubernetes/autoscaler 9926). kubernetes version console $ kubectl version v1.37.0 (also v1.36.1) cloud provider n/a os version console on linux: $ cat /etc/os-release paste output here $ uname -a paste output here on windows: c:\> wmic os get caption, version, buildnumber, osarchitecture paste output here install tools container runtime (cri) and version (if applicable) related plugins (cni, csi, ...) and versions (if applicable)

explore publishing an aggregated openapi v3 schema for downstream consumers what would you like to be added? explore publishing a single, merged openapi v3 document in the repo (or as a release artifact) alongside the existing per-group-version files under api/openapi-spec/v3/. this would only be a static file for offline consumers, not a new endpoint served by kube-apiserver. why is this needed? with /openapi/v2 deprecation being discussed in 141455, many downstream projects still rely on api/openapi-spec/swagger.json instead of openapi v3. for example, the official client generators in kubernetes-client/gen (python, java, javascript, c , etc.), the rust k8s-openapi crate, kustomize, and pulumi-kubernetes all consume swagger.json. a big reason these consumers have not moved to v3 is that api/openapi-spec/v3/ is split across dozens of per-group-version files with shared types like objectmeta duplicated in each file. most code generators expect a single openapi document, so migrating to v3 currently requires every downstream project to write custom logic to parse and merge all the group-version files themselves. or they can adopt fetching each document separately and processing there but that's a bigger change. publishing a pre-merged openapi v3 spec would make it much easier for client libraries and tooling to migrate off swagger.json without affecting kube-apiserver runtime memory. /sig api-machinery /cc @seans3

apimachinery yaml: last line silently dropped when its length is a multiple of the buffer size what happened? k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/yaml silently drops the last line of a stream when that line has no trailing newline and its length is an exact multiple of the reader's buffer size (4096 in newyamlorjsondecoder(r, 4096)). no error is returned, the last document is just truncated. cause: bufio.reader.readline never returns data and an error together, so for such a line linereader.read reads it as full-buffer prefix chunks, then gets io.eof on one extra call and returns the accumulated bytes with io.eof. yamlreader.read treats io.eof as end of data and discards line. what did you expect to happen? the final line is returned, whatever its length. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? go for , n := range []int{4095, 4096, 4097} { last := "b: " + strings.repeat("x", n-3) r := yaml.newyamlreader(bufio.newreadersize(strings.newreader("a: 1\n---\n"+last), 4096)) r.read() doc, err := r.read() fmt.println(n, len(doc), err) } // 4095 4096 // 4096 0 eof anything else we need to know? hit in production through argo cd: its config-management-plugin server trimsuffixes the plugin output's trailing newline before splitting it with newyamlorjsondecoder(..., 4096). a helm chart whose last rendered line was a 16384-byte json spec: (victoria-metrics-operator-crds 0.15.0) was applied without its spec, and the api server rejected the object. present on master and in every release i tested (v0.34.1 to v0.36.1). fix with a regression test to follow. kubernetes version library bug, reproduced with k8s.io/apimachinery v0.34.1, v0.35.3, v0.36.0, v0.36.1 and master. cloud provider n/a (library). /sig api-machinery

dra: resourceslice validation panics on a zero with an extreme negative exponent in capacity.requestpolicy.validvalues what happened? with drafractionalcapacityrange enabled (beta, on by default since 1.37), validating a resourceslice whose device capacity has requestpolicy.validvalues containing 0e-2147483647 panics inside validateresourceslice: runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range parsequantity("0e-2147483647") is accepted (a zero on the inf.dec backend with scale 2147483647), and validaterequestpolicyvalidvalues keys the values with quantitykeyasdec, which calls asdec().string(); inf.dec.string allocates scale+2 bytes for a value below one (gopkg.in/inf.v0/dec.go:442) and overflows. reproduced on master (6c1c7702 and later) with a unit probe in pkg/apis/resource/validation: go featuregatetesting.setfeaturegateduringtest(t, utilfeature.defaultfeaturegate, features.drafractionalcapacityrange, true) bad := apiresource.mustparse("0e-2147483647") cap := testdevicecapacity(apiresource.mustparse("1"), testcapacityrequestpolicy(ptr.to(apiresource.mustparse("1")), []apiresource.quantity{bad, apiresource.mustparse("1")}, nil)) slice := testresourceslice("slice", "node", "driver.example.com", 1) slice.spec.devices[0].allowmultipleallocations = ptr.to(true) slice.spec.devices[0].capacity["memory"] = cap validateresourceslice(slice) // panics validatemultiallocatabledevicecapacity panic: runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range validateresourceslice panic: runtime error: makeslice: cap out of range in the apiserver the panic is recovered by the handler, so the request fails with a 500 instead of a validation error. release-1.37 has the same quantitykeyasdec key function (validation.go:1420,1755) with the gate on by default, and parsequantity accepts the input there too, so v1.37 is affected as well. what did you expect to happen? a validation error, or acceptance of the value as zero; no panic. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? the probe above, or a resourceslice with spec.devices[].capacity. .requestpolicy.validvalues: ["0e-2147483647"] and allowmultipleallocations: true against a cluster with the gate enabled. anything else we need to know? 142355 removes quantitykeyasdec and keys every value through quantitykeyint, which does not call asdec().string(), so it fixes this as a side effect; a regression row for 0e-2147483647 in validation device capacity test.go would pin it. related: 141166 (quantity int64/int32 tracker); the parser accepting a zero with an out-of-range exponent is 142452. kubernetes version master 6c1c7702 (2026-09-27); the gate is beta and on since v1.37. /kind bug /sig node

cloud-controller-manager accepts the nativehistograms feature gate but never applies it what happened? nativehistograms (kep-5808) is beta and enabled by default since v1.37. each component must call metricsfeatures.applyfeaturegates() for histograms to pick up the gate state: this is done in kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kube-proxy and kubelet, the five components listed in kep-5808. however, k8s.io/cloud-provider/app also registers the metrics feature gates, so cloud-controller-manager accepts --feature-gates=nativehistograms=true and defaultfeaturegate.enabled(nativehistograms) returns true, but nothing calls applyfeaturegates: so on every cloud-controller-manager built on k8s.io/cloud-provider/app, the gate reports as enabled (by default since v1.37) but has no effect, and histograms stay classic-only. the same is true in v1.37.0. what did you expect to happen? either cloud-controller-manager histograms are exposed in both classic and native formats when nativehistograms is enabled, like the other control-plane components, or, if cloud-controller-manager is intentionally out of scope, the gate should not silently appear enabled there with no effect. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? no cluster is needed. this test drives the real newcloudcontrollermanagercommand and checks, from the cloudinitializer hook (which runs after config()), whether a newly created histogram is native: test snippet go cloudinitializer := func( config.completedconfig) cloudprovider.interface { gateenabled := utilfeature.defaultfeaturegate.enabled(metricsfeatures.nativehistograms) nativebefore := histogramisnative(t, "repro before seconds") // newhistogram + gather, checks schema != nil metricsfeatures.applyfeaturegates(utilfeature.defaultfeaturegate) nativeafter := histogramisnative(t, "repro after seconds") // ... } cmd := app.newcloudcontrollermanagercommand(s, cloudinitializer, app.defaultinitfuncconstructors, names.ccmcontrolleraliases(), cliflag.namedflagsets{}, stopch) cmd.setargs([]string{"--kubeconfig= ", "--cloud-provider=fake", "--feature-gates=nativehistograms=true", "--secure-port=0", "--webhook-secure-port=0"}) output at master (6c1c7702cf2): nativehistograms gate enabled in ccm: true histogram native after ccm startup (config done): false histogram native after calling applyfeaturegates: true i'm happy to share the full test. anything else we need to know? i noticed that kep-5808 lists only five components, so i'm not sure whether leaving out cloud-controller-manager was a deliberate scoping decision. either way, the gate currently looks enabled but silently does nothing there, which seems worth resolving in one of two ways: 1. wire it up: call features.applyfeaturegates(utilfeature.defaultfeaturegate) in the cloud-controller-manager rune, right after logsapi.validateandapply. that is before s.config() builds rest clients and informers, so it also avoids the ordering problem described in 142379. a cloud-controller-manager case could be added to test/integration/metrics/nativehistograms/metrics test.go. 2. if cloud-controller-manager is intentionally out of scope, make that explicit, for example in the kep or the feature-gate docs, so cloud-provider maintainers aren't surprised. happy to send a pr for option 1 if that's the preferred direction. related: 128842, 142379, 142377. ai tools assisted with the investigation; i reviewed the code and ran the reproduction myself. /sig cloud-provider /sig instrumentation kubernetes version reproduced from source at master 6c1c7702cf2052245ef10e699d45f071af306f59 (v1.38 development). confirmed the same code is in v1.37.0 (applyfeaturegates is not called in k8s.io/cloud-provider/app). cloud provider any cloud-controller-manager built on k8s.io/cloud-provider/app. reproduced with a unit test, so no cloud is involved. os version windows 11 (build 26200), go1.27.1. not os-specific. install tools n/a, reproduced from source container runtime (cri) and version (if applicable) n/a related plugins (cni, csi, ...) and versions (if applicable) n/a

leverage remote partitions for exclusive cpus (linux 6.7+) linux 6.7 added support for "remote partitions" to sync cpu allocation to containers. it manages a default set, and every container that doesn't have exclusive cpus gets assigned the default set. the default set is updated (for every container) to remove cpus as they're allocated exclusively. problems with this approach: 1. eventual consistency: when an exclusive cpu is assigned, there is up to 10s (or more!) delay before that cpu is removed from the default set of other containers. 2. no protection from system processes: only containers managed by the kubelet are excluded from using the assigned cpus. system processes (e.g. the kubelet itself) can still be scheduled to it. 3. every static cpu assignment (or release) requires updating every other container on the node. these are all done through updatecontainerresources requests, and are subject to global nri locks. 4. container reconciliation outside of syncpod: the reconcile loop calls updatecontainerresources directly. normally, all direct container operations like that happen within syncpod. performing the operation outside of syncpod makes this more prone to race conditions. proposal 1. the full set of assignable cpus is written to cpuset.cpus.exclusive on the full cgroup tree (kubelet.slice, kubelet-kubepods.slice), and pod-level cgroups. 2. when a container is assigned exclusive cpus, it sets cpuset.cpus.exclusive to the assigned set, and cpuset.cpus.partition=root (some specialized workloads like dpdk may want isolated). this is set on container creation, or in dopodresizeaction on resize, both of which are in syncpod. 3. remove the cpu manager reconciliation loop: it's no longer needed. /sig node /kind feature /cc @pravk03 @ffromani @dchen1107 @chunxia202410 @lukaszwojciechowski @esotsal

client-go: add support for connection pool what would you like to be added? i would like to propose adding a support to client-go library for creating multiple connections to the same endpoint and using some naive load balancing (such as round robin or power of 2) to send traffic. the option cloud be set using one of the following mechanisms: in kubeconfig, via option similar to 'disablecompression' we have today in golang, by setting respective value, e.g. via rest.config flag goal: in many environments, the endpoint specified in kubeconfig is an l4 load balancer that picks backend randomly. by opening multiple connections we can split the traffic from a single client / controller to multiple kube-apiserver replicas and avoid single kube-apiserver instance becoming overloaded while the other replicas are idle. avoid single-replica pinning issue -- improve client experience in case of single kube-apiserver replica slowdown / unhealthiness. e.g. today kubelet sends traffic only to a single kcp replica. if the replica is slow or unhealthy (e.g. not able to process requests but alive), all connections are persistent and all kubelet's retries are still going to that replica, leading to marking the replica as unhealthy. by sending traffic to multiple replicas, we increase chances (both must be unhealthy). out of scope: multiple endpoint support (we still want client-go to open connections to single endpoint -- we rely on l4 load balancer to assign connections to multiple backends) endpoint discovery: client-go somehow finds out what are the ips for kube-apiserver instances. why is this needed? this is important use case for performance-heavy controllers / schedulers and similar technique is widely used by the components (see e.g. transporthack. by moving this concept to core client-go library we can help the controllers to avoid this "transporthack" or similar technique. by standardising this pattern, we can make this opinionated and ensure that controllers are behaving in expected way and automatically benefit from potential improvements in this area.

was leaving nativehistogramminresetduration unset in component-base intentional? first of all, thank you for landing native histogram support in v1.37 — it's been a really welcome addition on my side. in my own testing on a kind cluster, scraping the control plane metrics as native-only cut the number of stored series by roughly 75%, and no longer being bounded by the classic bucket boundaries has already changed how i'm approaching sli design. while evaluating it, i ran into something i wasn't sure how to read. apologies in advance if this has already been discussed somewhere i've missed. component-base sets two of the native histogram options: go var defaultnativehistogramoptions = nativehistogramoptions{ bucketfactor: 1.1, maxbucketnumber: 160, } nativehistogramminresetduration is left at zero. as far as i can tell, that means once a histogram exceeds maxbucketnumber, maybereset() is skipped and only doublebucketwidth() runs, so the reduced resolution stays in place for the lifetime of the process: go // - any increased zero threshold or reduced resolution is reset back // to their original values once nativehistogramminresetduration has // passed (since the last reset or the creation of the histogram). a few other projects in the ecosystem do set it to 1h: | repo | org | bucketfactor | maxbucketnumber | minresetduration | |---|---|---|---|---| | controller-runtime | kubernetes-sigs | 1.1 | 100 | 1h | | cluster-api | kubernetes-sigs | 1.1 | 100 | 1h | | prometheus | prometheus | 1.1 | 100 | 1h | that said, i can imagine a reason not to: maybereset() also clears sum, count and the classic buckets, which may well be something you'd want to avoid for stable metrics. kep-5808 explains the reasoning behind bucketfactor and maxbucketnumber but doesn't touch on reset behaviour, so i couldn't tell whether this was weighed and set aside, or simply hasn't come up yet. could you help me understand which it is? i'd be glad to open a pr if it turns out to be just an oversight, though i wanted to ask first in case there's context i'm missing. /sig instrumentation /kind bug

kube-apiserver keep using a stale webhook configuration after an update what happened? the kube-apiserver kept calling admission webhooks with an old version of validatingwebhookconfiguration, even though the object had been updated. it kept doing so until the object was updated again. there is a recurring e2e flake in cluster api, which most likely is related to this cache race. right after the providers are installed, every webhook fails with: failed calling webhook "validation.cluster.cluster.x-k8s.io": failed to call webhook: post " tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority following the time from one failing run cert-manager issues the serving certificate (signle revision) (17:22:16) clusterctl creates the validatingwebhookconfiguration without a cabundle. in the same time, cert0manager caininjector sets the cabundle on all webhooks. the object ends at generation: 2 and it is never modified again. (17:22:19) the webhook server loads the serving certificate. (17:22:23 --> end of the test) every call from the kube-apiserver fails with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. the webhook server logs remote error: tls: bad certificate for the same connections. a dump of the objects after the failure shows cabundle equal to ca.crt of the serving certificate secret, meaning that the stored object was correct for the failing duration, but the kube-apiserver, probably, kept serving with the version that had no cabundle. it seems that the race is in configurationscache, sync.map, in the webhook managers code (validating/mutating). the cache is built with keys derived only by configuration name. the informer updatefunc runs configurationscache.delete(name) and then lazy.notify(). getvalidatingwebhookconfigurations builds accessors from a lister snapshot and runs configurationscache.store(name, accessors) without checking which version they were built from. what did you expect to happen? after a webhook configuration is updated, the kube-apiserver uses the latest version. accessors built from an older version are never cached in the way that they will outlive an update event. how can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? stale repos - gopkg.in/inf.v0 (github.com/go-inf/inf) following the same pattern as 132312, for a different dependency. gopkg.in/inf.v0 is a direct dependency of k8s.io/apimachinery, where inf.dec backs the arbitrary-precision path of resource.quantity: go type quantity struct { // i is the quantity in int64 scaled form, if d.dec == nil i int64amount // d is the quantity in inf.dec form if d.dec != nil d infdecamount ... } it is also part of apimachinery's exported surface -- func (q quantity) asdec() inf.dec and func newdecimalquantity(b inf.dec, format format) quantity, so it is compiled into essentially every go program that talks to a kubernetes api server, not only kubernetes itself. what i am not claiming there is no cve (osv reports zero for gopkg.in/inf.v0), no bug report, and no urgency. the package is 760 lines across dec.go and rounder.go, has no external dependencies at all , just math/big, fmt, io, strings, and uses neither unsafe nor reflect. decimal arithmetic is a stable problem, and "no commits since 2018" is not by itself alarming for code of this shape. this is materially lower-risk than the json-iterator situation in 132312, and i do not think it should be treated with the same urgency. i am also not proposing removal. inf.dec is in a ga go api on one of the most widely used types in the ecosystem, so removing it would need k8s.io/apimachinery/v2. that is not what this issue is asking for. what the actual concern is it is bus factor, not code quality. as far as i can tell there is currently nobody able to publish a release under this import path: - last commit: 2018-03-27 . last release: v0.9.1, 2018-03-26 . only two versions were ever tagged. - sole author is péter surányi (@speter, per the license copyright line); the only other commit in the repo's history is a one-line gofmt change from 2017. his last authored commit in any public repo is 2020-03-28 . - the go-inf organisation has zero public members , no org email, and one repo. it was created in 2015 purely to back this vanity import path after google code shut down (see 26231). the original speter.net domain no longer resolves. - go-inf/inf 8 would return a different named type. 3. deprecate asdec/newdecimalquantity now and drop the dependency at a hypothetical apimachinery v2. cleanest, slowest. "the risk is acceptable, leave it alone" is a perfectly good answer too — i would just like it to be a decision on the record rather than something nobody has looked at. happy to do the legwork on any of these if it is useful. cc @thockin (you have both dep-approvers and pkg/api/resource hats, and may remember the 2016 speter.net migration) @dims (you filed 132312) @jpbetz (flagging so this does not surprise the quantity burndown in 141166 — this issue is not a proposal to change that code) /sig architecture /sig api-machinery /area dependency /kind cleanup

[fg:inplacepodverticalscalingexclusivecpus] need to track actuated changes iiuc, cpus are assigned during the admission stage when allocating a pod resize. during upsize, this is not a problem, but when downsizing the unallocated cpus are returned to the available pool before the runtime has actually updated the container. this could cause a race condition where those cpus are assigned to a different pod before the previous pod has actually released them. i think cpu manager needs to track not-yet-released cpus separately from what's been allocated to ensure they aren't reassigned before they're released. /sig node /assign @esotsal /cc @ffromani @natasha41575

global allocators are unsoundly allowed to return memory from the global allocator i've been thinking about this weird edge case that might happen to someone on accident when we introduce unsafe trait globalallocator: allocator to replace globalalloc. a globaalloc impl can call global.allocate()/alloc::alloc(), and then return that memory. this causes the allocator to recurse if it is registered as the [global allocator]. there is currently nothing in the docs of globalalloc or globalallocator that forbids this. the section on reentrance, this becomes much less clear in generic code. for example, consider an allocator myalloc that does something like this: - for small sizes, call allocator a with a larger size, and return that allocation. - for large sizes, call allocator b. now, if we (or downstream) set myalloc as the global allocator, and call box::new(small object), we get the same situation as above. ----- this is also relevant to prior discussions about a nativeallocator wrapper for allocator, which would get support from llvm intrinsics to allow box to be noalias. we believed that [the safety requirements of staticallocator are enough for that]( but i suspect llvm will also not be a fan of these "logical double frees". cc @ralfjung @rustbot label a-docs a-allocators i-unsound a-global-allocator-reentry t-libs t-opsem

[proposal] add a "low-resource / hdd-optimized" compilation mode with explicit memory and thread limits 背景 / background rust 编译器在高性能硬件（nvme ssd、32gb+ 内存、多核 cpu）上表现优异，但仍有大量开发者在资源受限环境中工作，尤其是使用机械硬盘（hdd）和低内存（如 4-8gb）的用户。当前 cargo 的默认配置倾向于最大化并行度和吞吐量，这在 hdd 和低内存机器上反而会导致严重的 i/o 争用和 oom 问题。 rust compiler performs excellently on high-end hardware (nvme ssds, 32gb+ ram, multi-core cpus), but many developers still work in constrained environments, especially those using mechanical hard drives (hdds) and limited memory (e.g., 4-8gb). current cargo defaults prioritize maximum parallelism and throughput, which can cause severe i/o contention and oom issues on hdds and low-memory machines. 提案内容 / proposal 建议在 cargo 中新增一个可选的低资源编译模式（例如 --profile low-resource 或环境变量 cargo low resource=1 ），该模式强制应用以下配置约束： i propose adding an optional low-resource compilation mode to cargo (e.g., --profile low-resource or environment variable cargo low resource=1 ) that enforces the following constraints: 1. 最大编译内存限制 / maximum compilation memory limit 配置项： max-compilation-memory （整数 gb，范围 1-1024） 建议默认值： 4 （即 4gb） 作用：限制编译器进程的内存使用上限，防止在低内存机器上触发 oom，同时为 ide（如 rust-analyzer）留出足够的内存空间。 configuration: max-compilation-memory (integer gb, range 1-1024) suggested default: 4 (i.e., 4gb) purpose: cap the compiler process memory usage to prevent oom on low-memory machines, while leaving sufficient memory for ides (e.g., rust-analyzer). 2. 线程数限制 / thread count limit 配置项： compiler-threads （整数，范围 1-16） 建议默认值： 2 作用：限制编译器可申请的并发线程数。在机械硬盘上，过多的并发线程会导致磁头频繁寻道（thrashing），反而降低整体 i/o 效率。双线程模型可以在保持基本并行度的同时，最小化磁盘争用。 configuration: compiler-threads (integer, range 1-16) suggested default: 2 purpose: limit the number of concurrent threads the compiler can request. on mechanical hard drives, excessive concurrent threads cause frequent head seeking (thrashing), reducing overall i/o efficiency. a dual-thread model minimizes disk contention while maintaining basic parallelism. 3. 缓存块大小优化 / cache block size optimization 配置项： cache-block-size （固定 16mb） 作用：将增量编译缓存文件对齐到 16mb 的固定块大小，减少机械硬盘上的文件碎片化，将随机读取转化为更接近顺序读取的模式，从而提升 hdd 上的缓存命中率。 configuration: cache-block-size (fixed at 16mb) purpose: align incremental compilation cache files to a fixed 16mb block size, reducing file fragmentation on mechanical hard drives and converting random reads into more sequential-like access patterns, thereby improving cache hit rates on hdds. 预期收益 / expected benefits hdd 用户编译速度提升约 2x：通过减少磁盘 i/o 争用和文件碎片化。 低内存机器稳定性提升：4gb 内存限制可防止 oom，让 4-8gb 内存的机器能够正常编译中小型项目。 可预测的编译时间：减少因磁盘争用导致的编译时间波动。 2x speedup for hdd users: by reducing disk i/o contention and file fragmentation. improved stability on low-memory machines: the 4gb memory cap prevents oom, enabling normal compilation of small-to-medium projects on 4-8gb ram machines. predictable build times: reduced variance caused by disk contention. 注意：此模式明确不适用于 ssd/高端用户，在这些环境下其性能可能低于默认的高并行模式。 note: this mode is explicitly not intended for ssd/high-end users, where its performance may be lower than the default high-parallelism mode. 实施建议 / implementation suggestions 作为可选的 profile 或 flag 实现，不影响现有默认行为。 在 .cargo/config.toml 中提供对应的配置键，方便用户手动启用。 收集 hdd 和低内存环境下的 benchmark 数据，验证加速效果。 implement as an optional profile or flag, without affecting existing default behavior. provide corresponding configuration keys in .cargo/config.toml for manual enablement. collect benchmark data in hdd and low-memory environments to validate the speedup. 开放问题 / open questions 编译器团队是否愿意接受一个针对特定硬件场景的"受限模式"？ 现有的增量编译缓存系统是否支持固定块大小的对齐策略？ would the compiler team be open to a "constrained mode" targeting specific hardware scenarios? does the existing incremental compilation cache system support fixed block size alignment?

runtime: stack switching on wasm go wasm stack switching as an experiment in the webassembly backend, under a gowasm feature-flag, retarget the compilation of goroutine switching to use webassembly's experimental suspend and resume instructions. why the existing method for switching stacks (goroutines) in go wasm is to insert code to manage the stack explicitly and step by step. to this end, every function call is checked for a switching boolean return and stack frames are returned one by one. every function has a jump table at the top which allows explicit representation of resume-points within the function, but which muddies the debuggability of the generated wasm code, and has a run-time cost. the experimental suspend/resume instructions in wasm are designed precisely to give a direct way to compile things like thread (goroutine) switching. "suspend" captures a current stack, up to some point, and "resume" installs a given stack that was captured earlier. behavior and compatibility a prototype has been implemented that shows how the suspend/resume instructions can integrate into the go runtime and compiler. using suspend/resume should make it possible to remove the checks on every call routine and the top-of-function jump table, making for much more straightforward compilation and code reading. the change is intended to be invisible to programmers and only to streamline the compiler implementation. however, the webassembly feature is not universally deployed, so the new work needs to be kept in an experiment.

x/pkgsite: use accurate same-module test for package imports when we count the number of packages importing some package p, we want to exclude other packages in p's module, because they don't tell us about the popularity of p. previously, we didn't have module information at the place we were doing the counting, so we approximated this check syntactically, using path prefixes. this could give the wrong counts in some cases, for example when modules where nested. we've rewritten the counting logic and now it's easy to be precise about module boundaries. we haven't made the change yet, however, because it will change many numbers and we want to avoid that while we're also introducing module counts. we also want to understand its effect better. once that's all happened, we should use the more accurate logic.
