cmd/compile: specialize instantiations of "certain" generic functions currently, generic functions are (almost) always shaped when instantiated, regardless of size. shapes functions get the following overhead: 1. dictionary calls: any interface operation has to go through the dictionary, and this costs eight bytes of binary size per itab; any generic call must also have a dictionary entry for its relevant dictionary. 2. interface wrappers: interface calls to non-generic methods of generic type need a wrapper to shift the input registers and stick the dictionary in rax or whatever. this tradeoff has three benefits: 1. improved icache pressure because there are simply less functions. this helps mitigate overhead (1). 2. smaller binaries, which means faster link times (some people care a lot about this, although it is hard to know when to justify it over performance -- for the sake of disclosure, i only care about benefit (2) for the sake of (1)). 3. faster build times, because fewer functions hit ssa and ultimately produce assembly that the linker has to copy around. my personal opinions aside (read: i come from c++), this is a pretty sound tradeoff between code density and performance for average code. however, i think we can do better. --- a function is specialized when rather than being shaped , a brand new, non-shaped function is stamped "as if it were a macro". specialization can coexist with shaping in the following way: 1. shaped -> specialized. requires a dictionary entry, except that this entry is a function pointer rather than a dictionary entry. 2. specialized -> shaped. exactly the same as calling a shaped function from monomorphic code: static call + pc-relative load of the dictionary. so the question is, when do we specialize[1]? i am interested in investigating the following: 1. specialization of small functions (say, inline cost <80 or <40), especially those which only call other specialized functions. 2. "hot" functions, as reported by pgo. pgo does not currently record tparams of profiled functions, although we could, in theory, reconstruct this from the symbols of monomorphic functions called through a dictionary. 3. known-hot generic functions in the standard library, via a standard-library only //go:specialize pragma. (1) and (3) are the easiest to investigate; (3) seems like it will have the easiest wins per code bloat (for example, specializing slices.sort for ints and strings). i do not know of any issues that are precisely about this topic, although 48849, 75056 appear relevant? i plan to investigate these avenues and get some performance numbers to see if there is some sensible middleground. [1]: @dr2chase told me some time ago that "there is some function somewhere in the compiler for forcing specialization of an ir.func given tparams", but i can't find such a thing. perhaps it got ripped out.

cmd/compile: omit or normalize line numbers in export data (.x) for incremental build pruning background & motivation build systems that split cmd/compile outputs into a small export data file (-o pkg.x, containing .pkgdef) for downstream compile actions and a full linker object (-linkobj pkg.a, containing go .o) for link actions can skip recompiling reverse dependencies when pkg.x is unchanged. however, because unified ir encodes source line/column numbers (src.pos) and internal linker symbol indices into .pkgdef, internal edits to a source file—such as adding comments, blank lines, or unexported functions above an exported declaration—shift line numbers and change pkg.x. when a core library with many reverse dependencies is edited, this forces all downstream packages to recompile even when the exported api and inlineable function bodies are unchanged. discussion context from cl 837805 in cl 837805 from .x export data while preserving full source positions in the package's own go .o (.a) archive. in the review discussion on [cl 837805]( it was noted that because export data includes the bodies of functions that can be inlined across packages, omitting line numbers from .x causes cross-package inlined frames in stack backtraces to lose their inner line numbers. we'd like to discuss whether there is an approach here that would be acceptable to the go toolchain—for example, explicitly indicating in stack traces/diagnostics when a line number was omitted due to -nolinenum, or another way to stabilize .x export data across line shifts without degrading stack backtraces.

(startcpuprofile // then warns that the rate is already set; that is expected.) runtime.setcpuprofilerate(1000) pprof.startcpuprofile(io.discard) go func() { for { runtime.gc() } }() for start := time.now(); time.since(start) the 71818 builder logs show the same thing: a crash report, then "test killed: ran too long (4m0s)". the hang has nothing to do with wow64. any fault inside winthrow can trigger it: 1. winthrow marks the process as panicking with panicking.store(1) directly, so m.dying stays 0. 2. its tracebacktrap faults on the garbage context (pc=0, sp=0). the nested throw → startpanic m sees dying == 0, so it increments panicking to 2. 3. dopanic m decrements it to 1, concludes that "some other m is panicking", and calls lock(&deadlock) twice. that thread waits forever for itself. a full dump of a hung process shows the throwing thread in dopanic m → lock2 → semasleep. what did you expect to see? the process exits with status 2 after printing the crash report. fix (@prattmic, 2022) changes winthrow to use startpanic m, which fixes this hang for the reproducer (its 2022 trybot run failed testg0stackoverflow on windows, so it needs re-checking against current master). with it applied to master be1160f2a4, all 237 runs exited promptly with status 2. 235 showed the exception 0x100c7 crash; the other 2 failed with "unexpected return pc", which is the same corruption. possibly related: 50144.

proposal: all: add goriscv64ogo enviornment variable for riscv64 proposal details abstract add a new environment variable, goriscv64ogo ( go riscv64 o ptimization g uidance o ptions), for goarch=riscv64. it declares performance guarantees , not just feature availability. the first two options are oilsm and ovlt, matching risc-v international's pow - optimization guidance options proposal. background goriscv64 only says which risc-v features exist. it does not say whether they are fast. as a result, go must generate pessimistic code on riscv64: it avoids unaligned memory accesses and uses conservative vector lmul settings. risc-v pow introduces optimization guidance options to express performance contracts: - oilsm : hardware handles unaligned scalar/vector memory accesses efficiently. - ovlt : vector execution time depends on dynamic vl, not static vlmax. see: risc-v pow - optimization guidance options oilsm: not formally adopted by gcc or llvm. gcc models related behavior through machine properties; see [gcc pr target/126640]( llvm has +unaligned-scalar-mem and +unaligned-vector-mem, but explicitly warns that misaligned accesses may still be slow; see [llvm issue 110454]( ovlt: not formally adopted. llvm merged a related tuning feature, +vl-dependent-latency, in [llvm pr 146746]( the commit message says it can be renamed to +ovlt if ratified. gcc discussions mention adopting ovlt after approval. implication: go can lead here, but should track pow ratification and align goriscv64ogo with gcc/llvm once they finalize their syntax. compatibility fully backward compatible. default empty. older go versions ignore unknown environment variables. non-riscv64 platforms ignore it. implementation 1. parse goriscv64ogo in src/internal/buildcfg/cfg.go. 2. emit riscv64.oilsm and riscv64.ovlt build tags. 3. add assembly macros in src/runtime/asm riscv64.h. 4. update compiler backend and runtime assembly under those tags. 5. wait for risc-v pow ratification before freezing names. open issues - should runtime verify declared performance guarantees?

crypto/internal/fips140/tls12: mastersecret records sha-384 as non-approved go version go1.27.1; also present on master as of 2026-09-30. what did you do? read mastersecret in src/crypto/internal/fips140/tls12/tls12.go, which records the service indicator for the tls 1.2 extended master secret: go case sha512.digest: if h.size() != 46 && h.size() != 64 { fips140.recordnonapproved() } what did you expect to see? sha-384 recorded as approved. the comment above quotes the condition "p hash uses either sha-256, sha-384 or sha-512", and sha-384's output size is 48 bytes (sha512.size384). what did you see instead? h.size() is never 46, so a tls 1.2 extended master secret computed with sha-384 (e.g. any tls ecdhe with aes 256 gcm sha384 suite) records non-approved in fips 140-3 mode. sha-512 is recorded correctly. the fix is a one-character change: diff - if h.size() != 46 && h.size() != 64 { + if h.size() != 48 && h.size() != 64 { found while running go's crypto tests against an alternative module implementation; a test asserting the indicator for mastersecret with sha512.new384 would have caught it.

postgresql: endless time ranges no longer round-trip since 8.1 (silent no-op updates when the range is in the primary key) since rails 8.1 the postgresql adapter writes an endless date/time range (t...) as [t,infinity) instead of [t,), but only when the bound's class is exactly date, datetime or time. an activesupport::timewithzone in utc still writes [t,). ranges read back from the database have a time begin, so writing one back encodes [t,infinity), which postgres treats as a different value from the stored [t,). as a result: - querying by a range read from a row misses that row - update!, save! and destroy on a record whose primary key includes the range affect no row, while still reporting success this started with 51920 in 8.1.0 and is not in the 8.1 release notes or upgrade guide. it also happens on main. steps to reproduce needs an empty postgresql database (database url, default postgres:///rails range bug). ruby frozen string literal: true require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "rails" if you want to test against edge rails replace the previous line with this: gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main" gem "pg" end require "active record/railtie" require "minitest/autorun" any empty postgresql database. env["database url"] ||= "postgres:///rails range bug" class testapp < rails::application config.load defaults rails::version::string.to f config.eager load = false config.logger = logger.new($stdout) config.secret key base = "secret key base" config.active record.encryption.primary key = "primary key" config.active record.encryption.deterministic key = "deterministic key" config.active record.encryption.key derivation salt = "key derivation salt" end rails.application.initialize! activerecord::schema.define do create table :events, force: true do |t| t.tstzrange :period, null: false end create table :rules, primary key: [:key, :period], force: true do |t| t.integer :key, null: false t.tstzrange :period, null: false t.string :name end end class event < activerecord::base end class rule < activerecord::base end class bugtest < activesupport::testcase def test endless range is stored the same whatever the class of its begin time = time.current with time with zone = event.create!(period: time...) with time = event.create!(period: time.utc...) assert equal stored period(with time with zone), stored period(with time) end def test endless range read back finds its own row event = event.create!(period: time.current...) period = event.find(event.id).period assert event.where(id: event.id, period:).exists? end def test updating a record whose primary key holds an endless range rule.create!(key: 1, period: time.current..., name: "before") rule.find by!(key: 1).update!(name: "after") assert equal "after", rule.find by!(key: 1).name end private aliased so active record doesn't cast it back to a range, which hides the difference. def stored period(event) event.where(id: event.id).pick(arel.sql("period::text as stored")) end end expected behavior all three tests pass, as they do on 8.0.5.1: 1. an endless range is stored the same way whatever the class of its begin. 2. a range read back from a row finds that row. 3. updating a record whose primary key includes an endless range updates it. actual behavior all three fail on 8.1.4 and on main (5afc71aa29): 1. the same endless range is stored differently depending on the class of its begin: -"\"2026-10-02 12:23:14.436961+00\",)" +"[\"2026-10-02 12:23:14.436961+00\",infinity)" 2. event.where(id: event.id, period: event.find(event.id).period).exists? is false. 3. update! returns true, but the row is unchanged: expected: "after" actual: "before" cause [ 51920 writes infinity for a nil end when date or time range? is true. that method compares range.begin.class and range.end.class with [date, datetime, time], so the encoding depends on the bound's exact class: - time, datetime and date get infinity. - an activesupport::timewithzone in utc passes through the attribute type unchanged and gets an empty bound. in any other zone, the type converts it to a time with getutc, so it gets infinity. reading goes through oid::range cast value, which returns t...nil for both t,) and [t,infinity), with a time begin. writing that value back, as a bind or as a primary key in a where, therefore encodes [t,infinity) and no longer matches the stored [t,). rows that mean "open-ended" also end up in two forms, and upper inf() and upper(col) is null (partial indexes, check constraints, scopes) see only the empty-bound form. on 8.1.4, destroy on a record whose primary key includes the range likewise reports success and leaves the row. on main, [ 56062). go back to an empty bound for the end of an exclusive range and for a nil begin, which a ruby range can't exclude anyway. detect date and time bounds by behaviour (acts like?(:date) || acts like?(:time)) rather than by exact class. every value rails reads would then encode to what is stored, except rows already written with an infinite bound by 8.1 or main. a config option choosing between empty bounds and ±infinity would also work for us. system configuration rails version : 8.1.4; also main (8.2.0.alpha, 5afc71aa29). 8.0.5.1 passes. ruby version : 3.3.11 postgresql version : 18.4

exceptionwrapper build backtrace copies every resolver template cache on each exception, including routing errors ( 13 mb per 404 on 8.1, 7 mb on main) steps to reproduce on 8.1, actiondispatch::exceptionwrapper initialize calls build backtrace ( 58686 made it lazy on main, see below), which walks actionview::pathregistry.all resolvers and calls resolver.built templates on each of them, to map backtrace frames that fall inside a compiled template back to the template source: filesystemresolver built templates is @unbound templates.values.flatten.flat map(&:built templates): concurrent::map values copies the whole map, and @unbound templates holds one entry per looked-up template path, misses included — so every resolver searched before the one holding a template gets an entry for it. the cost therefore grows with templates × resolvers, and it is paid by every exception, twice per request with the production error pages (once by debugexceptions, once by showexceptions). a routing error, whose backtrace can never go through a template, pays it too — which makes every 404 from a vulnerability scanner allocate megabytes. the script below renders 5,000 templates once each (what a long-running process ends up doing, or what actionview::precompiler now does at boot on main), with 15 extra view paths standing in for engines, then measures one 404 with the production error pages. ruby frozen string literal: true require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "rails", "8.1.4" end require "action controller/railtie" require "objspace" require "tmpdir" templates: templates rendered once each, as a long-running process ends up doing (or as actionview::precompiler does at boot on main). resolvers: view paths searched before the one holding the templates, as engines and gems add. templates = integer(env.fetch("templates", "5000")) resolvers = integer(env.fetch("resolvers", "15")) root = dir.mktmpdir view paths = array.new(resolvers) { |i| file.join(root, "engine {i}", "app", "views").tap { |p| fileutils.mkdir p(p) } } app views = file.join(root, "app", "views") fileutils.mkdir p(file.join(app views, "pages")) templates.times { |i| file.write(file.join(app views, "pages", "page {i}.html.erb"), " page \n") } class testapp < rails::application config.root = root config.load defaults 8.1 config.eager load = false config.enable reloading = false config.secret key base = "secret" config.hosts.clear config.logger = logger.new(nil) production error pages: no debug page, only showexceptions. config.consider all requests local = false config.action dispatch.show exceptions = :all routes.append { get "/pages/:id", to: "pages show" } end class pagescontroller < actioncontroller::base def show render "pages/page {params[:id]}" end end pagescontroller.view paths = view paths + [app views] testapp.initialize! def request(path) testapp.call(rack::mockrequest.env for(path)) end templates.times { |i| request("/pages/ {i}") } cached = actionview::pathregistry.all resolvers.sum { |r| r.instance variable get(:@unbound templates)&.size.to i } puts "rails {rails.version}, {actionview::pathregistry.all resolvers.size} resolvers, {cached} cached template lookups" 3.times { request("/wp-login.php") } gc.start gc.disable objectspace.trace object allocations { request("/wp-login.php") } bytes = 0 objectspace.each object { |o| bytes += objectspace.memsize of(o) if objectspace.allocation sourcefile(o) } gc.enable puts "one 404: {(bytes / 1 048 576.0).round(2)} mb allocated, status {request('/wp-login.php').first}" n = 100 started = process.clock gettime(process::clock monotonic) n.times { request("/wp-login.php") } puts " {n} x 404: {((process.clock gettime(process::clock monotonic) - started) 1000 / n).round(2)} ms per request" expected behavior a 404 costs the same whatever the number of templates the process has compiled: the backtrace of an actioncontroller::routingerror has no template frame to map. actual behavior ruby 4.0.7, rails 8.1.4, 16 resolvers: | | allocated by one 404 | time per 404 | | --- | --- | --- | | templates=0 | 0.06 mb | 0.18 ms | | templates=5000 | 13.33 mb | 27.65 ms | | templates=5000, with the change below | 0.05 mb | 0.14 ms | on our production application (about 81,000 cached lookups across 15 resolvers, templates precompiled at boot), measured on a staging container: 10.0 mb allocated and 16.9 ms per 404, of which 9.7 mb are allocated by built templates (the concurrent::map values copies and the arrays built from them). with the change below, 0.24 mb and 0.9 ms. on main, 58686 builds the backtrace lazily, which removes the showexceptions half. but build backtrace itself is unchanged, and debugexceptions log error still reads wrapper.exception trace whenever rescued responses are logged, which is the default. replaying the script above on 8.1.4 with the change from 58686 copied in: | | allocated by one 404 | time per 404 | build backtrace calls | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 8.1.4 | 13.33 mb | 27.65 ms | 2 | | 58686, default settings | 7.08 mb | 14.05 ms | 1 (debugexceptions) | | 58686, log rescued responses = false | 0.03 mb | 0.09 ms | 0 | so with the default settings every 404 still walks every resolver once. main also has actionview::precompiler, which fills these caches at boot, so a process pays that cost from its first exception. possible fix a compiled template method is named by actionview::template method name, " {identifier method name} {@identifier.hash} { id }" with - replaced by , where identifier method name only keeps [a-z ]: so the resolvers only need to be walked when at least one frame has that shape; otherwise no frame can be mapped, and the original method returns the locations unchanged anyway. this is what we run as a patch: ruby template method name = /\a [a-z ] \d+ \d+\z/ def build backtrace locations = @exception.backtrace locations || [] return super if locations.any? { |location| template method name.match?(location.base label) } locations.dup end the pattern accepts negative hashes ( before the digits) and does not match ordinary underscore-prefixed methods such as run process action callbacks; a false positive only falls back to the current behavior. a sturdier fix in rails itself could avoid depending on the method name format altogether, for instance by keeping a registry from method name to template filled when a template is compiled, instead of rebuilding it from every resolver on each exception. happy to open a pr for whichever approach you prefer. system configuration rails version : 8.1.4 (build backtrace and built templates identical on main) ruby version : 4.0.7

activemodel::type::biginteger cast truncates large integer strings to 16 bytes, silently corrupting the value steps to reproduce ruby require "active model" type = activemodel::type::biginteger.new type.cast("18446744073709551615") also reproducible through activerecord::type::decimalwithoutscale (used automatically for decimal columns without a scale, e.g. t.decimal "my field", precision: 20), since it now subclasses activemodel::type::biginteger. expected behavior returns 18446744073709551615 actual behavior returns 1844674407370955 the value is silently truncated to 16 significant digits and corrupted, instead of raising or returning the full integer. root cause: activemodel::type::integer cast value now truncates the input string to limit 4 bytes before calling .to i (added in 8.1.4 as a dos mitigation). biginteger overrides max value/min value to remove the range limit, but does not override limit, so it still falls back to default limit = 4 → truncates to 16 bytes. this silently corrupts any big integer attribute, or any decimal column without a scale, holding a value longer than 16 digits. not sure on how you want this to be fixed. system configuration rails version: 8.1.4 ruby version: 4.0.7 context column affected: decimal(20,0) (postgres numeric(20), no scale) — used to store a client-side uint64 that doesn't fit in a signed bigint. workaround ruby in the model attribute :my field, :decimal, precision: 20 this forces activemodel::type::decimal casting instead of the auto-inferred activerecord::type::decimalwithoutscale (which subclasses the buggy biginteger), avoiding the truncation.

activesupport::isolatedexecutionstate.share with shallow-copies nested state, leaking mutations (e.g. activerecord's connected to stack) across threads steps to reproduce ruby require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "activesupport", "8.0.5.1" end require "active support" require "active support/isolated execution state" activerecord::core.connected to stack stores its stack under exactly this key, and actioncontroller::live calls share with to copy a streaming request's execution state into the thread it spawns for the response body (actionpack/lib/action controller/metal/live.rb): activesupport::isolatedexecutionstate.share with(t1, except: self.class.live streaming excluded keys) main thread = thread.current main thread.active support execution state = { active record connected to stack: [] } spawned thread = thread.new do activesupport::isolatedexecutionstate.share with(main thread) the spawned thread pushes a frame onto what it believes is its own, isolated connected to stack (mirrors activerecord::core connected to). activesupport::isolatedexecutionstate[:active record connected to stack] :spawned thread shard}] same object? false actual behavior isolatedexecutionstate.share with builds the copy with other.active support execution state.dup, which is a shallow hash dup. any mutable value nested inside that hash, in particular the concurrent::array that activerecord::core.connected to stack stores under :active record connected to stack, is not copied; the same array object ends up referenced from both threads' state hashes. mutating the stack from either thread (pushing/popping a connected to frame) is visible from the other thread as well: main thread stack: [{:shard=>:spawned thread shard}] spawned thread stack: [{:shard=>:spawned thread shard}] same object? true in production this surfaces through actioncontroller::live, which spawns a thread per streaming response and calls share with to copy the original thread's execution state into it. because the connected to stack array is shared by reference rather than copied, a connected to/shard-swapping block entered on one of the two threads can push or pop a frame that the other thread then also observes, letting the streaming thread and the request thread corrupt each other's view of the current shard/role, rather than staying isolated as share with intends. concretely, this ends up failing requests because at least one of them then fails to lookup a record from the database. suggested fix changing state.dup to state.deep dup in share with fixes the reproduction above: each thread ends up with its own connected to stack array, and mutating one doesn't affect the other. we've been running with this patched in locally (monkey-patching isolatedexecutionstate.share with via prepend) without issue. one thing worth weighing before landing a blanket deep dup, though: not every value stashed in this state hash is stack-shaped, per-thread data. some keys hold what look like intentionally shared, live singletons, e.g. active record connection handler, which owns the process's connection pools via activerecord::connectionadapters::connectionhandler. only array and hash override deep dup to recurse; everything else falls back to object deep dup (duplicable? ? dup : self). connectionhandler doesn't opt out of duplicable? (that's reserved for method/unboundmethod and classes including singleton), so a blanket deep dup on the state hash would call plain dup on it: a new connectionhandler object whose internal @connection name to pool manager still points at the same underlying concurrent::map. the spawned thread would end up with a distinct object identity for something that's arguably supposed to stay the exact same object across threads. we didn't hit a concrete failure from that in our case, but the question i discussed with @tenderlove at railsworld: should share with deep-copy the whole state hash indiscriminately, or should the copy-vs-share behavior be declared per key (similar to how except: already opts individual keys out of the copy entirely)? if the latter, how would that be configured for the different frameworks? system configuration rails version : 8.0.5.1 (reproduces on main/8.1.3 too; isolatedexecutionstate share with in activesupport/lib/active support/isolated execution state.rb still does state.dup there, it was just reshaped to take a block) ruby version : 3.4.8 (also reproduces under 3.3.x and 4.0.6; not ruby-version-specific)

activesupport::timezone mapping inaccurate for manitoba activesupport::timezone::mapping maps human-friendly zone names to iana time zone identifiers: ruby "central time (us & canada)" => "america/chicago", this name implies that the us and canadian regions it covers keep the same clock. that has been true historically because manitoba and the us states in the central time zone changed their clocks on the same schedule. it will no longer be true in the near future: - per the announcement on sept 17, 2026, manitoba will remain on daylight saving time permanently and will not fall back on nov 1, 2026: america/chicago will keep observing seasonal dst. so starting nov 1, 2026, "central time (us & canada)" will resolve to america/chicago (cst, utc-6), while manitoba is actually on utc-5. any app or user using time.zone = "central time (us & canada)" as a proxy for manitoba will compute times an hour off for those users every winter, affecting scheduling, timestamps, notifications, and so on. this is the same situation as with british columbia and alberta in 58316, which was resolved in 58321 by adding "pacific time (canada)" and "alberta" entries while keeping the existing pacific time (us & canada) and mountain time (us & canada) entries for compatibility. note that the iana tz database does not yet include manitoba's change (it is not in 2026d), so correct offsets for america/winnipeg will also require a future tzdata release. the friendly name mapping is needed either way, since there is currently no friendly name for america/winnipeg. steps to reproduce ruby activesupport::timezone["central time (us & canada)"].tzinfo.name => "america/chicago" activesupport::timezone.all.find { |zone| zone.tzinfo.name == "america/winnipeg" } => nil expected behavior following 58321, a "manitoba" => "america/winnipeg" entry should be added to activesupport::timezone::mapping, with "central time (us & canada)" kept mapped to america/chicago for compatibility. actual behavior "central time (us & canada)" exclusively resolves to america/chicago, and there is no friendly name for america/winnipeg, so manitoba users have no accurate option in activesupport::timezone.all (e.g. in time zone select). system configuration rails version : 8.1.3.1 ruby version : 4.0.6

normalizes with apply to nil: true is ignored by where(attr: nil) the docs state two things: normalization applies to the keyword arguments of finder methods, and apply to nil: true applies normalization to nil. together those imply that where(attr: nil) queries the normalized value. it does not. a raw nil always generates is null. steps to reproduce ruby class createwidgets "" the normalizer, not a column default widget.where(name: nil).to sql => ... "name" is null widget.where(name: "").to sql => ... "name" = '' expected behavior both queries generate the same sql, as they already do for a normalizer running in the opposite direction. actual behavior they differ. queryattribute nil? returns early on value before type cast.nil?, so the normalizer is never consulted, even though type.serialize(nil) returns "". why this looks inconsistent rather than intended 53564 and 53580 established that a normalized attribute's query should reflect the normalized value, and added a test asserting where(name: nil).to sql == where(name: "").to sql. that assertion holds for a normalizer that maps blank to nil, and fails for one that maps nil to blank. there is no test, no doc note and no comment covering the other half. the practical consequence is dead sql. on a not null column, where(attr: nil) can never match a row, and where.not(attr: nil) matches every row. the second one fails silently, which is how we hit it. system configuration rails version: 8.1.3.1 ruby version: 4.0.6 reproduced on both sqlite3 and postgresql.

ruby schema dumper drops create schema for schemas required by extensions but outside schema search path steps to reproduce given a postgresql database where an extension is installed into a schema that is not part of schema search path: > example: postgis tiger geocoder installed into a tiger schema, while schema search path is only public, postgis > > this is a setup postgis itself recommends, since tiger/topology define many generically-named functions that can shadow ones in public. ruby config/database.yml development: adapter: postgresql database: my app development schema search path: public, postgis ruby a migration, run once, outside of schema search path's reach class installtigergeocoder ' db/schema.rb:13:in ' ' root cause 50020 (merged for 8.1) made the :ruby format schema dumper finally honor activerecord.dump schemas, which was previously only respected by the :sql (structure.sql) dumper. that's correct and desired on its own. but it means postgresql::schemadumper schemas now only emits create schema for schemas in @dump schemas (connection.current schemas, driven by schema search path when activerecord.dump schemas == :schema search path, the default): ruby def schemas(stream) schema names = @dump schemas - ["public"] ... end before 50020, this method (or its equivalent) dumped create schema for every schema that actually exists in the database, regardless of schema search path — which is exactly what's needed for a schema that a migration created and an extension depends on, but that the app deliberately keeps out of its search path. workarounds considered and their downsides: - activerecord.dump schemas = :all it restores the missing create schema lines, but also makes the dumper iterate every schema for tables/types (within each schema) which for tiger/topology dumps thousands of internal postgis/tiger geocoder tables into schema.rb that were never meant to be there. it also flips relation name into its multi-schema mode (@dump schemas.size > 1), which prefixes every table/enum name with public., producing a massive, unwanted diff. - monkeypatching postgresql::schemadumper schemas to add back the specific schemas required by extensions, without touching @dump schemas (so within each schema/relation name are unaffected) ruby module activerecord module postgisextensionschemadumper extension schemas = %w[tiger tiger data topology].freeze def schemas(stream) super extra schemas = (extension schemas & @connection.schema names) - @dump schemas return if extra schemas.empty? extra schemas.sort.each { |name| stream.puts " create schema {name.inspect}" } stream.puts end end end activesupport.on load :active record do activerecord::connectionadapters::postgresql::schemadumper.prepend activerecord::postgisextensionschemadumper end it works but requires reaching into a private rails internal. system configuration rails version : 8.1.3.1 ruby version : 4.0.5 postgresql version : 18.4 database adapter : activerecord-postgis-adapter related issues - 50020 — the pr that introduced this regression as a side effect of a legitimate fix - 49926 — the bug 50020 fixes (schema dumper ignoring dump schemas entirely, causing schemas to be over -dumped) - 30990 — older, related: extensions installed into non-default schemas losing their schema qualification in schema.rb - 17157 — same tension for structure.sql: extensions get skipped when schema search path is narrower than the database's actual schemas

should classify this as a write (it contains a stacked drop table), " \ "but it returns false because build read query regexp only checks the prefix of the string." end end on postgresql specifically, this isn't just a misclassification — sending the same string through connection.execute with no bind params (libpq's simple query protocol runs every ;-separated statement) while wrapped in activerecord::base.while preventing writes actually executes the drop table, with no readonlyerror raised: ruby activerecord::base.while preventing writes do activerecord::base.connection.execute("select 1; drop table users; --") end verified live against a real postgresql 17 database — table was gone afterward, no error. not reproducible on sqlite3 (its default execute path only runs the first statement). expected behavior write query?("select 1; drop table users; --") returns true. under while preventing writes, executing it raises activerecord::readonlyerror before anything runs. actual behavior write query? returns false. no error is raised. on postgresql, the drop table executes. cause: build read query regexp only checks that the string starts with a read keyword, with no end-anchor: ruby activerecord/lib/active record/connection adapters/abstract adapter.rb l103-l110 def self.build read query regexp( parts) :nodoc: parts += default read query parts = parts.map { |part| / {part}/i } /\a(?:[(\s]| {comment regex}) {regexp.union( parts)}/ no \z end anything after the first recognized keyword is never checked. suggested fix: add an end-anchor (or reject a bare top-level ; followed by further content) so the whole string is validated, not just the prefix. system configuration rails version : reproduced on main (a63debae6081630294cfe21554984abfbd346f43), 8.1.3.1, and 7.2.2.2 ruby version : 3.3.8

active storage fails to start on a new mac without libvips installed (cursor agent using cursor grok helped me debug this problem and prepare this issue, but i have read it all and vouch for what it says.) steps to reproduce - buy a new mac - install the ruby-vips gem - don't install libvips - try to boot the app, eg. bin/setup it will crash with: undefined method 'analysis=' for nil (nomethoderror) active storage.queues.analysis = :active storage analysis the same crash is reproduced by this script (it stubs the loaderror ruby-vips actually raises when glib is missing, so you don’t have to uninstall system libraries): ruby frozen string literal: true require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "rails", "8.1.3.1" gem "ruby-vips", "2.2.1" end module kernel alias method :require without vips stub, :require def require(name) if name == "ruby-vips" raise loaderror, << msg could not open library 'glib-2.0.0': dlopen(glib-2.0.0, 0x0005): tried: 'glib-2.0.0' (no such file). could not open library 'libglib-2.0.0.dylib': dlopen(libglib-2.0.0.dylib, 0x0005): tried: 'libglib-2.0.0.dylib' (no such file). msg end require without vips stub(name) end end require "rails/all" class bugapp < rails::application config.load defaults 8.1 end expected behavior rails boots. missing libvips is optional: set activestorage::vips available = false and skip vips-backed variants/analysis. that already happens when the error message matches /libvips|ruby-vips/. actual behavior boot fails with: undefined method 'analysis=' for nil (nomethoderror) active storage.queues.analysis = :active storage analysis that error is a red herring. what actually happens: 1. ruby-vips ffi-loads glib before libvips, so the loaderror mentions glib-2.0.0, not libvips. 2. activestorage/lib/active storage/vips.rb only swallows messages matching /libvips|ruby-vips/, so it re-raises. 3. rails/all rescues that loaderror, so active storage/engine stops half-way: config.active storage exists, config.active storage.queues was never set. 4. load defaults then does active storage.queues.analysis = … on nil. my agent thinks the fix is to just drop the matcher: ruby begin gem "ruby-vips" require "ruby-vips" activestorage::vips available = true rescue loaderror activestorage::vips available = false end i'd probably prefer a second opinion from @flavorjones before making a pr. system configuration rails version : 8.1.3.1 ruby version : 3.4.2 (arm64-darwin)

connection checkout can block for up to 100s regardless of checkout timeout when queued behind background maintenance connectionpool try to queue for background connection waits up to a hardcoded 100 seconds for a connection tied up in background maintenance, ignoring the pool's configured checkout timeout entirely: ruby def try to queue for background connection return unless @maintaining > 0 synchronize do return unless @maintaining > @available.num waiting @available.poll(100) end end if maintenance (e.g. a keepalive ping via conn.active?) stalls because the database server or a network hop is slow or unresponsive, checkout blocks for up to 100 seconds regardless of what checkout timeout is set to -- effectively a lock. reproduction from @nateberkopec: we hit this in production at gusto during a rails 8.1 upgrade, triggered by latency on one database. raised originally in 54175. pr incoming that bounds the wait to checkout timeout instead of the hardcoded 100.

keepalive: false in database.yml is silently ignored hashconfig keepalive treats a literal keepalive: false in database.yml the same as the key being absent, since false is falsy in ruby: ruby def keepalive keepalive = (configuration hash[:keepalive] || 600).to f keepalive if keepalive > 0 end ruby hashconfig.new("test", "primary", { adapter: "trilogy", keepalive: false }).keepalive => 600.0, not nil we hit this at gusto: after our first rails 8.1 upgrade attempt caused connection pool contention in production, we added keepalive: false believing it disabled keep-alive pings, and only found out it was still fully active (with the default threshold) while investigating a separate checkout-blocking bug. keepalive: 0 is the only value that actually disables it (0.to f > 0 is false), which isn't obvious from the option's own boolean-sounding name. raised originally in 54175, pr incoming.

sqlite table reconstruction cascade-deletes child rows inside transactional migrations steps to reproduce this is my first time working with sqlite, so i may be missing something obvious about the expected migration setup or behavior. this reproduces on active record 8.1.3.1 and on rails main at bd885fa do source " gem "activerecord", "8.1.3.1" gem "sqlite3", " > 2.1" gem "minitest" end require "active record" require "minitest/autorun" require "tmpdir" class sqlitecascademigrationtest 0", name: "authors name present" ) connection.create table(:books) do |table| table.references :author, null: false, foreign key: { on delete: :cascade } end connection.execute("insert into authors (id, name) values (1, 'douglas adams')") connection.execute("insert into books (id, author id) values (1, 1)") migration directory = file.join(directory, "migrate") dir.mkdir(migration directory) file.write( file.join(migration directory, "20260909000000 remove author name check.rb"), << ruby class removeauthornamecheck < activerecord::migration[8.1] def change remove check constraint :authors, name: "authors name present" end end ruby ) migration context = activerecord::migrationcontext.new( migration directory, activerecord::base.connection pool.schema migration, activerecord::base.connection pool.internal metadata ) migration context.migrate assert equal 1, connection.select value("select count( ) from authors") assert equal 1, connection.select value("select count( ) from books"), "the migration must not cascade-delete books while rebuilding authors" ensure activerecord::base.connection pool.disconnect! end end end expected behavior removing the check constraint rebuilds the authors table without deleting records from the referencing books table. both assertions pass. actual behavior the authors row survives, but the books row is deleted: text the migration must not cascade-delete books while rebuilding authors. expected: 1 actual: 0 this appears related to 55866 and 55907. that fix moved disable referential integrity outside the sqlite adapter's internal reconstruction transaction. however, the migration runner has already opened an outer transaction because sqlite reports support for transactional ddl. sqlite treats pragma foreign keys = off as a no-op while that transaction is active, so dropping the original parent table still fires the cascade. the regression tests added by 55907 call adapter methods directly rather than running the operation through activerecord::migrationcontext, so they do not exercise the outer migration transaction. adding disable ddl transaction! to the generated migration makes this reproduction pass, but i could not find that requirement documented for ordinary sqlite schema operations. system configuration rails version : active record 8.1.3.1; also reproduced on rails main at bd885fa ruby version : 4.0.6 sqlite3 gem version : 2.9.6 sqlite version : 3.53.2

activesupport::json.decode raises argumenterror with json gem >= 3.0 (positional options arg removed) steps to reproduce 1. new rails 8.1.3.1 app (default propshaft + cookie session store), ruby 4.0.6. 2. do not pin the json gem — bundler resolves it to whatever is newest/bundled (currently 3.0.0, released 2026-09-07). 3. load any page once so a session cookie is set (e.g. get /). 4. request the same page again, sending that session cookie back. ruby minimal repro outside a full request cycle require "active support" require "active support/json" activesupport::json.decode('{"foo":"bar"}') argumenterror: wrong number of arguments (given 2, expected 1) expected behavior the cookie/session (or any signed/encrypted payload using activesupport::json.decode) decodes normally, as it does with json = 3.0 def parse(source, on load: nil, object class: nil, array class: nil, options); end but activesupport::json.decode still calls it positionally (activesupport/lib/active support/json/decoding.rb:25 data = ::json.parse(json, options) ... since options defaults to {}, this previously worked fine as the positional-hash form; with json 3.0 it now raises argumenterror: wrong number of arguments (given 2, expected 1) whenever it's ever called with a non-empty argument list (it's always called with 2 args here, json and options, regardless of whether options is empty). this affects activesupport::messageencryptor/messageverifier message reading in particular, so anything that decrypts/verifies a previously-issued signed payload breaks — session cookies, csrf token metadata, signed active storage/global ids, etc. because a freshly issued cookie is only ever encrypted (write path), not decrypted (read path), this only manifests on repeat requests carrying an existing cookie — which made it look at first like a browser-vs-curl or environment-specific issue, when it's actually 100% reproducible any time a payload gets decoded. suggested fix update activesupport::json.decode (and any other internal callers passing a positional options hash to json.parse) to use options instead: ruby def decode(json, options) data = ::json.parse(json, options) ... workaround pinning gem "json", " > 2.21" in the gemfile restores the old positional-argument json.parse signature and resolves the issue until rails ships a release compatible with json >= 3.0.

nameerror: uninitialized constant activesupport::ractors::ractor on jruby steps to reproduce save the following script as repro.rb and run ruby repro.rb on jruby 10.1.0.0. the minitest pin only avoids an unrelated native extension issue with the prism dependency of minitest 6 on jruby. ruby require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "activesupport", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main" gem "minitest", " = "4.0". jruby 10 reports ruby version as "4.0.0" but does not define the ractor constant, so the shims delegate to a constant that does not exist. there are further references behind that first one (a module-level ractor.respond to?(:store if absent) check, and ractors.main? reached from activesupport::notifications at load), so the constant is required as soon as the active support core extensions load. active support/ractors.rb was introduced in 57526, and the call in the backtrace above comes from 57857. i am aware of the earlier discussion about jruby support in i am filing this issue to document the reproduction, and whether to address it is open for discussion.

bin/docker-entrypoint not working when passing parameters to bin/rails server hi, using docker-image alpine:ruby for installation, podman instead of docker, and installing rails 8.1.3.1: usually i do use my own entrypoint script when running rails in docker, but for testing purposes i just built a docker image of a clean upstream rails installation, i.e. just gem install rails rails new app which creates a bin/docker-entrypoint containing if running the rails server then create or migrate existing database if [ "${@: -2:1}" == "./bin/rails" ] && [ "${@: -1:1}" == "server" ]; then ./bin/rails db:prepare fi where "${@: -2:1}" is the second last, and "${@: -1:1}" the very last parameter passed to the entrypoint. i.e. it needs to be run with cmd set to ./bin/rails server as the last two parameters to match this condition. which does not work for standard networking, i.e. not using host mode. why? by default a rails app run with puma binds to 127.0.0.1:3000 and thus cannot be reached from outside the container e.g. with port 3000:3000, because by default ports from outside to connect to the ip address of the virtual docker environment and not 127.0.0.1. therefore, it must be run as ./bin/rails server -b 0.0.0.0 (or the ip address of the docker container) but then, the condition in the entrypoint script is not met and thus db is not prepared. since docker treats containers working together (e.g. docker compose) differently and puts them all on the same machine, connecting each other as 127.0.0.1, while podman creates a pod with virtual machine addresses, this might work with docker, but not with podman. since you can't know what a user will use to run a container once it is build, it is considered a bug when a container works with one (docker or podman) and not both. why does this condition use the second last and very last command parameter, instead of first and second, thus making it impossible to pass any additional parameters (such as -b 0.0.0.0) ? even when using plain docker, there could be good reasons to pass additional command line parameters to bin/rails server. regards

ractor.store if absent deadlock in schemacontext attributes schemacontext attributes uses ractor.store if absent to initialize an attributes object. however, attributes.new calls attributeregistration apply pending attribute modifications, which walks up the superclass chain and applies attribute modifiers from them (e.g. from encryptablerecord). those modifiers call columns hash on the superclass, which triggers load schema, which calls schemacontext attributes again, thus calling ractor.store if absent, causing a deadlock. this issue was introduced by 51a2a815a2663b3a35f6af862b27b1dbd2287528. steps to reproduce ruby frozen string literal: true require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "rails", path: '/home/kyrofa/src/gems/rails' gem "sqlite3" end require "active record/railtie" require "minitest/autorun" env["database url"] = "sqlite3::memory:" class testapp < rails::application config.load defaults rails::version::string.to f config.eager load = false config.logger = logger.new($stdout) config.secret key base = "secret key base" config.active record.encryption.primary key = "primary key" config.active record.encryption.deterministic key = "deterministic key" config.active record.encryption.key derivation salt = "key derivation salt" end rails.application.initialize! activerecord::schema.define do create table :base models, force: true do |t| t.string :encrypted attr end end class basemodel < activerecord::base encrypts :encrypted attr end class childmodel < basemodel end class bugtest < activesupport::testcase def test store if absent deadlock activerecord::base.connection.transaction do childmodel.create!(encrypted attr: "test") raise activerecord::rollback end assert true, "no deadlock" end end expected behavior this should work just fine. actual behavior it deadlocks ever since 51a2a815a2663b3a35f6af862b27b1dbd2287528: threaderror: deadlock; recursive locking. system configuration rails version : main ruby version : v3.4.9

repro.rb 1) failure: bugtest test streaming worker thread releases its connection: expected ["action controller.live-worker-1"] to be empty. in production this exhausted the pool: five concurrent applicationrecord.connected to(role: :writing) stops lifting the readonly guard after activerecord::base re-establishes the primary pool summary an application that sets primary abstract class and calls connects to names its primary connection pool "applicationrecord". applicationrecord.connected to(role: :writing) then lifts the readonly guard correctly. if any code re-establishes that same pool through activerecord::base, the pool descriptor is renamed to "activerecord::base". from that point applicationrecord.connected to(role: :writing) no longer lifts the guard, and the write raises activerecord::readonlyerror. only activerecord::base.connected to(role: :writing) still works. activerecord::migration.maintain test schema! performs such a re-establish, so the guard behaves one way in a booted application and the other way under rails/test help. steps to reproduce the script below needs no rails application. run it with ruby repro.rb. ruby require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "activerecord", "8.1.3.1" gem "sqlite3" end require "active record" require "minitest/autorun" db = "/tmp/railsbug/test.sqlite3" file.delete(db) if file.exist?(db) activerecord::base.configurations = { "default env" => { "primary" => { "adapter" => "sqlite3", "database" => db }, "primary replica" => { "adapter" => "sqlite3", "database" => db, "replica" => true } } } class applicationrecord < activerecord::base primary abstract class connects to database: { writing: :primary, reading: :primary replica } end class post < applicationrecord; end activerecord::base.connected to(role: :writing) do applicationrecord.lease connection.create table(:posts, force: true) { |t| t.string :title } end def descriptor name applicationrecord.lease connection.connection descriptor.instance variable get(:@name) end what the databaseselector middleware wraps every get in, and what an action does when that get must write. def write under readonly request activerecord::base.connected to(role: :writing, prevent writes: true) do applicationrecord.connected to(role: :writing) do post.create!(title: "x") end end end class applicationrecordlifttest < minitest::test def test lift works then stops working after a primary class reestablish assert equal "applicationrecord", descriptor name write under readonly request puts "before: descriptor= {descriptor name.inspect} write=ok" exactly what activerecord::tasks::databasetasks with temporary pool does, by way of activerecord::migration.maintain test schema! in rails/test help. db config = activerecord::base.configurations.configs for(env name: "default env", name: "primary") activerecord::base.connection handler.establish connection(db config) puts "after: descriptor= {descriptor name.inspect}" write under readonly request puts "after: write=ok" end end expected behavior applicationrecord.connected to(role: :writing) lifts the readonly guard on the primary database both times. the script prints two write=ok lines. actual behavior before: descriptor="applicationrecord" write=ok after: descriptor="activerecord::base" activerecord::readonlyerror: write query attempted while in readonly mode: insert into "posts" ("title") values (?) returning "id" the one establish connection call between the two writes is the only difference. analysis two behaviours combine. 1. the adapter guard compares the frame by class name , not by class identity. ruby active record/core.rb:205 def self.preventing writes?(class name) connected to stack.reverse each do |hash| return hash[:prevent writes] if !hash[:prevent writes].nil? && hash[:klasses].include?(base) return hash[:prevent writes] if !hash[:prevent writes].nil? && hash[:klasses].any? { |klass| klass.name == class name } end false end with the stack [{prevent writes: true, klasses: [activerecord::base]}, {prevent writes: false, klasses: [applicationrecord]}] and class name == "activerecord::base", the applicationrecord frame matches neither branch. the lookup falls through to the outer frame and returns true. applicationrecord.current preventing writes matches by class identity, so it returns false at the same moment. the two apis disagree. 2. the descriptor name is whichever primary class established the pool last. ruby connection adapters/abstract/connection handler.rb:131 update the pool config's connection class if it differs. this is used for ensuring that activerecord::base and the primary abstract class use the same pool. without this granular swapping will not work correctly. if owner name.primary class? && (existing pool config.connection descriptor != owner name) existing pool config.connection descriptor = owner name end activerecord::base.primary class? is also true, so a re-establish through activerecord::base renames the application's descriptor. the result is the failure the comment sets out to prevent, in the other direction. activerecord::tasks::databasetasks with temporary pool is one such re-establish. its ensure restores the original db config but not the original descriptor: ruby active record/tasks/database tasks.rb:558 def with temporary pool(db config, clobber: false) original db config = migration class.connection db config migration class == activerecord::base pool = migration class.connection handler.establish connection(db config, clobber: clobber) yield pool ensure migration class.connection handler.establish connection(original db config, clobber: clobber) end activerecord::migration.maintain test schema! reaches it through load schema if pending! and any schema needs update?. rails/test help calls maintain test schema! at require time, so every test process starts with the descriptor renamed. impact an application that follows the multiple databases guide, enables config.active record.database selector, and writes during a get sees the documented granular form work in development and production, then fail in tests. activerecord::base.connected to works in both, but it lifts the guard on every database rather than on the one the application names. an oauth callback is the common case, because the provider redirects back with a get that must store a token. related - 40559, preventing writes? does not work in the test environment - 41030, fix preventing writes for applicationrecord that fix introduced the descriptor and the connection handler.rb:131 clause above. this report is about a path that still renames the descriptor after the fact. system configuration rails version: 8.1.3.1 ruby version: 3.4.1

activerecord::coders::json encode options raises nameerror on stable/main summary activerecord::coders::json.new(encode options: ...) raises nameerror on 8-1-stable and current main because the initializer merges an undefined local named options instead of its encode options keyword. this appears to come from 58601. reproduction ruby require "active record" activerecord::coders::json.new(encode options: { escape html entities: false }) nameerror: undefined local variable or method options the affected line is: ruby encode options = encode options ? default encode options.merge(options) : default encode options changing merge(options) to merge(encode options) preserves defaults and the caller override. verification a one-line source candidate passes: - six standalone checks with json 3.0.0.rc1; - the same six checks with rails' currently locked json 2.21.2; - the focused active record json coder suite (4/4). rails 8.1.3.1 predates this regression, so no consumer pin is proposed. songstats does not call this nodoc coder api directly; this report is for the stable/current regression itself.

activemodel integer string cap drops values after leading zeroes current main commit 57368 limits activemodel::type::integer cast value by taking the first limit 4 bytes before to i. that changes valid conversions when whitespace or zero padding consumes the prefix, while serialize still calls to i on the complete string and does not share the new bound. examples on current main with the default 16-byte cap: ruby type = activemodel::type::integer.new type.cast("0" 100 + "1") => 0, expected 1 type.cast(" \t-" + "0" 100 + "12tail") => 0, expected -12 type.serialize("0" 100 + "1") => 1 (different path) a focused candidate uses one bounded conversion helper for casting and serialization. it consumes ascii to i whitespace/sign/leading-zero syntax, passes at most limit 4 significant digits to to i, and preserves the current cap for a 17-digit significant value. verification on ruby 4.0.6: - current main reproduces both lost-value cases - six-check external model passes the candidate, including receiver-size instrumentation showing serialize never passes more than 16 bytes to to i - focused active model integer suite: 22 runs / 63 assertions / 0 failures - ruby syntax and git diff --check pass the stable 8.1.3.1 release predates 57368, so this is an unreleased-main regression plus consistency follow-up. i have not opened a pr because this audit is constrained from adding the rails regression tests expected for bug-fix pull requests; the executable model and source candidate are available for maintainer review.

sourceannotationextractor.enumerate mutates caller options rails::sourceannotationextractor.enumerate deletes :dirs from the caller's options hash, then display adds :indent to that same hash. reusing or inspecting options after enumeration therefore observes unrelated internal normalization. executable reproduction on rails 8.1.3.1 and current main: ruby require "rails/source annotation extractor" require "stringio" require "tmpdir" dir.mktmpdir do |dir| file.write(file.join(dir, "example.rb"), " todo: preserve options\n") options = { dirs: [dir], tag: true } expected = options.dup stdout = $stdout $stdout = stringio.new begin rails::sourceannotationextractor.enumerate("todo", options) ensure $stdout = stdout end raise "mutated: {options.inspect}" unless options == expected end both the release and current main change the hash to { tag: true, indent: 1 }. a focused source candidate duplicates options at the public enumerate boundary and uses options.merge(indent: ...) inside display. the model then passes while rails notes output is unchanged. ruby syntax and git diff --check pass. i have not opened a pr because this audit is constrained from adding the upstream regression test expected for rails bug-fix pull requests; the complete executable case and two-line source correction are provided here for maintainer review.

dependent: :destroy async on has many :through destroys target records instead of join records summary dependent: :destroy async behaves differently from synchronous dependency handling on a has many :through association. the documentation says that when :through is used, the join records are deleted rather than the associated target records. however, the asynchronous path collects ids from the final target model and activerecord::destroyassociationasyncjob destroys those target records. this can unexpectedly delete shared records and run their destruction callbacks. reproduction ruby class team false expected behavior only the join record connecting team one and user should be destroyed. the user and the second team's membership should remain: ruby user.exists?(user.id) => true membership.exists?(team: team two, user: user) => true this would match the documented behavior and the synchronous has many :through deletion path. actual behavior the asynchronous dependency handler obtains ids from the final target model (user) and enqueues them for destruction. the job consequently destroys the shared user itself rather than the join record. relevant locations: - activerecord/lib/active record/associations.rb - activerecord/lib/active record/associations/has many association.rb - activerecord/lib/active record/associations/has many through association.rb - activerecord/lib/active record/destroy association async job.rb - activerecord/test/activejob/destroy association async test.rb the existing active record test appears to expect the target records to be destroyed, while the documentation says the join records should be destroyed. could maintainers clarify which behavior is intended? this was previously reviewed by the rails security team, classified as a non-security issue, and directed to the public tracker. i would be happy to prepare a pull request once the intended behavior is confirmed.

postgresql primary key introspection includes include columns steps to reproduce ruby frozen string literal: true require "bundler/inline" gemfile(true) do source " gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main" gem "pg" end require "active record" require "minitest/autorun" activerecord::base.establish connection( env.fetch("database url", "postgresql://localhost/activerecord unittest") ) class coveringprimarykeytest < minitest::test def test primary keys exclude included columns connection = activerecord::base.connection connection.execute "drop table if exists covering pk records" connection.execute "create table covering pk records (tenant id integer not null, id integer not null, name text)" connection.execute "create unique index covering pk on covering pk records (tenant id, id) include (name)" connection.execute "alter table covering pk records add primary key using index covering pk" assert equal ["tenant id", "id"], connection.primary keys("covering pk records") ensure connection&.execute "drop table if exists covering pk records" end end expected behavior primary keys("covering pk records") returns only the constrained key columns: ruby ["tenant id", "id"] actual behavior it also returns the non-key column added with include: ruby ["tenant id", "id", "name"] active record currently reads pg index.indkey, which contains both key and included columns. this can cause bulk upserts to treat included columns as read-only and silently omit their updates. proposed fix: 58555 system configuration rails version : main; also reproduced with rails 7.2.3.2 ruby version : 3.3.12 postgresql version : 11 or newer

sql server: failed savepoint rollback hides the original error and leaves a stale transaction level, so later transactions never commit laravel version 13.34.0 (also current 13.x; managestransactions is unchanged) php version 8.4.26 (reproduction); also seen on 8.5.10 in production database driver & version sql server 2022 (mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest), pdo sqlsrv 5.13.3, odbc driver 18 for sql server description some sql server errors roll back the entire transaction on the server, not just the failing statement. examples: merge error 8672 (which upsert() compiles to when a source key repeats and already exists), a trigger that runs rollback transaction, or any error under set xact abort on. when one of these happens inside a nested db::transaction(), the savepoint is gone, and three things go wrong: 1. the real error is lost. rollback() runs rollback transaction trans2, which fails with sqlstate[25000] cannot roll back trans2. no transaction or savepoint of that name was found. handlerollbackexception() rethrows that, and the original exception is dropped (it is not set as previous). each enclosing transaction() then retries the same savepoint and fails the same way, so the caller only ever sees the rollback error. 2. the transaction level is never reset. $this->transactions = $tolevel only runs when performrollback() succeeds, so after the exception escapes, transactionlevel() is still 2. meanwhile, the odbc driver (manual-commit mode) has opened a new server transaction: @@trancount is 1. 3. later writes on the same connection are silently never committed. the next top-level db::transaction() sees level 2, so it only creates and releases a savepoint and never issues commit. it returns normally, but its writes are rolled back when the connection closes. in a queue worker or octane, every later transaction on that connection is lost without an error. the deadlock path already accounts for "the server rolled back everything" (handletransactionexception() skips the savepoint rollback for concurrency errors and decrements the level), but the other sql server errors that do the same are not handled. for comparison, a statement-level error in the same position (a duplicate-key insert) behaves correctly: the original uniqueconstraintviolationexception surfaces, the level returns to 0, and later transactions commit. this is probably the same root cause as 49514, which was closed for lack of a reproduction. below is a self-contained docker one. possible direction: when a savepoint rollback fails, check whether the server transaction still exists (select @@trancount, or the driver's equivalent). if it is gone, reset the level to 0, roll back the stray driver transaction, and rethrow the original exception with the rollback failure attached, instead of the rollback failure alone. steps to reproduce save these four files in an empty directory and run docker compose run --rm app (sql server runs under amd64 scheduler wakes scaled-to-zero app at wrong hour for monthly tasks across dst change laravel version 12.66.0 php version 8.4.25 database driver & version no response description environment: laravel cloud, app cluster with scale to zero and scheduler enabled. laravel 12.66.0, app.timezone = europe/berlin. what happened: a monthly task schedule::command('billing:run')->monthlyon(1, '06:00') did not run on 2026-10-01. laravel considers it due at 04:00 utc (06:00 cest). the cloud dashboard showed it as 0 6 1 "at 6:00 am utc". the app was asleep at 04:00 utc and was woken at 06:00 utc, when the task was no longer due. it was silently skipped: no log entry, no exception. root cause: illuminate\console\scheduling\cronexpressiontimezoneconverter::offsetcomponents() returns null when the utc offset differs between the next run and the run after it. forevent() then falls back to the unconverted expression, and that expression is presented as utc. for monthly tasks this happens every time the next two runs are on opposite sides of a dst change (deploys in september and march). reproduction: carbon::settestnow(carbon::parse('2026-09-30 12:00', 'utc')); $event = (new schedule('europe/berlin'))->command('x')->monthlyon(1, '06:00'); cronexpressiontimezoneconverter::forevent($event, new datetimezone('utc')); // ['0 6 1 '] – expected ['0 4 1 '] (next run 2026-10-01 06:00 cest = 04:00 utc) // same call on 2026-08-15 or 2026-10-15 converts correctly (0 4 / 0 5). impact: with scale to zero, cloud wakes the app at the wrong hour, and laravel's own due check (which correctly uses the event timezone) then skips the task. daily tasks are rarely affected because their consecutive runs almost never straddle a dst change. suggested fix: cloud could derive wake-up times from nextrundate() in utc instead of a converted cron expression. alternatively, the converter could signal "not convertible" instead of returning the raw expression as if it were in the target timezone. workaround: schedule monthly tasks explicitly in utc (->timezone('utc')), so no conversion is needed. steps to reproduce a) framework only (no cloud needed) create a fresh laravel 12 app and set 'timezone' => 'europe/berlin' in config/app.php. add a monthly task to routes/console.php: schedule::command('inspire')->monthlyon(1, '06:00'); set the system clock to a date where the next two runs fall on opposite sides of a dst change, e.g. 2026-09-30 (next run 2026-10-01 in cest, the run after that 2026-11-01 in cet). with faketime: faketime '2026-09-30 12:00:00' php artisan schedule:list --timezone=utc actual: 0 6 1 (the europe/berlin expression, shown unchanged under utc). expected: 0 4 1 (2026-10-01 06:00 cest = 04:00 utc). repeat on a date without a dst change between the next two runs: faketime '2026-08-15 12:00:00' php artisan schedule:list --timezone=utc this correctly shows 0 4 1 . b) on laravel cloud deploy the app from a) to an environment whose app cluster has scale to zero and scheduler enabled, with no wake-up interval. deploy between 2026-09-02 and 2026-10-01 (or between 2026-03-02 and 2026-04-01), so that the next two runs of the monthly task straddle a dst change. open environment → app cluster → scheduler → scheduled tasks. the task is listed as 0 6 1 "at 6:00 am utc on day 1 of the month". let the environment sleep, and send no traffic around 04:00 utc on the 1st. actual: the app is woken at 06:00 utc. schedule:run does not consider the task due (laravel expects 04:00 utc), so the task never runs. there is no log entry and no exception. expected: the app is woken at 04:00 utc and the task runs.

[octane] requestterminated is not dispatched when client::respond() throws, so once() leaks into the next request laravel version 13.33.0 php version 8.5.7 database driver & version no response description laravel/octane v2.20.0 (the same code is on 2.x today); reproduced in process with octane's fakeworker, and the code path in worker::handle() is shared by every server. in worker::handle(), $gateway->terminate($request, $response) runs after $this->client->respond(...). if respond() throws, the catch calls handleworkererror() and requestterminated is never dispatched for that request, so the listeners on it - flushonce, flushtemporarycontainerinstances, and anything else on the terminated event - do not run. the next request on the same worker then reads the failed request's once() values, and the base application keeps scoped instances that should have been forgotten. steps to reproduce a route that returns a once() value from the request: php route::get('/once', fn () => once(fn () => request()->query('v'))); a client whose first respond() throws, as a dropped connection might: php $client = new class([]) extends fakeclient { public int $sends = 0; public function respond(requestcontext $context, octaneresponse $octaneresponse): void { if (++$this->sends === 1) { throw new runtimeexception('client went away'); } parent::respond($context, $octaneresponse); } }; $worker = new fakeworker(new applicationfactory(base path()), $client); $worker->boot(); $client->requests = [ request::create('/once?v=first'), request::create('/once?v=second'), request::create('/once?v=third'), ]; $worker->run(); the two responses the client receives have the bodies first and third - the second request was answered with the first request's once() value - and requestterminated is dispatched 2 times for 3 requests. expected: second and third, and a terminated event for every request that was handled. dispatching the termination (or at least running the flush listeners) from the finally when the request was handled would close it.
